Martin County's contracted transit provider walked away from its agreement Thursday, halting all MARTY bus service and laying off 29 employees with no warning to riders or county leaders.Martin County issued an official statement acknowledging the disruption and pledging to work toward a solution."Martin County is actively working to identify solutions to restore transit service as quickly as possible and minimize the impact on our riders." Martin County said."We understand the importance of MARTY services to our community and apologize for the disruption." Martin County said.Martin County Transit, the company contracted to operate the MARTY system, blamed rising operating costs for the decision. In a statement, CEO Karen Deigl said, "we entered this contract in good faith and made every effort to find a path forward. We understand how important MARTY is to its riders and the community, and this decision was not made lightly.”Martin County Transit also acknowledged the abruptness of the shutdown."We understand that this news may feel sudden to riders and residents. As strong advocates for reliable public transportation, we are disappointed that we are unable to continue to operate the MARTY system," Martin County Transit said.In an afternoon press conference County leaders explained they were in negotiations after the vendor asked for a significant increase in the cost of the contract. Two weeks ago, the company gave notice it planned to leave in 180 days and instead, it walked away Thursday.Jim Gordon, Martin County's Public Works Director, said the county had no warning the cancellation was coming."We were not given advanced notice that they were going to cancel service today," Jim Gordon said.For Joe, a 67-year-old veteran and Martin County resident, losing MARTY service means losing his lifeline. Joe sat at the bus stop Thursday expecting his regular pickup, but no buses came. He relies on the transit system daily."[I use it] to go to work sometimes and to go down to the homeless place, the church that feeds us food," Joe said.Joe said he received no notice before service was cut."No warning at all, nothing, zero." Joe said.Physical limitations make alternative transportation all but impossible for Joe."I've had two broken necks, three broken backs, I can't feel my feet, so I'm not getting anywhere," Joe said.Tony Argudo, a Martin County resident, said the transit company's handling of the shutdown lacked transparency."I don't think letting people go first thing this morning was a good idea. There should have been more transparency and the people should have had some kind of notice so they could have made other plans," Argudo said.George Stokus, Martin County's Assistant County Administrator, said county officials are working urgently to restore service."We're doing everything we can humanly due to restore service as soon as we can," George Stokus said.In the meantime, the United Way of Martin County is stepping in through its Ride United program, which provides free, pre-scheduled Lyft rides to eligible residents for trips to work, grocery stores, medical appointments and other essential services.The organization said it was already facing financial challenges due to increased demand and other funding reductions before the MARTY service interruption and is now anticipating even greater need.Carol G. Houwaart-Diez, president and CEO of United Way of Martin County, emphasized the critical importance of transportation access for those who depend on it."Transportation isn't a luxury for the people who depend on it. It's how they get to work, receive medical care and put food on the table. When a critical service like this disappears, the need doesn't disappear with it," Houwaart-Diez said.Houwaart-Diez said the United Way is committed to being there for riders during the disruption."This is important for people to be able to get to the doctors to get to wherever they need to go so we want to be there," Houwaart-Diez said.Ashley Capital has committed an initial $2,500 donation to help support the Ride United program's response, alongside a contribution from another donor. Since launching in September 2022, Ride United has provided thousands of rides for Martin County residents facing transportation barriers. However, United Way emphasized that the program cannot fully replace MARTY's fixed-route bus and paratransit services and that its response is only a temporary solution dependent on available funding.Martin County said it will continue providing updates as it works to restore public transit service. Information about MARTY can be found on the county's transit website.Residents seeking transportation assistance can call the United Way of Martin County at 772-283-4800 or click here to visit their website.Residents seeking paratransit transportation assistance can call 772-463-2822.This story was reported on-air by a journalist and has been converted to this platform with the assistance of AI. Our editorial team verifies all reporting on all platforms for fairness and accuracy.

For the first time, the family of a man set to be executed for the 1986 murder of an Indian River County sheriff's deputy is speaking publicly about their effort to save his life.William Reaves has spent nearly four decades on death row for shooting and killing 29-year-old Deputy Richard Raczkowski. Reaves' execution is scheduled for Oct. 20.WATCH BELOW: As execution nears, Reaves' family asks DeSantis to spare his lifeNow, with less than two weeks remaining, Reaves' family is asking Gov. Ron DeSantis to grant him clemency and commute his death sentence to life in prison."I mean, he's my uncle, and I love him," Reaves' nephew, Meredith Farrington, told WPTV investigative reporter Kate Hussey.Farrington said his family does not dispute the gravity of Reaves' crime or the pain Raczkowski's family has endured."I can't be upset. I can't be mad at the governor or the decision," Farrington said. "I mean, my uncle did take a life."But Farrington added, "I just want the governor to look at the whole picture."That story stretches back to Sept. 23, 1986.According to court records, Reaves called 911 from a convenience store in Indian River County after he was unable to get a taxi.Raczkowski responded and was attempting to help Reaves call a cab when a gun fell from Reaves' pants. A struggle followed.Reaves shot Raczkowski four times in the back, killing him.For nearly 40 years, Raczkowski's brother, Marc Raczkowski, has lived with the loss."Why? Why?" he said while speaking with WPTV near his brother's gravesite. "It's something I wouldn't wish on anybody." A stretch of road near where the deputy was killed now bears Raczkowski's name — a memorial to a life taken and a crime that continues to reverberate through two families four decades later."The pain will still always be there," Marc Raczkowski said.DeSantis signed Reaves' death warrant Sept. 22, scheduling his execution for Oct. 20.Farrington is not asking the governor to pardon his uncle or release him from prison. Instead, he wants DeSantis to commute Reaves' death sentence so the now-77-year-old can spend the rest of his life behind bars.Central to his plea is Reaves' history as a decorated Vietnam War veteran and questions raised during decades of appeals about his mental health, substance abuse and legal representation.Court records show Reaves repeatedly challenged his conviction and death sentence, including claims that his trial attorney failed to adequately investigate and present evidence concerning his drug use and mental health."The attorney wasn't an effective attorney for that type of case," Farrington said. "That was his first death row case."At Reaves' sentencing, testimony described him as suffering from what was then called "Vietnam syndrome," rather than post-traumatic stress disorder.Years later, other experts testified that Reaves suffered from PTSD, substance abuse and other impairments.Farrington said none of that excuses the murder."I'm not going to say that his PTSD, his drug use, his being on cocaine and all the other stuff excuses what he did," Farrington said. "I mean, he's being punished by being in prison, and he's 77. The governor can let him stay in prison for the rest of his life, and still he's being punished without killing him and taking another life."Farrington also acknowledges that his family is not the only one carrying grief into Oct. 20.On the other side is Raczkowski's family, which has spent four decades living with the consequences of Reaves' actions."I mean, trying to understand what he feels — there's no way I could do that," Farrington said of Raczkowski's brother.He said he understands why the deputy's family may want the execution to proceed."I know that the family, the officer ... I would probably want the same thing, and I can't even imagine," Farrington said.For the Raczkowski family, the case is about a life taken nearly 40 years ago.For Reaves' family, it is now about whether another life should end."But we're praying," Farrington said.Reaves has already lost his latest attempt to stop the execution in Indian River County court. He has appealed that decision to the Florida Supreme Court.For now, his execution remains scheduled for Oct. 20 unless a court intervenes or DeSantis grants clemency.If carried out, Reaves' execution will mark the 18th in Florida in 2026.

As Hurricane Isaias heads toward the Florida Panhandle, homeowners across the state will see hurricane deductibles go into effect on their insurance policies."The trigger in this case for most policies is a (hurricane) watch or (hurricane) warning anywhere in the state of Florida," Robert Norberg of Arden Insurance in Lantana said.WATCH BELOW: Isaias triggers Florida insurance deductibles that could cost homeowners thousandsHurricane deductibles are common in Florida and are used for hurricane-related claims. They also have a much higher deductible than the usual deductibles on insurance policies."Typically, it's 2 to 3 percent of the property's insured value — not 2 to 3 percent of the claim — so it can be pretty extensive; some people even have 5 or 10 percent deductibles," Norberg said.A 2 percent deductible on a $300,000 home can run about $6,000.And that deductible applies anywhere in the state as long as a hurricane is posted somewhere in Florida."Any type of wind damage that causes a claim — say you're in Palm Beach County, those people will be subject to the wind deductible," Norberg saidThe hurricane deductible, according to state statute, expires 72 hours after the last hurricane warning is lifted.RELATED COVERAGE:

Lucie County Fire District has hit a snag in its effort to create a new policy for handling complaints against its own top leaders as fallout continues from a controversial hazing investigation. During a Fire District Board workshop Wednesday morning, board members had hoped to hear from outside law firms about helping draft a new complaint policy.WATCH BELOW: Fire district's new complaint policy effort stalls amid hazing falloutInstead, St. Lucie County Commissioner and Fire District Board Member Jamie Fowler said one of the law firms contacted never returned her calls, while another disclosed a potential conflict of interest."I appreciated her honesty and forthrightness on that issue," Fowler said of the attorney during the meeting. "That being said, she did provide two references, both on the West Coast." The board discussed now reaching out to additional law firms in hopes of securing outside legal help ahead of its next meeting Oct. 21."I think we'd be doing ourselves an injustice if we at least we don't have a courtesy conversation with these other firms, so that we're at least prepared just in case these two firms aren't available, non-responsive," Board Member and Fort Pierce City Commissioner Curtis Johnson said. "I think we all have some sense of urgency of getting this thing closed, and and I don't want to delay any further." The effort follows a heated special board meeting Sept. 30, when members publicly acknowledged what they described as a significant gap in district policy: There is no clear process for independently handling complaints made against some of the district's own contract employees. "Since this district's inception, we have not had a policy on how they handle complaints against themselves," Fowler said during that meeting. "They — being those positions — have essentially been able to investigate themselves."Those positions include the fire chief, district attorney, clerk treasurer and medical director.The issue came under increased scrutiny amid fallout from a hazing investigation involving three veteran firefighters.A third-party investigator concluded that videos showing firefighters using a modified bug zapper to shock probationary firefighters depicted hazing.Three veteran firefighters — Doug Boudrias, Jordan Hutchinson and Christopher Baldwin — were fired as a result.Hutchinson and Boudrias previously told WPTV they did not consider the conduct hazing and said there was no intent to hurt anyone."It was just us in our downtime, joking around, having fun," Hutchinson said."We're all still friends," Boudrias said. "Us and the victims, there was no ill intent."The controversy has also raised questions about how complaints involving district leadership have been handled.Months before the hazing incident came to light, Baldwin and Hutchinson filed a complaint against Fire Chief Jeff Lee and then-District Attorney Kim Sabol in September 2025. District officials ultimately denied it. Baldwin and Hutchinson later filed additional complaints, including an amended complaint to investigators alleging the hazing investigation and their subsequent terminations were part of a broader pattern of retaliation. Lucie County Fire District told WPTV it is not currently in receipt of any official retaliation complaint from any party involved in this matter."That's not a good process," Fowler previously told WPTV.Sabol submitted her notice of retirement Sept. 30, just minutes after the special board meeting, effective 90 days from her notice. The District stated she will continue to provide services during that 90-day period. Lee previously acknowledged the district lacks a clear complaint process and told WPTV investigative reporter Kate Hussey that he welcomed outside scrutiny."I'm glad this board is finally taking this as a serious issue," Lee said, adding that he "welcomes any investigation from any agency."Lee also defended Sabol following her notice of retirement, calling it a "sad day" and saying she had been a "tremendous attorney for the district."Meanwhile, firefighters have been casting ballots in a union vote of no confidence in Lee."It basically says whether or not they trust and believe in him to lead this district," Fowler previously said. "So that is a huge thing if you have the majority of the men and women underneath you saying they can no longer serve under you, that's a pretty impactful message."Lee previously said he would wait for the results before commenting further on the vote."We'll see what the men and women decide," Lee said. "I came up on the labor side; I've always fought for our men and women on the line."The union is also continuing its legal fight to reinstate Boudrias, Hutchinson and Baldwin.During the Sept. 30 meeting, Fowler questioned whether the fire board itself may have the authority to bring the three firefighters back rather than waiting for the arbitration process to play out."I think we might actually," Fowler said at the time.Board members are expected to continue searching for an outside law firm to help develop the new policy before the Fire District Board meets again Oct.

Florida Panthers captain Aleksander Barkov received the Key to the City of Boca Raton at a ceremony Thursday afternoon.It was awarded to Barkov by Mayor Andy Thomson. Barkov has lived in Boca Raton since he was 18, his first year with the Panthers.Watch report from Mike TrimWPTV Florida Panthers Anchor and Panthers 360 host Mike Trim connected with Barkov at the ceremony.Trim asked, why is Boca Raton so special to you? Barkov said “Because I live there, I live there in my whole career which is almost half of my lifetime so, I only live into two places. It’s back home in Finland and focus so this is a special place for me.” Trim then asked, “Are there any Barky favorites in Boca Raton, places that you really like to go?”Barkov said, “There's a lot. I play a lot of tennis, so every park has a tennis court. I love a lot of different restaurants. Mizner Park is super nice. There's so many good things about it. I will be here all day explaining.”Panthers television play-by-play announcer Steve Goldstein emceed today’s event. Many fans also met Barkov. The Panthers all-time franchise points leader, Barkov, is currently out 6-8 weeks rehabbing a leg injury but tells Trim he is excited to get back on the ice. Trim asked, “A lot of fans in Palm Beach county are wondering how your doing after what happened on the road trip. Is there anything you want to say about that?"Barkov said, “I mean, I got really good news after the road trip, so really looking forward to trying to come back as soon as possible. We have good doctors, they take really good care of me, so I'm really lucky about that.”

Lucie County jury convicted former Fort Pierce City Manager Nick Mimms of official misconduct Thursday, finding he improperly obstructed, delayed or prevented information about a possible felony involving the city from being communicated. Jurors found Mimms not guilty of bid tampering, the first count he faced. But they found him guilty on the official-misconduct count and specifically determined the misconduct involved obstructing, delaying or preventing communication of information related to a possible felony that directly involved or affected the government entity he served. The verdict followed a trial that began Sept. 29 and centered on allegations that Mimms improperly influenced the city’s bidding process for two vacant Lincoln Park-area lots. Prosecutors alleged Mimms steered the process toward Lincoln Park Young Professionals , a nonprofit whose board included his niece and another city employee. The organization sought a lease involving the properties, near the Lincoln Theater. During trial, FDLE Agent Derek Brisky testified about emails, city records and the request-for-proposals process. Prosecutors pointed to communications showing Mimms continued to discuss the RFP’s evaluation criteria and committee after the matter had been referred to the city’s purchasing department. The defense argued the purchasing department controlled the RFP’s publication and administration, and challenged the state’s claim that the process amounted to an improper sole-source arrangement. See also: 4 people arrested after drugs, 26 firearms found at North Palm Beach home Court records show Circuit Judge Michael James Linn denied the state’s request to have Mimms taken into custody pending sentencing. Mimms was allowed to remain free on bond. Sentencing is scheduled for 9:30 a.m. Lucie County Circuit Court.

Lucie residents are dealing with the aftermath of heavy rain that flooded roads and swales Tuesday, leaving vehicles stranded and prompting city officials to prepare for more potential rainfall. Barricades remain in place as a precaution, according to city officials. Resident Tommy Fry shared a video of his flooded driveway, saying, "This is the end of the driveway and, you know, two plus feet of water." "It poured, you know, it came down pretty quick, probably 45 minutes of rain," Fry said, describing the rapid accumulation of water. He also described the extent of the flooding. "Just insanity, you know, it's just water two feet deep in the middle of California Boulevard and a waterline 15 feet up my driveway from the street and, of course, the swale over here that's been like that. I can't mow it," Fry said. Drone footage captured severe flooding near Savona and California boulevards, showing streets covered in water after the afternoon rain. Some vehicles became stranded while attempting to navigate the flooded streets. City officials reported that most of the water had receded by 8 p.m. However, some residents are still seeking relief, and officials acknowledge their concerns. "We're responsible for a very wide network of swales, right, so we try to get to as much as we can," said Scott Samples, the city's strategic communications team leader. Deep Dive: WPBF 25 News Investigates Samples explained that public works crews check drains before storms but noted the challenges of managing heavy rainfall. We try to do as much as we can. We know that Mother Nature sometimes is going to win, and we try to do the best that we can to make sure that first of all, people are safe and the inconvenience lasts as little as possible," Samples said. City officials are also exploring long-term projects to address flooding. "So, we're looking at how can we change some of the stormwater management across the city. These are longer-term projects that, you know, I know people would like to have solutions right now. But again, our goal is to try to do this as well as we possibly can for the long term," Samples said. City officials emphasized that crews and equipment are on standby in case of additional heavy rainfall. Lucie County courtroom found former Fort Pierce city manager Nicholas Mimms not guilty of bid tampering and guilty of official misconduct on Thursday, Oct. Sentencing is scheduled for December 11. Jurors deliberated in the trial of former Fort Pierce city manager Nicholas Mimms, who is accused of bid tampering and official misconduct involving city-owned properties and a nonprofit linked to his niece. Prosecutors said Mimms used his position as city manager to help Lincoln Park Young Professionals, a nonprofit co-founded by his niece, secure a lease to develop two city-owned properties. Stay up-to-date: The latest headlines and weather from WPBF 25 The defense denied Mimms did anything wrong, arguing that he and his niece, Caleta Scott, have a distant relationship. The prosecution argued there was a conflict of interest, saying Scott was granted special treatment because of her relationship with Mimms. Deliberations began late yesterday after closing arguments from both sides and resumed at 9 a.m. Jurors have broken for lunch but have not yet reached a verdict. A Flood Advisory is in effect for St. Lucie County until 4:30 p.m. A flood watch is in effect until 11 p.m. Thursday for parts of the Treasure Coast and Central Florida, including Indian River, Martin, St. Lucie and Okeechobee counties. The National Weather Service said numerous showers and thunderstorms are expected to develop Thursday afternoon and continue into the early evening. Some storms could bring 2 to 4 inches of rain, with isolated totals of 5 to 7 inches possible. Forecasters warned the heavy rain could lead to flash flooding, particularly in areas that have already received significant rainfall recently. Excessive runoff could flood rivers, creeks, streams and other low-lying areas. Urban locations and places with poor drainage may also see flooding, while storm drains and ditches could become clogged with debris. Residents should avoid driving through flooded roadways and be prepared for rapidly changing conditions through Thursday night.

MARTY public transit service in Martin County came to an abrupt halt Thursday, leaving residents who depend on the transit system without regular transportation as county officials scramble to find a solution. Martin County officials told WPBF's Caleb Califano they were given no advance warning that service would stop Thursday. According to the county, MARTY’s operator, Martin County Transit LLC, had requested a significant increase in its contract. The company says rising insurance, fuel and maintenance costs have led to significant financial losses since it began operating the service in July 2025. Despite negotiations with the county, the two sides were unable to reach an agreement. County officials said the company provided a 180-day notice to terminate its contract approximately two weeks ago. However, Thursday morning, Martin County Transit LLC notified the county that it was immediately discontinuing service. The sudden shutdown has left residents who rely on MARTY to get around the county without their regular transportation option. George Stokus, assistant Martin County administrator, said officials are now exploring both short-term and long-term solutions to restore service. "We are doing everything we can humanly do right now to restore service as soon as we can," Stokus said. "It’s just not an easy operation or switch to turn it back on. It’s going to take some time, and we are working to get to that." In the meantime, county officials say they are working with community partners, including United Way, to help residents impacted by the shutdown. The county has not provided a timeline for when MARTY operations could resume. Officials say they will continue posting updates on social media and will notify residents as soon as a solution is reached. Riders react Leticia Chaclan, of Martin County, waited for the bus in Stuart on Thursday, but it never came. She was unaware that the MARTY bus had been suspended until WPBF's Jasimine Yasmine Julmisse informed her. Chaclain says she's been riding the bus for years and that it's a staple for many members of the community. "We really need the bus," she said. "Especially people within the Hispanic community, who don’t have a driver’s license, and need it to go to places like the clinic, to go to the hospital, and for other things we need. It’s very necessary, and we use the bus a lot. In my case, I don’t drive. But I really need the bus, and I use it a lot. I don’t drive, and we go everywhere to shop." The sudden suspension of service impacted riders including Steven Godell, who said he was on his bicycle Thursday because he didn't see the MARTY bus come Thursday morning. As Hunger Action Month comes to a close, Feeding South Florida is continuing to raise awareness about food insecurity affecting families and seniors across South Florida.WPTV's monthlong series visited four hunger-relief organizations throughout the region, wrapping up at Feeding Palm Beach County in Boynton Beach, where leaders highlighted the growing need for food assistance and the programs helping vulnerable residents."There are 1.7 million people all the way from Tequesta down to Key West struggling to put food on the table," said Paco Vélez, president and CEO of Feeding South Florida. “Now we find ourselves in a situation where prices are soaring, not just for fuel, but also for all the goods and services, especially for food.”Vélez said rising transportation and supply costs continue to increase demand at food distribution sites and partner agencies across South Florida."So many families are coming to us, so many families are coming to our partner agencies," Vélez said.At the organization’s Community Kitchen in Boynton Beach, Susan Taves, culinary director for Feeding South Florida, demonstrated how meals are prepared for seniors throughout the region."We make nutritionally balanced meals for mostly non-ambulatory seniors, and we deliver them frozen," Taves said. "They're nutritionally balanced so that by the end of the week they’ve gotten all of their daily requirements."Taves said Feeding South Florida’s culinary and wellness teams work together to ensure meals meet health and nutrition standards."We have a registered dietitian who's the director of health and wellness," Taves said. "She does a great job of making sure that we meet all the requirements."Feeding South Florida says its 5,000-square-foot Community Kitchen can produce up to 10,000 meals each day for seniors, after-school programs, medically tailored meal services and disaster response efforts.The organization serves Palm Beach, Broward, Miami-Dade and Monroe counties through direct-service programs and a network of more than 350 nonprofit and community partners.Vélez encouraged community members to support hunger-relief efforts by volunteering, donating or participating in fundraising campaigns."Feedingsouthflorida.org is the best way to get involved," Vélez said. "Go there to find out volunteer opportunities not only to pack food boxes but also to help prepare meals, as well as events and matching fund campaigns."The need remains significant as many South Florida households continue struggling with the rising cost of food, housing and transportation. Hunger-relief organizations say continued community support is critical heading into the holiday season.This story was reported on-air by a journalist and has been converted to this platform with the assistance of AI. I visited Love, Hope & Healing Inc. to learn more about IGNITE: The Father & Son Grill Challenge, an event built around mentoring, communication and creating stronger relationships between young men and the adults who support them.While the event includes grilling and friendly competition, organizers say the larger goal is helping fathers, sons, mentors and mentees spend meaningful time together."We will have what we call the Fire Circle, where we will have a therapist-led session, and we're talking about some of these conversations that fathers and sons need to have, but rarely have and don't know how to have," said Donte Bates, co-founder and executive director of Love, Hope & Healing Inc. "So we're creating that space for them to actually talk about it."Yolanda Bates, CEO of Love, Hope & Healing Inc., said events like IGNITE help strengthen relationships that can have a lasting impact on young people."Fathers and sons, they need to create these bonds where these young men can have these experiences and the leadership and mentorship as they grow," she said.One of the organizations supporting the effort is United Way of Palm Beach County. Gwynette Williams, vice president of mentoring, said relationship-building is at the heart of the organization's mission."It's important to make sure that we are building relationships between adults and young people all over Palm Beach County," Williams said. "That's really what we do all day long."Williams also summed up one of the event's unique attractions with a smile."You can't go wrong with men and meat," she said.Mentor Bruce Lewis said his involvement is rooted in helping young men see a positive path forward."It's serving as a positive role model for the young African American males who really need that, giving them a good pathway to success," Lewis said. "I look forward to helping them build their futures."His mentee, Nate, said he's excited about both the experience and the opportunity to grow."I'm looking forward to making friends and having a better bond," he said.The event's presenting partner, Lowe's Home Improvement, is providing a grill and supplies for participating teams."We're in the community, and we're for the community," said David Territo, a Lowe's store manager.ABOUT IGNITE: THE FATHER & SON GRILL CHALLENGEOn Oct. 17, dozens of fathers, father figures, mentors, sons and mentees will gather at Gaines Park Recreation Center in West Palm Beach for IGNITE: The Father & Son Grill Challenge. Organized by Love, Hope & Healing Inc. and supported by Lowe's Home Improvement, the event uses grilling as a way to bring people together, creating opportunities for mentorship, teamwork and meaningful conversations. Along with a hands-on grill challenge, participants will take part in "The Fire Circle," a therapist-led discussion designed to help fathers and sons talk about topics that often go unspoken, from communication and accountability to emotional wellness and support systems. Jupiter Fire Rescue began its first day of municipal service Thursday by responding to four calls after midnight and unveiling Jupiter's first ladder truck, which carries a tribute to FDNY Ladder 10 and the six members who died in the Sept. 11 terrorist attacks.Fire Chief Darrel Donatto said the department's first calls unfolded as its members had prepared."They went perfectly, exactly as planned," Donatto said. "We've been planning for this moment for three years, and everything is perfect."The launch marks a new chapter for public safety in Jupiter, with locally controlled fire rescue and emergency medical services operating from stations serving the town's eastern, central and western communities.Jupiter's new ladder truck is based at Station 10, located at 500 N. Highway 1 near Burt Reynolds Park. It is the first ladder truck based in Jupiter, according to Donatto.Donatto said the equipment is important because of the town's oceanfront high-rises and multi-story residential developments."Jupiter has a lot of high-rise buildings all along the oceanfront here, plus a lot of three-story type townhomes all through the Abacoa community," Donatto said. "And so a ladder truck is vital to protecting those, those type of occupancies."Palm Beach County Fire Rescue continues to serve nearby unincorporated areas, including county pockets near the Jupiter Inlet, DuBois Park and Jonathan's Landing, Donatto said.Jupiter's first ladder truck features an American flag design and imagery of the Jupiter Lighthouse. The truck carries the number 10 as a tribute to FDNY Ladder 10, whose firehouse sits across from the World Trade Center site in New York City.Following the Sept. 11, 2001 terrorist attacks, FDNY Ladder 10's replacement truck was wrapped in an American flag design honoring the firefighters who responded that day. Before adopting the tribute, Town of Jupiter officials contacted FDNY Ladder 10 to seek their blessing.Rodman Leas, a firefighter with Jupiter Fire Rescue, explained the significance behind the tribute."Today marks a brand new chapter in Jupiter fire history as we roll out 10 Truck, our community is, like you said, our community's very first ladder truck ever," Leas said. "It carries the number 10 badge ... as we honor FDNY Truck 10, whose firehouse stands directly across from the Sept. 11th World Trade Center site." Leas said six members of FDNY Ladder 10 made the ultimate sacrifice on Sept. 11."I took an inspiration from their American flag design as well ... as a constant reminder of the bravery, courage, brotherhood that defined the fire service," Leas said.Battalion Chief Jason Bohan said Jupiter Fire Rescue worked with Palm Beach Gardens as crews prepared for the new department's launch."We've had an incredible partnership with Palm Beach Gardens," Bohan said. "We've been using their training facility, and because of that partnership over the last couple of months, they and us have been training, getting ready for today."That preparation includes learning to put on approximately 60 pounds of protective equipment quickly when an emergency call comes in.Bohan said the most exciting part of launch day was bringing the new department together around its public service mission."Getting us all together, knowing what we're called to do, which is to protect and save people," Bohan said. "So now that it finally came today, we're all really excited."For Lt. Christian Lainhart, joining Jupiter Fire Rescue also represents a personal homecoming. Lainhart previously worked for Martin County Fire Rescue and described himself as a sixth-generation Jupiter pioneer."I'm super excited, very blessed to be here," Lainhart said.Lainhart said his family's roots in the Jupiter area extend to the 1890s. He grew up and attended school in Jupiter and is now raising his family there."It's just truly remarkable," Lainhart said. "Growing up here, I'm a sixth-generation pioneer, so that really means something here. Grew up here, went to school here, currently raising my family, and now I'm here serving the community that I know and love."While Jupiter's new stations, apparatus and equipment are central to the launch, Donatto said the department's personnel are what make the milestone meaningful."The most exciting thing is the people in it," Donatto said. "We've just been so incredibly blessed to hire some of the best people in the world. They're excited to serve the town of Jupiter."By 5 a.m. Thursday, Jupiter Fire Rescue's firefighters and paramedics had already answered four calls while introducing the community to the people and equipment behind the new department.This story was reported on-air by a journalist and has been converted to this platform with the assistance of AI. A 14-year-old Treasure Coast High School student is in critical condition after being struck by a vehicle while walking to school Wednesday morning, according to the Port St. Lucie Police Department.Police said the crash happened around 6 a.m. near the intersection of Southwest Port St. Lucie Boulevard and Southwest Squirrel Avenue.WATCH BELOW: Student critically injured after being struck by SUVInvestigators said the freshman was walking northbound along Port St. Lucie Boulevard on his way to school and was near the edge of the roadway alongside construction barrels in the area when he was struck from behind by a 2002 Ford Excursion driven by a 72-year-old man.According to police, the driver initially believed he had hit a construction barrel and did not realize he had struck a person. Authorities said the driver later made a U-turn at the next location where it was safe to do so and returned to the scene.Once back in the area, the driver activated his hazard lights and found the teen unconscious on the side of the roadway. Police said he immediately called 911 and has remained cooperative throughout the investigation.The student suffered life-threatening injuries and remains hospitalized in critical condition, according to police.Investigators said there were no apparent signs of impairment involving the driver, though they noted the assessment is preliminary and could change as the investigation continues.The crash remains under investigation.Police are asking anyone who witnessed the incident or who may have dash camera, surveillance or other video footage from the area around the time of the crash to come forward.Anyone with information is asked to contact the Port St. Lucie Police Department at 772-871-5000.Howard Shapiro lives across the street from where the crash occurred.Shapiro said this stretch of Port St. Lucie Boulevard can be dangerous."I don't walk around here is no lighting outside at nighttime," said Shapiro. "Kids walk along all the time because there's school back there, school down there."Though crews are improving the roadway, Shapiro said lights would make it safer."They are putting in a sidewalk, so that's going to be helpful. But streetlights need to follow," said Shapiro.Celine Gabriel lives off nearby Becker Road and said she avoids Port St. Lucie Boulevard altogether."I don't even come down this road no more," said Gabriel. "I go all the way down to I-95, come up on Gatlin to take my child to school.

Lucie County Fire District has hit a snag in its effort to create a new policy for handling complaints against its own top leaders as fallout continues from a controversial hazing investigation. During a Fire District Board workshop Wednesday morning, board members had hoped to hear from outside law firms about helping draft a new complaint policy.WATCH BELOW: Fire district's new complaint policy effort stalls amid hazing falloutInstead, St. Lucie County Commissioner and Fire District Board Member Jamie Fowler said one of the law firms contacted never returned her calls, while another disclosed a potential conflict of interest."I appreciated her honesty and forthrightness on that issue," Fowler said of the attorney during the meeting. "That being said, she did provide two references, both on the West Coast." The board discussed now reaching out to additional law firms in hopes of securing outside legal help ahead of its next meeting Oct. 21."I think we'd be doing ourselves an injustice if we at least we don't have a courtesy conversation with these other firms, so that we're at least prepared just in case these two firms aren't available, non-responsive," Board Member and Fort Pierce City Commissioner Curtis Johnson said. "I think we all have some sense of urgency of getting this thing closed, and and I don't want to delay any further." The effort follows a heated special board meeting Sept. 30, when members publicly acknowledged what they described as a significant gap in district policy: There is no clear process for independently handling complaints made against some of the district's own contract employees. "Since this district's inception, we have not had a policy on how they handle complaints against themselves," Fowler said during that meeting. "They — being those positions — have essentially been able to investigate themselves."Those positions include the fire chief, district attorney, clerk treasurer and medical director.The issue came under increased scrutiny amid fallout from a hazing investigation involving three veteran firefighters.A third-party investigator concluded that videos showing firefighters using a modified bug zapper to shock probationary firefighters depicted hazing.Three veteran firefighters — Doug Boudrias, Jordan Hutchinson and Christopher Baldwin — were fired as a result.Hutchinson and Boudrias previously told WPTV they did not consider the conduct hazing and said there was no intent to hurt anyone."It was just us in our downtime, joking around, having fun," Hutchinson said."We're all still friends," Boudrias said. "Us and the victims, there was no ill intent."The controversy has also raised questions about how complaints involving district leadership have been handled.Months before the hazing incident came to light, Baldwin and Hutchinson filed a complaint against Fire Chief Jeff Lee and then-District Attorney Kim Sabol in September 2025. District officials ultimately denied it. Baldwin and Hutchinson later filed additional complaints, including an amended complaint to investigators alleging the hazing investigation and their subsequent terminations were part of a broader pattern of retaliation. Lucie County Fire District told WPTV it is not currently in receipt of any official retaliation complaint from any party involved in this matter."That's not a good process," Fowler previously told WPTV.Sabol submitted her notice of retirement Sept. 30, just minutes after the special board meeting, effective 90 days from her notice. The District stated she will continue to provide services during that 90-day period. Lee previously acknowledged the district lacks a clear complaint process and told WPTV investigative reporter Kate Hussey that he welcomed outside scrutiny."I'm glad this board is finally taking this as a serious issue," Lee said, adding that he "welcomes any investigation from any agency."Lee also defended Sabol following her notice of retirement, calling it a "sad day" and saying she had been a "tremendous attorney for the district."Meanwhile, firefighters have been casting ballots in a union vote of no confidence in Lee."It basically says whether or not they trust and believe in him to lead this district," Fowler previously said. "So that is a huge thing if you have the majority of the men and women underneath you saying they can no longer serve under you, that's a pretty impactful message."Lee previously said he would wait for the results before commenting further on the vote."We'll see what the men and women decide," Lee said. "I came up on the labor side; I've always fought for our men and women on the line."The union is also continuing its legal fight to reinstate Boudrias, Hutchinson and Baldwin.During the Sept. 30 meeting, Fowler questioned whether the fire board itself may have the authority to bring the three firefighters back rather than waiting for the arbitration process to play out."I think we might actually," Fowler said at the time.Board members are expected to continue searching for an outside law firm to help develop the new policy before the Fire District Board meets again Oct.

For the first time, the family of a man set to be executed for the 1986 murder of an Indian River County sheriff's deputy is speaking publicly about their effort to save his life.William Reaves has spent nearly four decades on death row for shooting and killing 29-year-old Deputy Richard Raczkowski. Reaves' execution is scheduled for Oct. 20.Now, with less than two weeks remaining, Reaves' family is asking Gov. Ron DeSantis to grant him clemency and commute his death sentence to life in prison."I mean, he's my uncle, and I love him," Reaves' nephew, Meredith Farrington, told WPTV investigative reporter Kate Hussey.Farrington said his family does not dispute the gravity of Reaves' crime or the pain Raczkowski's family has endured."I can't be upset. I can't be mad at the governor or the decision," Farrington said. "I mean, my uncle did take a life."But Farrington added, "I just want the governor to look at the whole picture."That story stretches back to Sept. 23, 1986.According to court records, Reaves called 911 from a convenience store in Indian River County after he was unable to get a taxi.Raczkowski responded and was attempting to help Reaves call a cab when a gun fell from Reaves' pants. A struggle followed.Reaves shot Raczkowski four times in the back, killing him.For nearly 40 years, Raczkowski's brother, Marc Raczkowski, has lived with the loss."Why? Why?" he said while speaking with WPTV near his brother's gravesite. "It's something I wouldn't wish on anybody." A stretch of road near where the deputy was killed now bears Raczkowski's name — a memorial to a life taken and a crime that continues to reverberate through two families four decades later."The pain will still always be there," Marc Raczkowski said.DeSantis signed Reaves' death warrant Sept. 22, scheduling his execution for Oct. 20.Farrington is not asking the governor to pardon his uncle or release him from prison. Instead, he wants DeSantis to commute Reaves' death sentence so the now-77-year-old can spend the rest of his life behind bars.Central to his plea is Reaves' history as a decorated Vietnam War veteran and questions raised during decades of appeals about his mental health, substance abuse and legal representation.Court records show Reaves repeatedly challenged his conviction and death sentence, including claims that his trial attorney failed to adequately investigate and present evidence concerning his drug use and mental health."The attorney wasn't an effective attorney for that type of case," Farrington said. "That was his first death row case."At Reaves' sentencing, testimony described him as suffering from what was then called "Vietnam syndrome," rather than post-traumatic stress disorder.Years later, other experts testified that Reaves suffered from PTSD, substance abuse and other impairments.Farrington said none of that excuses the murder."I'm not going to say that his PTSD, his drug use, his being on cocaine and all the other stuff excuses what he did," Farrington said. "I mean, he's being punished by being in prison, and he's 77. The governor can let him stay in prison for the rest of his life, and still he's being punished without killing him and taking another life."Farrington also acknowledges that his family is not the only one carrying grief into Oct. 20.On the other side is Raczkowski's family, which has spent four decades living with the consequences of Reaves' actions."I mean, trying to understand what he feels — there's no way I could do that," Farrington said of Raczkowski's brother.He said he understands why the deputy's family may want the execution to proceed."I know that the family, the officer ... I would probably want the same thing, and I can't even imagine," Farrington said.For the Raczkowski family, the case is about a life taken nearly 40 years ago.For Reaves' family, it is now about whether another life should end."But we're praying," Farrington said.Reaves has already lost his latest attempt to stop the execution in Indian River County court. He has appealed that decision to the Florida Supreme Court.For now, his execution remains scheduled for Oct. 20 unless a court intervenes or DeSantis grants clemency.If carried out, Reaves' execution will mark the 18th in Florida in 2026.

Family, friends, teachers and classmates gathered at Farm & Flame in Vero Beach on Wednesday to remember 17-year-old Sulliman “Sulli” Bah, who was fatally shot during a meetup at Garcia Boat Ramp last week, according to the Indian River County Sheriff's Office. No arrests have been made, and investigators are examining whether the shooting may have involved self-defense. The celebration of life was held at the Vero Beach restaurant where Bah worked. Through tears and memories, those who knew him described the Sebastian River High School student as kind, funny, hardworking and someone who could light up a room.As rain poured down Wednesday evening, flowers, candles and photographs filled Farm & Flame while people who knew Bah stood together to honor his life.Isaac Rodriguez, who knew Bah, said Bah made an impact on everyone around him. “He touched everybody’s heart and he was just really kind and he always lit up the room,” Rodriguez said.Bah's close friends told WPTV he was focused on his future and enjoyed spending time with the people closest to him.Alex Cortez said he and Bah boxed together, spent time together and shared many memories. “He was a very positive guy. He was always about working, he was intelligent, he had a big future,” Cortez said.Friend Xavi Espinosa remembered Bah as someone who could immediately make others feel welcome. “Even when I first met him, I felt he was such a good soul,” Espinosa said.The Indian River County Sheriff's Office said Bah was at a meetup at Garcia Boat Ramp on Friday when shots were fired. The sheriff's office said investigators are looking into whether the shooting was self-defense. No arrests have been made.Bah's mother, Chelynn Godfrey, described her son as a loving and caring teenager who had his entire life ahead of him. She said she wants investigators to consider all the facts as they determine what happened.“I just ask that law enforcement truly looks at the big picture. I just want them to really look at the facts and I hope that they get this right,” Godfrey said. “I hope his shooter is arrested and I hope he goes to jail.”During the celebration, people took turns sharing memories of Bah and the impact he had on their lives.Angela Sanders, one of Bah's former sixth grade teachers, remembered his personality and smile. “His personality is amazing, his smile lit up a room,” Sanders said.Myan Agosto said Bah was the type of friend who regularly checked on the people around him. “He never failed to make sure everybody was okay,” Agosto said. “He was just a really good friend.”Another friend, Zani Zoutten, remembered spending time with Bah during sixth period and described him as a happy person.The memories shared Wednesday showed how many people Bah touched during his 17 years.“He may not have lived so many years in this room, but the days he made on this earth — look at this room,” another speaker said during the celebration.Bah's funeral is scheduled for Saturday.

Two women in Fort Pierce are accused of animal neglect after a dog died on their watch, according to arrest reports from the Fort Pierce Police Department . FPPD says that Samya Shanice Bryant, 25, and Danielle Amanda Potts, 28, were arrested on Oct. 2 in connection with the neglect and death of a dog at Pine Creek Apartments. Officers found the dog days before on Sept. 29 lying outside an apartment. The dog was severely underweight with visible ribs, infected sores on his paws, and no food or water. Bryant told the officers that the dog was hers, and that he had been sick for weeks after another man allegedly poured boiling water on him. FPPD says that both women who each lived in the apartment had control of the dog but did not get him veterinary treatment. See also: Trump touts West Palm golf club as possible Camp David-style retreat for future presidents Animal Control took the dog for emergency care, but the dog had to be euthanized on Oct. 2 because of injuries, infections and organ failure. Both Bryant and Potts were arrested and are being charged with aggravated animal cruelty and confining/impounding an animal without sufficient food or water.

Former Fort Pierce city manager Nick Mimms was found guilty of a third-degree felony of official misconduct and not guilty of a second-degree felony of bid tampering on Thursday.Mimms was arrested in 2024 on charges of bid tampering and official misconduct.WATCH BELOW: Former Fort Pierce city manager found guilty of official misconductAccording to the Florida Department of Law Enforcement, Mimms was accused of rigging the bidding process for two vacant parcels of land along Avenue D, adjacent to the Lincoln Theater, in favor of a local nonprofit, Lincoln Park Young Professionals.Among that nonprofit's board was Caleta Scott, Mimms' niece, and also a city employee.The nonprofit had been awarded a $500,000 grant from Allegheny Franciscan Ministries for a community center project, but nothing was ever built.Johnathan Bridges, special assistant state attorney and Brandon White, major crimes attorney for the 19th Circuit, said there was a mountain of evidence, including emails and city documents that incriminated Mimms."What we learned is millions of dollars have been wasted by this city hall under the leadership of Nick Mimms, and for too long, it went unchecked,” said White. Pierce deserve better, and I think this verdict shows the corruption that was happening under Nick Mimms. It's about time someone was held accountable."WPTV pressed Mimms and his attorney for comment as they left the courtroom but did not get a response.Mimms was granted a pre-sentencing investigation and is scheduled to be sentenced on Dec. Lucie County Courthouse.Prosecutors said he could face a maximum of five years in prison.

The detention center Florida dubbed "Alligator Alcatraz" may have shut down, but questions remain about who will ultimately pay for it.Last year, the federal government awarded Florida more than $600 million through FEMA to help fund operations at the immigration detention facility built in the Everglades. WATCH ALLIGATOR ALCATRAZ, IS FEDERAL FUNDING AT RISK?While state leaders touted the project and President Donald Trump praised it shortly after opening, only a portion of the promised funding has been distributed so far.Now, two federal reports are putting renewed attention on whether that money could be withheld and Florida could face additional scrutiny before receiving the rest of the funds."I think what these reports and the findings in them do is create a potential basis for scrutiny," said Stetson University law professor Anthony Palermo, who specializes in contracts.The questions stem from two separate federal reviews examining the facility's operations.A report from the Department of Homeland Security's Office of Inspector General found the detention center failed to meet several basic standards related to environmental health, safety, medical care, food service and hygiene.According to the report, some detainees reported lacking access to clean drinking water. Inspectors also documented detainees being confined in what were described as "small metal enclosures."A separate Government Accountability Office report highlighted concerns about spending and potential waste. The report found Immigration and Customs Enforcement had not finalized a contract or formal agreement with Florida before immigrants began arriving at the facility.Without pre-negotiated rates in place, the state sought reimbursement at significantly higher costs. The GAO found Florida's approved reimbursement rate was $249 per detainee per day, compared with ICE's reported median detention bed rate of $92 per day, a difference of 171%.So far, neither report concludes Florida violated the terms of its FEMA grant. That distinction could prove important.Palermo says federal agencies typically look first at whether grant recipients complied with the specific requirements attached to funding."Just because there is some sort of deviation from the anticipated standard doesn't necessarily mean that any funding will be withheld," Palermo explained.While the grant excludes typical termination language, it requires Florida to provide a detailed cost breakdown and justification for each reimbursement request.He noted that FEMA retains the authority to review spending, conduct audits and potentially challenge reimbursements if costs are deemed unreasonable. "There is always a chance that there could be an audit or even an investigation into reimbursement that was granted that could potentially lead to a reversal," Palermo said.Federal regulations also give agencies avenues to revisit previously issued payments."There is usually a chance under federal regulations for the government to potentially audit, investigate, review funds that have been paid out and make sure that they were reasonable and could potentially claw them back," he said.Gov. Ron DeSantis dismissed the findings in the federal reports and defended the state's handling of the facility.He also told us last month that additional federal funding continues to flow to the state. To date, just over $134 million has been dispersed from the grant according to USAspending.gov.Neither the Governor's office nor Florida's Department of Emergency Management responded to our inquiries about how the federal reports could impact funding for the facility.The detention center is closed. The federal money is still in question. And until federal officials determine whether all reimbursement requests meet grant requirements, Florida taxpayers have no guarantee they won't end up responsible for part of the final bill.

As Hurricane Isaias heads toward the Florida Panhandle, homeowners across the state will see hurricane deductibles go into effect on their insurance policies."The trigger in this case for most policies is a (hurricane) watch or (hurricane) warning anywhere in the state of Florida," Robert Norberg of Arden Insurance in Lantana said.WATCH BELOW: Isaias triggers Florida insurance deductibles that could cost homeowners thousandsHurricane deductibles are common in Florida and are used for hurricane-related claims. They also have a much higher deductible than the usual deductibles on insurance policies."Typically, it's 2 to 3 percent of the property's insured value — not 2 to 3 percent of the claim — so it can be pretty extensive; some people even have 5 or 10 percent deductible," Norberg said.A 2 percent deductible on a $300,000 home can run about $6,000.And that deductible applies anywhere in the state as long as a hurricane is posted somewhere in Florida."Any type of wind damage that causes a claim — say you're in Palm Beach County, those people will be subject to the wind deductible," Norberg saidThe hurricane deductible, according to state statute, expires 72 hours after the last hurricane warning is lifted.RELATED COVERAGE:

A 14-year-old Treasure Coast High School student is in critical condition after being struck by a vehicle while walking to school Wednesday morning, according to the Port St. Lucie Police Department.Police said the crash happened around 6 a.m. near the intersection of Southwest Port St. Lucie Boulevard and Southwest Squirrel Avenue.WATCH BELOW: Student critically injured after being struck by SUVInvestigators said the freshman was walking northbound along Port St. Lucie Boulevard on his way to school and was near the edge of the roadway alongside construction barrels in the area when he was struck from behind by a 2002 Ford Excursion driven by a 72-year-old man.According to police, the driver initially believed he had hit a construction barrel and did not realize he had struck a person. Authorities said the driver later made a U-turn at the next location where it was safe to do so and returned to the scene.Once back in the area, the driver activated his hazard lights and found the teen unconscious on the side of the roadway. Police said he immediately called 911 and has remained cooperative throughout the investigation.The student suffered life-threatening injuries and remains hospitalized in critical condition, according to police.Investigators said there were no apparent signs of impairment involving the driver, though they noted the assessment is preliminary and could change as the investigation continues.The crash remains under investigation.Police are asking anyone who witnessed the incident or who may have dash camera, surveillance or other video footage from the area around the time of the crash to come forward.Anyone with information is asked to contact the Port St. Lucie Police Department at 772-871-5000.Howard Shapiro lives across the street from where the crash occurred.Shapiro said this stretch of Port St. Lucie Boulevard can be dangerous."I don't walk around here is no lighting outside at nighttime," said Shapiro. "Kids walk along all the time because there's school back there, school down there."Though crews are improving the roadway, Shapiro said lights would make it safer."They are putting in a sidewalk, so that's going to be helpful. But streetlights need to follow," said Shapiro.Celine Gabriel lives off nearby Becker Road and said she avoids Port St. Lucie Boulevard altogether."I don't even come down this road no more," said Gabriel. "I go all the way down to I-95, come up on Gatlin to take my child to school.

A former CIA agent convicted Tuesday of defrauding the government of $194 million reportedly used the majority of the money to acquire properties in Palm Beach and Hobe Sound. According to CBS Miami , court filings say 49-year-old David J. Rush of Virginia, a former high-ranking federal employee, directed $145 million to a holding company he controlled, and that $102 million was used to purchase four Florida properties: Two Palm Beach homes: $21.9 million and $27 million One Palm Beach parcel: $13.65 million One Hobe Sound parcel: $40 million Prosecutors allege Rush intended to eventually resell the properties for a profit. How the scheme unfolded According to the Department of Justice , Rush, of Ashburn, Virginia, pleaded guilty Tuesday, Oct. 6, to wire fraud in federal court in Alexandria, Virginia. According to prosecutors, Rush used his senior-level government position and "Top Secret" clearance to create fictitious government authorities and obtain federal money for his own benefit. Between November 2025 and March 2026, he directed approximately $145 million to a holding company established at his direction, according to court documents. The money was then used to purchase the properties. The Justice Department says Rush fraudulently obtained approximately $193.6 million in government funds. The South Florida real estate was only part of the alleged scheme. Gold bars Prosecutors say Rush separately created a fake "sensitive government activity" to justify acquiring hundreds of gold bars. On May 19, 2026, FBI agents searched Rush's Virginia home and recovered 298 gold bars, approximately $2.1 million in cash, €104,795, and numerous luxury watches. The gold had cost the government approximately $46 million, according to the Justice Department. Rush has agreed to forfeit the gold bars and cash, the Florida properties, luxury watches, and two 2026 BMW Alpina vehicles as part of his plea agreement. What's next Rush is scheduled to be sentenced Jan. He faces a maximum of 20 years in federal prison, along with possible restitution, forfeiture and a fine. The Justice Department said its investigation is continuing. The Director of National Intelligence has also requested an investigation by the Intelligence Community's inspector general. The allegations and admissions are detailed in federal court documents filed as part of Rush's guilty plea.

Brandee Anthony, known as the Vero Beach Mermaid, is an elite level PADI dive instructor, who teaches people of all ages to become mermaids — offering experiences that range from glamorous mermaid makeovers and beach photoshoots to poolside swimming lessons."I was a professional live streamer a long time ago, so I thought it would be really cool to take all my viewers underwater, but how can I make that interesting and magical?" Anthony said.That curiosity grew into a deep and lasting passion."That was 10 years ago and I'm a little in love with mermaiding for sure," Anthony said.The experience begins with a mermaid makeover, starting inside Anthony's custom fantasy closet — brimming with tropical-inspired tails, tops and accessories created just for mermaid gear."We're going to start with a mermaid makeover, which is one of my favorite parts," Anthony said. "Kate, so this is your magical closet."The closet features silicone tails that each weigh about 30 to 35 pounds. Accessories are on hand to complete every look."Mermaid crowns and armbands and embellishments, kind of the final touches to help people really feel like they have a full ensemble," Anthony said.Armbands come in a variety of styles, including options with a vibrant teal accent."We have a few options if you want to go with armbands. We have these, these are super cute and they have that nice teal," Anthony said.Anthony even offered a personalized recommendation while I was browsing through the options."I think with what you are wearing I would probably wear this one," she said.Browsing the closet felt like being a kid in a candy store — wanting more of everything. Anthony said that reaction is exactly the goal."That is exactly what you should feel like," she said. "So, we'll pick out a tail, a top, some accessories, and a crown, and then we'll head over to the beach."After settling on a look — including a tail Anthony called a "wind trader" and a stunning leafy sea dragon design — I was feeling the mermaid vibe and ready for the beach.Anthony, a professional photographer for 15 years, combines breathtaking backdrops and elaborate costumes to create magic where whimsy meets the water. Once suited up, I made my way toward the water, making my mermaid marks in the sand along the way."Like a sea turtle you are going to migrate towards the ocean," she said. "And then your going to turn toward me put your fin over here — we call it a fluke."Anthony walked me through the first poses on the shoreline."The seated is the easiest first pose — you can kind of just look at the ocean and relax and let the wind take your hair," she said. "Look out towards the beach — a little water love."Next, I headed poolside for a basic mermaiding class.Anthony caters to every client's ability, even those who are a little cautious about the experience."Once people get in a tail and they find their groove, it turns into a bunch of people just playing in a pool," she said.People come to the experience for all kinds of reasons."I've had people come to me for fun and some for deeper reasons," Anthony said."Coming on a retreat or take a course really did change their lives — or changed the trajectory of their lives. I've turned a few people into pro mermaids," Anthony said.In the pool, Anthony was ready to teach me how to mermaid — stripping back the glam and focusing on the fundamentals."So now you've had the photoshoot and the glam and now we are going to strip it back and just have some fun swimming as a mermaid," Anthony said.She walked me through every step of the movement."So you can flex your foot up towards the top of the water and then push it down…and just do that a few times….you can feel the resistance of the water and that's what propels you," Anthony said. "I'm going to have you back float in the tail — I'll kind of help you float there."The lesson even included a dive completely underwater."3.2.1. breathe out — we dive down and then pop up," Anthony said. "That was so good — that was fun — and that's how we shoot video underwater."For Anthony, the joy of mermaiding as an adult goes far beyond the water itself. "I think that's what mermaiding as an adult feels like is you don't have to act like a kid but you can be an adult that plays," she said. "And that's where it can be fun or it can be more — some people just want to feel empowered. Or good in their skin and they do a photo shoot or a bucket list thing."This story was reported on-air by a journalist and has been converted to this platform with the assistance of AI. Our editorial team verifies all reporting on all platforms for fairness and accuracy.

Florida officials are urging residents in the Panhandle to finalize their hurricane preparations as Hurricane Isaias strengthens in the Gulf of Mexico and heads toward the state's northwestern coast.During a news briefing Thursday, Gov. Ron DeSantis said the storm is expected to bring impacts as early as Friday afternoon, with landfall projected late Friday night into early Saturday morning.WATCH THE FULL NEWS CONFERENCE BELOW: While forecasters currently expect Isaias to make landfall as a Category 2 hurricane, state officials said they are preparing for a Category 3 storm."We're taking it very seriously," DeSantis said. "Our assumption is that it's going to hit strong as a probably lower-end Category 3, and then we work off that assumption."The governor warned that the storm's most dangerous conditions are expected to be on the eastern side of its track, putting much of the Florida Panhandle at risk for storm surge, tornadoes, flooding and damaging winds.Current forecasts show landfall somewhere between Mobile Bay and Navarre, though officials stressed the track could still change.State emergency officials said storm surge of 5 to 7 feet is possible along portions of the Panhandle. Evacuation orders have already been issued in several counties, primarily for Zones A and B, barrier islands and other low-lying areas."We want everybody to be prepared," DeSantis said. "There will be impacts all across the Florida Panhandle."Florida's Emergency Operations Center is operating at its highest activation level as agencies across the state prepare for response and recovery efforts.The Florida Division of Emergency Management has staged more than 1,000 generators, 500,000 gallons of gasoline, 1 million gallons of diesel fuel, more than 3 million meals ready to eat and 1.1 million bottles of water.More than 6,000 utility workers and restoration personnel are standing by to respond to power outages.The Florida Department of Transportation has also mobilized 900 personnel, nearly 260 pieces of heavy equipment and 100 pumps ahead of the storm. Tolls have been suspended on several Panhandle roadways to help facilitate evacuations and emergency response.Officials said approximately 5,000 members of the Florida National Guard are being activated, while the Florida State Guard has deployed 175 soldiers, aircraft and rescue vessels to support storm operations.Search-and-rescue assets, including airboats, shallow-water boats, swamp buggies and high-water vehicles, have also been pre-positioned throughout the anticipated impact area.Emergency managers said one of the biggest concerns is the potential for inland flooding.The Panhandle has already experienced significant rainfall in recent weeks, leaving many areas saturated before the storm's arrival."You're going to see rising water," DeSantis said. "You're going to see these interior places that I discussed."Florida Division of Emergency Management Executive Director Jared Perdue said officials are closely monitoring rivers, streams and drainage systems that could overflow as additional rain falls."We're viewing this as it could be a Category 3 major hurricane, and we want to be prepared for that," Perdue said.Officials are encouraging residents to complete preparations immediately, including filling gas tanks, securing supplies and reviewing evacuation plans.DeSantis said residents in the storm's path should assume power outages are likely and be prepared with enough water and nonperishable food to last several days.Emergency managers also reminded residents not to leave pets behind during evacuations. Every county in Florida has at least one pet-friendly shelter, officials said.Residents are encouraged to follow guidance from local emergency management agencies and heed all evacuation orders."Do not wait until conditions deteriorate to take action," Perdue said. "Make decisions now to keep yourself and your family safe."Officials also cautioned residents who plan to use generators after the storm to operate them outdoors and away from enclosed spaces to avoid potentially deadly carbon monoxide poisoning.The state said preparations and resource staging will continue as Hurricane Isaias approaches the Gulf Coast, with tropical-storm-force winds expected before landfall and hazardous conditions likely continuing into Saturday.

Martin County officials are scrambling to restore public transportation service after the county's contracted transit provider abruptly canceled its services, leaving Martin County Public Transit (MARTY) riders without transportation effective immediately. In a statement Thursday, Martin County said it is aware that its contracted transit service provider has canceled service and that MARTY transit operations are currently interrupted. "Martin County is actively working to identify solutions to restore transit service as quickly as possible and minimize the impact on our riders," the county said. "Additional information will be provided as it becomes available." Officials did not immediately identify the transit provider or explain why the service was canceled. "We understand the importance of MARTY services to our community and apologize for the disruption," the statement said. In response, United Way of Martin County said it is preparing for an increase in transportation assistance requests through its Ride United program, which provides free, pre-scheduled Lyft rides to eligible residents. Region Martin County "Transportation isn't a luxury for the people who depend on it. It's how they get to work, receive medical care and put food on the table," said Carol G. Houwaart-Diez, president and CEO of United Way of Martin County. "When a critical service like this disappears, the need doesn't disappear with it." United Way officials said the program was already facing financial challenges due to increased demand and other funding reductions before the MARTY service interruption. The organization is now anticipating an even greater need for transportation assistance. Ashley Capital has committed an initial $2,500 donation to help support Ride United's response to the outage. Since launching in September 2022, Ride United has provided thousands of rides for Martin County residents facing transportation barriers. However, United Way emphasized that the program cannot fully replace MARTY's fixed-route bus and paratransit services and that its response is only a temporary solution dependent on available funding. WPTV reached out to Martin County Transit who responded with this statement: "We understand that this news may feel sudden to riders and residents. As strong advocates for reliable public transportation, we are disappointed that we are unable to continue to operate the MARTY system." Martin County Transit told WPTV that 29 employees will be losing jobs as a result of the contract termination. Residents seeking transportation assistance can call 772-283-4800 or visit https://www.unitedwaymartin.org/rideunited for more information. Martin County said it will continue providing updates as it works to restore public transit service. Information about MARTY can be found on the county's transit website .

Palm Beach County Fire Rescue and Animal Care and Control are joining forces once again to help homeless animals find loving homes through a one-of-a-kind fundraiser.The annual Palm Beach County Fire Rescue calendar brings together firefighters, EMTs and adoptable animals for a photo shoot designed to raise money and awareness for animals in need. Organizers say the calendar has become much more than a collection of photos, helping support local animal welfare efforts while connecting pets with potential adopters.WATCH BELOW: Firefighters team up with adoptable pets for popular charity calendar fundraiserWhile posing for the camera may be outside their usual line of work, firefighters say they are happy to step out of their comfort zones for a good cause."I am excited but a little nervous, but it's for a great cause," firefighter Jose Besosa said.The fundraiser began last year and quickly gained momentum."Last year we started it, and it kind of took off from there, and it's become a huge event," said Bryan Brather, Second Legislative Vice President of Local 2928.According to organizers, proceeds from the calendar benefit Palm Beach County Public Safety Animal Care and Control. Last year, the fundraiser raised $10,000, and all of the dogs featured in the calendar were adopted."Last year we raised $10,000, and we would like to double that and do what we can to help out all the animals in Palm Beach County," Bryan Brather, Second Legislative Vice President of Local 2928. said.This year's kickoff event will give the public a chance to help decide which firefighter and dog duo is featured in each month of the calendar.Some of the firefighters are already campaigning for their preferred spots."I would like a summer month because that explains why I am so hot," firefighter and EMT Trey Gilbert joked.The event is about more than fundraising. It is also an opportunity to shine a spotlight on animals looking for a second chance."There are so many dogs and cats that go through unfortunate situations. Not only because people don't want them, but because people die, and they deserve to have second chances," said Palm Beach County Fire Rescue Capt. Janice Vassalotti.The calendar kickoff event is scheduled for Sunday from 6 p.m. at Renegades in West Palm Beach. Attendees can meet firefighters, learn about adoptable animals and help determine which firefighter-and-pet pairs will represent each month of the upcoming calendar.WPTV reporter Christy Waite will be emceeing the event and announcing which firefighter and animal duo were selected for which months.
