After viewer videos showed water covering roads and vehicles struggling through several Port St. Lucie neighborhoods, the city's own budget documents show where it plans to put money to reduce flooding. The city says that work is still in its early stages. Lucie has received about 4 inches of rain over the past 48 hours , and another 2 to 4 inches could fall by the end of the week. City crews are monitoring conditions as water recedes, and officials are reminding drivers and pedestrians to stay out of flooded roads because it is hard to tell how deep the water is. Frank Camarda, who has lived in the area for more than 20 years near SW California Boulevard and SW Plantation Terrace, said Tuesday night's flooding turned his street into a detour. He said drivers piled in while trying to bypass flooded roads, and he believes Savona Boulevard was also underwater. Camarda said he has not seen flooding on his own street before, but he has watched water pool near Oak Hammock a couple of times. He also said city crews used to clean the swale in front of his home about once a month, and he believes that has stopped. "I've been waiting for these guys to clean up. I haven't seen them," Camarda said. City spokesperson Scott Samples said the rain came in too fast for the system to keep up. He said the canals, swales and retention ponds were already full, which makes it harder for water to move. At one location the city monitored, he said, about two feet of water arrived in roughly 30 minutes. Samples said the water had receded from most roadways by about 8:30 p.m. Tuesday, and he described that as the stormwater system doing what it is designed to do. He said Public Works checks drainage before heavy rain and is working to keep swales, drains and canals clear, but there is only so much crews can do when that much water arrives at once. See also: Florida stages emergency supplies as Tropical Storm Isaias strengthens in Gulf Samples said residents who cannot get home should find other accomedations if they can, whether that be another place to stay or carpooling in vehicles that can handle minor flooding. He also said that the city is working closely with police on safety. The city's proposed capital plan for fiscal years 2027 through 2031, submitted to City Council on April 13, includes the Oak Hammock Watershed Improvement Project. It would add new retention ponds, pump systems, and upgraded valves. The plan shows $8 million in each of the first two years and $7 million in each of the next two, for $30 million in all, paid for through stormwater bond financing. Samples said the city has just begun early data analysis for Oak Hammock, which he placed in the California Boulevard area. He said the work will guide the design of a multi-phase project that could include new retention ponds, canal pumps, or even raising the roadway at California and Savona boulevards so water drains off. He said it is hard to predict when residents will see construction or a finished project, because the city must first gather data, settle on a design, and line up funding. He called Oak Hammock a priority for the city. "It will move as fast as it possibly can," Samples said. According to the city, the project covers a large area east of Interstate 95, north of the C-24 Canal and Port St. Lucie Boulevard, and west of Florida's Turnpike. The money would come partly from the $6 increase in the annual stormwater assessment. That went into effect Oct. 1 and raised the assessment from $189 to $195. The city says the assessment helps pay for five projects aimed at flooding and water flow: Oak Hammock, the Elkcam Basin, the E-8 Canal, Hogpen Slough, and faster replacement of swales and culverts. The city says its drainage system includes about 200 miles of canals, 1,200 miles of swales, and more than 6,000 culverts. It also notes that maintaining swales and driveway culverts, from the edge of the pavement to the property line, is the property owner's responsibility under city code.

After years of infertility, pregnancy loss and unanswered questions, one Jupiter mother is turning her personal journey into a source of hope for others.The inaugural Hope Rising 5K and Fun Walk will take place Oct. 17 at Carlin Park, bringing together families, wellness providers and community partners with a shared goal: ensuring that no one facing infertility or pregnancy loss feels alone.WATCH: Jupiter woman creates Hope Rising after infertility journeyFor founder Kimberly Malik, the event grew from her own experience navigating five miscarriages and four years of infertility."When you get told unexplained infertility, that's not really what you want to hear and that's not an answer I can accept," Malik said.She spent years researching, advocating for herself and searching for answers before ultimately learning she had a blood-clotting condition that contributed to her losses.Despite the heartbreak, Malik said the experience eventually led her to a larger purpose."Welcomed our rainbow baby on Nov. 8 of 2024, my husband's birthday, and I just felt this calling of don't let others walk alone," she said.That mission became the foundation of Hope Rising.Malik says one of the most difficult parts of infertility and pregnancy loss is the isolation many families experience.The Hope Rising event is designed to change that.Organizers are bringing together local businesses, wellness providers and community partners to create a Support Village where attendees can connect with resources and others who understand the journey firsthand."We can have those that unfortunately are on a fertility journey feel seen and supported," Malik said.Among those helping organize the event is Jenny Frattaruolo, owner of Jupiter Fit Club, who became part of Malik's support system during her fertility journey."Just having resources and having someone along the journey with you is everything," Malik said during an earlier interview.While the event centers around a 5K and fun walk, organizers say the focus extends far beyond race day.Participants will be able to leave messages of encouragement on wooden hearts, honor loved ones through remembrance activities and celebrate children born after pregnancy loss on a Rainbow Baby Wall.The event will also raise money for the Hope Rising Grant, which aims to help Florida families facing the financial challenges often associated with infertility treatment."Fitness is a great way to bring people together, so this race is going to bring a lot of women together and hopefully we can help them find resources," Frattaruolo said.Pregnancy loss remains a topic many families struggle to discuss openly, even though countless people are affected by it.Frattaruolo believes connection can make a meaningful difference."It's one of those, if you know, you know," she said. "I think we will all experience death and grief in our lifetime, but miscarriage is the only death you will experience inside your own body."For Malik, that understanding is exactly why Hope Rising exists.What began as a search for answers has evolved into a movement focused on support, community and hope.The Hope Rising 5K and Fun Walk will take place Oct. 17 at Carlin Park in Jupiter.This story was reported on-air by a journalist and has been converted to this platform with the assistance of AI. A 17-year-old boy died after a shooting late Friday close to a boat ramp near Fellsmere and Vero Beach, the Indian River County Sheriff's Office said Saturday. The Indian River School District said the unnamed teen recently withdrew from Sebastian River High School to homeschool and was not enrolled in the district at the time of the shooting. "We are deeply saddened by the loss of this young person, and our hearts are with his family, friends, and the Sebastian River High School community," district spokeswoman Kyra Schafte said in a statement to WPBF. In a follow-up email she wrote: "This remains an active investigation, and we are in constant communication with the Indian River County Sheriff’s Office. Please direct questions about the investigation to IRCSO. Our primary focus is supporting our students, staff, families, and community during this difficult time." A dance is scheduled for 7 p.m. Saturday at Sebastian River High. Read more at: https://www.miamiherald.com/news/article317482082.html#storylink=cpy At 11:24 p.m., deputies responded to reports of a juvenile shot in the area of Garcia's Boat Ramp in the 3700 block of County Road 512 and near the Fort Drum Marsh Conservation Area. Deputies located the teen and began lifesaving measures until Indian River County Fire Rescue arrived. He was taken to Sebastian River Medical Center and later flown to Holmes Regional Medical Center in Melbourne, where he died from his injuries, the sheriff's office said. "At this time, this appears to be an isolated incident, and there is no threat to the public," Lt. Kevin Jaworski wrote in an alert to the media. "This is an active investigation." He told WPBF that investigators have interviewed all parties involved in the case. Anyone with information about this incident is asked to call the Indian River County Sheriff’s Office (772-569-6700) or Treasure Coast Crime Stoppers (1-800-273-TIPS). Detectives from the Criminal Investigations Division and crime scene personnel were processing the scene and interviewing multiple witnesses. The area remains open to the public. Martin County officials are scrambling to restore public transportation service after the county's contracted transit provider abruptly canceled its services, leaving Martin County Public Transit (MARTY) riders without transportation effective immediately. In a statement Thursday, Martin County said it is aware that its contracted transit service provider has canceled service and that MARTY transit operations are currently interrupted. "Martin County is actively working to identify solutions to restore transit service as quickly as possible and minimize the impact on our riders," the county said. "Additional information will be provided as it becomes available." Officials did not immediately identify the transit provider or explain why the service was canceled. "We understand the importance of MARTY services to our community and apologize for the disruption," the statement said. In response, United Way of Martin County said it is preparing for an increase in transportation assistance requests through its Ride United program, which provides free, pre-scheduled Lyft rides to eligible residents. Region Martin County "Transportation isn't a luxury for the people who depend on it. It's how they get to work, receive medical care and put food on the table," said Carol G. Houwaart-Diez, president and CEO of United Way of Martin County. "When a critical service like this disappears, the need doesn't disappear with it." United Way officials said the program was already facing financial challenges due to increased demand and other funding reductions before the MARTY service interruption. The organization is now anticipating an even greater need for transportation assistance. Ashley Capital has committed an initial $2,500 donation to help support Ride United's response to the outage. Since launching in September 2022, Ride United has provided thousands of rides for Martin County residents facing transportation barriers. However, United Way emphasized that the program cannot fully replace MARTY's fixed-route bus and paratransit services and that its response is only a temporary solution dependent on available funding. WPTV reached out to Martin County Transit who responded with this statement: "We understand that this news may feel sudden to riders and residents. As strong advocates for reliable public transportation, we are disappointed that we are unable to continue to operate the MARTY system." Martin County Transit told WPTV that 29 employees will be losing jobs as a result of the contract termination. Residents seeking transportation assistance can call 772-283-4800 or visit https://www.unitedwaymartin.org/rideunited for more information. Martin County said it will continue providing updates as it works to restore public transit service. Information about MARTY can be found on the county's transit website .

Family, friends, teachers and classmates gathered at Farm Flame in Vero Beach on Wednesday to remember 17-year-old Sulliman “Sulli” Bah, who was fatally shot during a meetup at Garcia Boat Ramp last week, according to the Indian River County Sheriff’s Office. No arrests have been made, and investigators are examining whether the shooting may have involved self-defense. The celebration of life was held at the Vero Beach restaurant where Bah worked. Through tears and memories, those who knew him described the Sebastian River High School student as kind, funny, hardworking and someone who could light up a room. As rain poured down Wednesday evening, flowers, candles and photographs filled Farm Flame while people who knew Bah stood together to honor his life. Isaac Rodriguez, who knew Bah, said Bah made an impact on everyone around him. “He touched everybody’s heart and he was just really kind and he always lit up the room,” Rodriguez said. Bah’s close friends told WPTV he was focused on his future and enjoyed spending time with the people closest to him. Alex Cortez said he and Bah boxed together, spent time together and shared many memories. “He was a very positive guy. He was always about working, he was intelligent, he had a big future,” Cortez said. Friend Xavi Espinosa remembered Bah as someone who could immediately make others feel welcome. “Even when I first met him, I felt he was such a good soul,” Espinosa said. The Indian River County Sheriff’s Office said Bah was at a meetup at Garcia Boat Ramp on Friday when shots were fired. The sheriff’s office said investigators are looking into whether the shooting was self-defense . No arrests have been made. Bah’s mother, Chelynn Godfrey, described her son as a loving and caring teenager who had his entire life ahead of him. She said she wants investigators to consider all the facts as they determine what happened. “I just ask that law enforcement truly looks at the big picture. I just want them to really look at the facts and I hope that they get this right,” Godfrey said. “I hope his shooter is arrested and I hope he goes to jail.” During the celebration, people took turns sharing memories of Bah and the impact he had on their lives. Angela Sanders, one of Bah’s former sixth grade teachers, remembered his personality and smile. “His personality is amazing, his smile lit up a room,” Sanders said. Myan Agosto said Bah was the type of friend who regularly checked on the people around him. “He never failed to make sure everybody was okay,” Agosto said. “He was just a really good friend.” Another friend, Zani Zoutten, remembered spending time with Bah during sixth period and described him as a happy person. The memories shared Wednesday showed how many people Bah touched during his 17 years. “He may not have lived so many years in this room, but the days he made on this earth — look at this room,” another speaker said during the celebration. Bah’s funeral is scheduled for Saturday.

Julie Wallace Thomas of Delray Beach has been part of the WPTV First Alert Weather Spotters program since it began and a recent visit to the WPTV newsroom gave her a new appreciation for the role she plays.WATCH BELOW:I connected with Thomas and gave her a tour of the station to learn more about what brought her to the team.During the visit, Thomas learned that Weather Spotters have direct communication with the weather service and that their observations actively help the weather service do its job. She said finding that out was a turning point."I didn't know that," she said. "Knowing this now knows that helps me to understand that I can make a difference in other people's lives to confirm that there was a tornado in my neighborhood that it could make a difference means a lot to me." Her passion for weather stretches back to her childhood."I've always loved the weather ever since a kid in science class when they're teaching us about the different kinds of clouds," Thomas said. "More recently, to be able to see on the radar what the weather is coming up."As a spotter, Thomas has captured many memorable moments, from sunsets to stunning rainbow shots."The sunset shots, the rainbow shots. Our church goes out to Anchor Park in Delray for a beach baptism, and as my husband, the pastor of our church, took this man's wife out into the waters to baptize her, we were rewarded with this brilliant double rainbow," she said. "So, I got some great pictures."Weather Spotters play an important role in the community no matter what weather is headed our way.

The Soup Kitchen in Boynton Beach is seeing a surge in demand, with need up about 25% as residents struggle with rising gas prices, medical bills, and other monthly expenses.Marlene Mejia, CEO and executive director of The Soup Kitchen, said the need is increasing."I would say it's about 25% higher need," she said.People are telling the kitchen that tough times are getting tougher."They're telling us that the gas prices are killing them, that medication and the bills that they have to pay at the end of the month, it's not enough," Mejia said. "So, that's why we're coming in and filling in the gap." The Soup Kitchen is filling in the gap for every walk of life, including employed residents, who have homes and cars but are still not making ends meet at the end of the month."You can see people from all over and we call them the household person, which is asset limited income constrained," Mejia said. "But they're employed, so they have cars, they may have a house, they may have an apartment, and it's just not adding up at the end of the month." Yolanda Marcellus was among the dozens of people standing in a long line and walking through The Soup Kitchen for food."I just come here. They have good food every day. So, I'm thank God I'm here," Marcellus said.The kitchen is able to distribute hundreds of pounds of food every day through faithful volunteers, like Mary Webb."You just feel good helping out other people and it comes back to you," Webb said. "The goodness comes back to you." The Soup Kitchen is located at 8655 W. and they can be contacted at 561-732-7595.

A highly specialized team of firefighters from Palm Beach County is heading to Florida's Panhandle to assist with response efforts as Hurricane Isaias takes aim at the Gulf Coast.Palm Beach County Fire Rescue's Urban Search and Rescue (USAR) team deployed Thursday morning on its first-ever state mission, sending 30 firefighters to areas expected to be impacted by the approaching storm.TRACKING THE TROPICS: Hurricane Center | Hurricane GuideThe team specializes in conducting searches and rescues in some of the most dangerous disaster conditions, including collapsed buildings and fast-moving floodwaters.Fire Rescue officials said the crew is transporting multiple boats, search equipment and specialized rescue tools to support emergency operations before and after the hurricane makes landfall.The deployment came after the team was activated overnight by state officials.USAR teams are trained to respond to a wide range of disasters, including structural collapses, severe flooding and other emergencies that require advanced rescue capabilities.Firefighters could remain deployed for up to two weeks, depending on conditions and the level of need in affected communities.Isaias is forecast to make landfall Friday night.

Family and friends gathered Wednesday night at Farm and Flame restaurant in Vero Beach to remember 17-year-old Sulliman Bah, who was shot and killed last Friday during a teen party at the Garcia boat ramp in Fellsmere. Bah, known to many as Sully, had just finished his shift at the restaurant before going to the large gathering of more than 100 teens. A couple hundred people packed the restaurant, sharing stories about Bah’s kindness and the impact he had on their lives. Bah's mother, Chelynn Godfrey, described him as a loving son, brother and kind person. He was just joyful, happy all the time, Godfrey said. Godfrey said her son was the kind of person who made everyone around him feel like they mattered. "We've walked down the street, any stranger he saw, he'd greet them, 'How you doing today?' she said. "That was very important to him that he made people feel good, feel seen." Godfrey said Bah cared deeply about making people feel seen. Friends remembered him as funny and caring and kind. See also: Boynton Beach teen reunites with first responders after surviving lightning strike "He was never mean to nobody, and I hate that this happened to him because he doesn't deserve this," one friend said through tears. "Sully was a kind soul." Investigators say several fights broke out at the teen party before an 18-year-old who knew Bah shot him. Indian River County Sheriff Eric Flowers has said he believes the shooting was in self-defense. "Getting that call on a random Friday night that one of my best friends had just gotten shot...was probably one of the hardest things I've had to go through," another friend said. One of eight children, Bah's mother said he was just a credit and a half away from graduating high school and had big plans for the future. "He wanted to travel," Godfrey said. "He wanted to spend time in a big city. wanted to be an entrepreneur." As she begins to cope with the unimaginable loss of her son, Godfrey said she wants answers about what happened that night and accountability for his death. "His life is not being valued enough, and things are not being looked at seriously enough," she said. "I believe that my son was murdered, and I believe that the shooter needs to be punished for that." The sheriff’s office says the investigation remains open. No arrests have been made, and the State Attorney will decide whether charges will be filed.

Heavy rain flooded roads across Port St. Lucie Tuesday afternoon, leaving some vehicles stranded, forcing children to walk through standing water after school and prompting a response from police officers and city crews. According to the City of Port St. Lucie , a large amount of rain fell in a short period of time, leading to temporary road closures and flooding in multiple areas. Public Works crews responded to flooding near Savona Boulevard and California Boulevard, closing the roadway until it was safe for travel. The city also reported high-water conditions near Thornhill Drive and Floresta Drive, where Phase 3 construction is underway. On Southwest Thornhill Drive, school buses continued dropping off students despite flooded streets. CBS12 News saw children step off buses carrying their shoes and walk barefoot through standing water to reach home. Along Southwest Broadview Avenue near Crosstown Parkway, residents watched as water spilled across the roadway, making it difficult for drivers to tell where the street ended and floodwater began. "If you didn't see the grass here, you wouldn't know where the road is," resident Kevin Burke told CBS12 News. "It was steady sheets of rain for a good hour. Non-stop, and I mean heavy, heavy." Police officers directed traffic while Public Works crews set up barricades and monitored conditions during the evening commute. Burke said flooding in the area has become a familiar problem during heavy downpours. "When it rains heavy like it did today, it's like this all the time, from that canal coming up," he said. Burke said standing water presents concerns beyond traffic issues. "We have a pond over there by Crosstown and Bayshore. It's got signs all around it saying there are gators in it. It's a long shot, but it could happen, and that's what worries me, with kids and the animals," he said. For some residents, the flooding disrupted everyday tasks. "She has her elderly brother, who's 83 years old, and she's in her 60s, and she was going to run out and get Chinese food, and now she's still sitting here waiting because she can't get to it," Burke said. Earlier in the day, Port St. Lucie police reported flooding at several intersections, including SE Evans Avenue and SE Airoso Boulevard, SE Eyerly Avenue and SE Airoso Boulevard, SW Bayshore Boulevard and SW Thornhill Drive, and NE Floresta Drive and NE Ardsley Drive. See also: Opponents, supporters clash over Palm Beach County Israel Bonds investments City officials said Public Works crews continued monitoring conditions as water slowly receded Tuesday evening. Officials also reminded residents not to walk or drive through flooded roadways because it can be difficult to determine how deep the water is.

Jurors are deliberating in the trial of former Fort Pierce City Manager Nicholas Mimms, who is accused of bid tampering and official misconduct involving city-owned properties and a nonprofit linked to his niece. Prosecutors said Mimms used his position as city manager to help Lincoln Park Young Professionals, a nonprofit co-founded by his niece, secure a lease to develop two city-owned properties. The defense denied Mimms did anything wrong, arguing that he and his niece, Caleta Scott, have a distant relationship. The prosecution argued there was a conflict of interest, saying Scott was granted special treatment because of her relationship with Mimms. Deliberations began late yesterday after closing arguments from both sides and resumed at 9 a.m. Jurors have broken for lunch but have not yet reached a verdict. There is no set timeline for how long deliberations will take. Stay up-to-date: The latest headlines and weather from WPBF 25 Get the latest news updates with the WPBF 25 News app.

While many people are just beginning to think about the holidays, volunteers with Back to Basics are already hard at work making sure thousands of Palm Beach County children have gifts to open this Christmas.The nonprofit's annual Angel Program provides new sneakers, socks, underwear, and a toy to children in need throughout the county. "We provide new sneakers, socks, underwear, and a toy for all of them."Because of the large number of children served, preparations begin months before the holiday season arrives. Some gifts are already being sorted and wrapped as volunteers work to get ahead of the demand."The biggest part of our program is we can depend on the community to adopt these children," Kelly said. "About 7,000 will go out to the community each year and the rest of them we do in-house."The organization is encouraging local residents, businesses and civic groups to participate by adopting children, donating gifts or volunteering their time.Back to Basics is also celebrating another successful community initiative. The nonprofit recently completed its annual school uniform drive, which provided approximately 20,000 uniforms to students at more than 60 elementary and middle schools throughout Palm Beach County."We serve over 60 schools here in Palm Beach County," said board member Mike O'Dell. "Many of the children who go to school are required to have uniforms, and they just don't have the financial wherewithal to do that."Volunteers say community support is essential to the success of both programs and helps ensure local children have the resources they need to thrive both in school and during the holiday season."You're helping those in need, and this is a great way to have your children learn the generosity and the joy of giving," Santa Claus joked during WPTV's Shining A Light visit.As the holiday season approaches, Back to Basics hopes more people will step forward to help make Christmas brighter for thousands of Palm Beach County children.

For nearly 40 years, The Golden Girls have entertained audiences with humor, friendship and unforgettable characters. Now, those beloved ladies are coming to South Florida through the touring stage production "Golden Girls: The Laughs Continue."The show arrives at the Raymond F. Kravis Center for the Performing Arts in West Palm Beach on Oct. 25, bringing Dorothy, Blanche, Rose and Sophia back together in a new story that imagines the iconic friends still living under one roof decades after the original sitcom ended.Actor Vince Kelley, who portrays Blanche Devereaux, and Adam Graber, who plays Rose Nylund, say the comedy's enduring popularity comes from its ability to connect with people from all walks of life."It's a very multifaceted answer," Kelley said. "The generational appeal, the nostalgia and stuff like that."He said the sitcom remains a source of comfort for viewers who return to the familiar characters again and again."Women of a certain age who sometimes can feel forgotten or cast aside, this gives them a voice," Kelley said. "The LGBT community obviously has very strong ties. Everybody can kind of identify with one of the girls, so it's easy to see yourself in the show."Full Interview with CastAlthough the original sitcom was set in Miami, the cast believes its themes resonate throughout South Florida."The lifestyle is born from this area," Kelley said. "We're going to be in West Palm Beach. How many people in West Palm Beach are retirees of a certain age who are maybe living this life, living with friends? They have a timeshare; they're doing this."The actors said audiences across Florida often recognize elements of their own communities in the world created by the television series."It's all South Florida," Kelley said. "The alligators, the humidity, banana leaves."The performers also said Florida audiences have embraced the production since it first began touring in the state."We always look forward to coming to Florida because of how solid the fan base is," Kelley said.The production imagines a continuation of the television series rather than a simple tribute show.According to the cast, Sophia has been arrested for operating a drug ring at Shady Pines, while Blanche and Rose launch a dating app for seniors. Meanwhile, Dorothy is forced into the world of online dating and begins a relationship with the very attorney prosecuting Sophia.The result is a fast-paced comedy that blends modern humor with the personalities fans have loved for decades.The show also embraces some of the continuity quirks that longtime viewers know well.During the interview, the actors laughed about references in the original sitcom that seemingly placed Jupiter's Burt Reynolds Dinner Theatre just a short drive from Miami."None of it makes sense," Graber joked. "You just let it happen."For many fans, The Golden Girls represents more than comedy.The cast said audience members frequently share personal stories during meet-and-greet events, telling them how the show connected them with parents, grandparents and close friends.Others describe finding comfort in the sitcom during difficult periods of their lives.That emotional connection continues to help new generations discover Dorothy, Blanche, Rose and Sophia long after the series left the air.Whether viewers tune in for the one-liners, the friendships, or the nostalgia, the cast believes the secret is simple: everyone can find a little of themselves in one of the four friends.Golden Girls: The Laughs Continue comes to the Kravis Center on Sunday, Oct. 25, with performances at 2 p.m. and 7:30 p.m.Organizers recommend buying tickets directly through Kravis.org to avoid scams and third-party resellers.This story was reported on-air by a journalist and has been converted to this platform with the assistance of AI. Florida center Aleksander Barkov is expected to miss six to eight weeks with a left leg injury and will not require surgery, Panthers coach Paul Maurice said Tuesday.Barkov was hurt in the Panthers' overtime loss at San Jose on Thursday. It appeared his left knee — not the knee that needed to be surgically rebuilt last year — buckled on the play, and the Finnish captain immediately left the ice in obvious discomfort.WATCH: Barkov won't need surgery, out 6-8 weeks, Panthers sayThe timetable would suggest that Barkov will probably be out somewhere between 20 and 25 games before he could return."That’s our best window," Maurice said. "Could be a little less, could be a little more. But we think six to eight (weeks) is the right rehab time."Florida plays at Los Angeles on Tuesday to end a season-opening four-game road trip. Maurice revealed the timetable after the Panthers' morning skate in advance of that game.The Panthers placed Barkov on long-term injured reserve over the weekend, after it became clear his absence would last longer than 10 games. The Panthers weighed multiple options on how to proceed and Barkov saw team doctors Monday before a final plan was agreed upon.Barkov was injured 20 minutes into the team’s first training camp practice for the 2025-26 season and missed the entire campaign, one of many injury issues that played a role in Florida going from a back-to-back Stanley Cup champion to a team that missed the playoffs.If there is a silver lining, it’s that Florida is well-versed in how to play without Barkov — who isn’t just the team captain, but is generally considered to be the team’s best player."If he hadn’t been injured last year we would have thought, ‘Gee, six to eight weeks is a long time,’" Maurice said. "I think last year was six to eight months, so we’re taking it."Over his most recent 10 seasons — excluding when he missed last season — Barkov had 722 points, 485 hits and 463 blocked shots. No other NHL player reached those numbers in all three categories over those years; Toronto’s Auston Matthews and Winnipeg’s Mark Scheifele were the only others with at least 700 points, 400 hits and 400 blocks in that span.And the Panthers were clearly breathing a sigh of relief knowing that he will be back this season."It's good for everything, maybe most importantly for Barky," Maurice said. "He’s our captain and we miss him and he feels it when he’s not around. So, he's probably the happiest of all of us."

Florida Panthers forward Brad Marchand sustained a left leg injury in the second period of their 2-1 win against the Los Angeles Kings on Tuesday night.Marchand was not on the bench for the third period, and coach Paul Maurice did not have an update on his condition afterward."We'll get him looked at probably Thursday," Maurice said.Marchand was hurt after taking a stick to the face from Kings defenseman Brandt Clarke with 52.6 seconds remaining, which caused him to twist around and collide with the right post before his left leg bent back in an awkward way.Marchand was down on the ice for several minutes being examined by an athletic trainer before teammates Brady Tkachuk and Niko Mikkola helped him to the bench, with Marchand unable to put any weight on his leg. He was then helped back to the dressing room.Marchand, 38, is in his third season with the Panthers after playing his first 16 seasons with the Boston Bruins. He was traded to Florida in March 2025 and helped them win their second straight Stanley Cup that season.But the defense of those titles last season was scuttled by injuries, and now the Panthers have seen two key players injured on their four-game West Coast trip to start this season.Aleksander Barkov, one of the top two-way centers in hockey, hurt his left leg in an overtime loss at San Jose on Thursday. Maurice said earlier Tuesday that Barkov is expected to miss six to eight weeks and will not require surgery."I mean, we have a little experience with Sasha going down, so it wasn't quite as shocking the second time it happened," Maurice said. "We know we have good depth. And there's a threshold for any team, a number of injuries you just can't survive, and we passed that early last year. So, real good resolve here. The tank is deep right now. We had a big summer off, so we're strong."Clarke received a four-minute double-minor penalty. It was the second penalty of the game for Clarke, who was called for interference against Eetu Luostarinen earlier in the period. Luostarinen was shaken up on a cross-check from Clarke, sustaining a stinger, but was able to return to the game.

Family, friends, teachers and classmates gathered at Farm & Flame in Vero Beach on Wednesday to remember 17-year-old Sulliman “Sulli” Bah, who was fatally shot during a meetup at Garcia Boat Ramp last week, according to the Indian River County Sheriff's Office. No arrests have been made, and investigators are examining whether the shooting may have involved self-defense. The celebration of life was held at the Vero Beach restaurant where Bah worked. Through tears and memories, those who knew him described the Sebastian River High School student as kind, funny, hardworking and someone who could light up a room.As rain poured down Wednesday evening, flowers, candles and photographs filled Farm & Flame while people who knew Bah stood together to honor his life.Isaac Rodriguez, who knew Bah, said Bah made an impact on everyone around him. “He touched everybody’s heart and he was just really kind and he always lit up the room,” Rodriguez said.Bah's close friends told WPTV he was focused on his future and enjoyed spending time with the people closest to him.Alex Cortez said he and Bah boxed together, spent time together and shared many memories. “He was a very positive guy. He was always about working, he was intelligent, he had a big future,” Cortez said.Friend Xavi Espinosa remembered Bah as someone who could immediately make others feel welcome. “Even when I first met him, I felt he was such a good soul,” Espinosa said.The Indian River County Sheriff's Office said Bah was at a meetup at Garcia Boat Ramp on Friday when shots were fired. The sheriff's office said investigators are looking into whether the shooting was self-defense. No arrests have been made.Bah's mother, Chelynn Godfrey, described her son as a loving and caring teenager who had his entire life ahead of him. She said she wants investigators to consider all the facts as they determine what happened.“I just ask that law enforcement truly looks at the big picture. I just want them to really look at the facts and I hope that they get this right,” Godfrey said. “I hope his shooter is arrested and I hope he goes to jail.”During the celebration, people took turns sharing memories of Bah and the impact he had on their lives.Angela Sanders, one of Bah's former sixth grade teachers, remembered his personality and smile. “His personality is amazing, his smile lit up a room,” Sanders said.Myan Agosto said Bah was the type of friend who regularly checked on the people around him. “He never failed to make sure everybody was okay,” Agosto said. “He was just a really good friend.”Another friend, Zani Zoutten, remembered spending time with Bah during sixth period and described him as a happy person.The memories shared Wednesday showed how many people Bah touched during his 17 years.“He may not have lived so many years in this room, but the days he made on this earth — look at this room,” another speaker said during the celebration.Bah's funeral is scheduled for Saturday.

For this week's 'Where's Walter?', I visited Paris Ballet in Jupiter, where students are busy preparing for their upcoming performances of The Nutcracker. As soon as I walked into the studio, I knew I was stepping into a world that requires talent, discipline and plenty of hard work.Of course, I couldn't just stand on the sidelines.WATCH: The dancers and instructors invited me to join them on the floor, and after a quick warm-up, it was time to learn some ballet basics. Let's just say I quickly discovered there's a reason these students spend so much time training.I teamed up with several dancers, including Maya, who helped teach me a few of the moves from her role as the Sugar Plum Fairy. While she made everything look effortless, my legs had a different opinion.Then it was time to learn part of another routine with dancer Jay. He was kind enough to slow things down for me, but even at a beginner's pace, I realized just how much strength, balance and coordination ballet requires.I'll be honest: I'm no ballet dancer.But spending time with these young performers gave me a whole new appreciation for what they do. Every movement takes focus. Every routine requires practice. And every performance is the result of countless hours spent perfecting their craft.What impressed me most was the dedication of the students. Watching them rehearse, I saw firsthand the commitment and passion they bring to every class and every performance. Their talent shines on stage, but it's the hard work behind the scenes that truly makes it all possible.I also got a special look at preparations for this year's Nutcracker production. Seeing the dancers work together to bring the beloved holiday classic to life made me appreciate just how much effort goes into creating a ballet performance.While I don't think I'll be joining the cast anytime soon, I had an incredible time trying out a few moves and learning from some very talented young dancers.And after seeing their hard work up close, I can tell you one thing: The Nutcracker is in very good hands this holiday season.Tickets are on sale now for the Nutcracker on Nov. 21 at the Duncan Theater in Lake Worth Beach.

A West Palm Beach woman is turning her husband’s Huntington’s disease diagnosis into a mission to raise awareness and support families affected by the progressive neurological disease.Madison Donovan says her husband, Brian, was diagnosed with Huntington's disease at age 21, just four years ago. Now, she is helping organize the Hope for HD Walk this weekend outside the Spanish River Library in Boca Raton.The walk is scheduled for Saturday at 9 a.m. and aims to raise both awareness and money for people and families affected by Huntington’s disease.According to Donovan, Huntington’s disease is a hereditary and progressive neurological disease that can affect movement and behavior.For Donovan, the diagnosis has become a reason to help others better understand a disease she says affects everyday families."I want to spread awareness. It’s not just a disease that goes into the rare disease book. It's something that is affecting everyday people," Donovan said.Donovan is helping organize the Hope for HD Walk as part of an effort to bring more attention to Huntington’s disease and raise funds for those affected by it.Proceeds from the event will benefit the Huntington’s Disease Society of America, Donovan said.The fundraising goal is $10,000. Donovan says organizers are already halfway to that goal.The event will take place Saturday at 9 a.m. outside the Spanish River Library in Boca Raton.

A 14-year-old Treasure Coast High School student is in critical condition after being struck by an SUV while walking to school Wednesday morning in Port St. Officers with the Port St. Lucie Police Department say the crash happened around 6 a.m. near the intersection of SW Port St. Lucie Boulevard and SW Squirrel Avenue. PSLPD says the freshman was walking northbound along Port St. Lucie Boulevard near the edge of the roadway, alongside construction barrels in the area. The incident occurred on National Walk, Bike, & Roll to School Day . Lucie flooding problem renews focus on city's stormwater spending Officers said the teen was struck from behind by a 2002 Ford Excursion driven by a 72-year-old man. The driver initially believed he had hit a construction barrel and did not realize he had struck a person, according to investigators. Police said the driver made a U-turn at the next available location where he could safely turn around. He returned to the area, activated his hazard lights, and found the teen unconscious on the side of the road. The driver called 911 and has remained cooperative with investigators, police said. Investigators have not observed any apparent signs of impairment involving the driver. Police emphasized that assessment is preliminary and could change as the investigation continues. The teen suffered life-threatening injuries and remains in critical condition. The investigation remains active. Police are asking anyone who witnessed the crash or has dashcam, surveillance, or other video from the area around the time of the crash to contact PSLPD at 772-871-5000 .

While much of the attention surrounding Florida's November election has centered on Amendment 3, voters will also decide the fate of two other proposed constitutional amendments that could have significant impacts on the state's finances and agricultural industry.Amendment 1 would make major changes to Florida's Budget Stabilization Fund (Read the full text), often referred to as the state's "rainy day" fund.WATCH BELOW: Amendments 1 & 2: What to know about these lesser-known ballot measuresThe proposal would increase the maximum size of the fund from 10% to 25% of net general revenue collections. It would also require annual transfers of up to $750 million into the reserve fund and allow state lawmakers to use the money for certain critical needs.Supporters say the amendment would strengthen Florida's financial position during natural disasters, economic downturns and other emergencies by ensuring the state maintains a larger reserve of available funds.Opponents, however, argue that setting aside additional money in reserves could limit the state's ability to address immediate needs, including public services and infrastructure projects.Voters will also weigh Amendment 2, which focuses on tax relief for Florida's agriculture sector. (Read the full text)The measure would exempt agricultural equipment and certain farm-related property from property taxes. Supporters say the change would reduce costs for farmers, strengthen the agriculture industry and help preserve farming operations across the state.Those opposed to the amendment contend the tax exemptions could reduce revenue collected by local governments. Critics argue that loss of tax income could affect funding for public services and other community programs that rely on property tax dollars.Both amendments will appear on Florida's ballot this November, giving voters an opportunity to decide whether the proposed changes should be added to the state constitution. Amendment 3 increases the homestead exemption, for all non-school taxes, to $150,000 in 2027 and $250,000 in 2028, and adjusts for inflation thereafter. Officials are also reminding people to avoid driving or walking through flooded roads because it can be difficult to determine how deep the water is.

Senate candidate Angie Nixon visited Fort Pierce on Tuesday to speak with voters about reproductive health care, the economy, and other issues as part of her campaign across Florida ahead of the general election. Nixon, who represents a Jacksonville-area district in the Florida House of Representatives and describes herself as a Democratic Socialist, is holding town hall meetings across the state to connect with voters. Planned Parenthood President and CEO Alexis McGill Johnson hosted the Fort Pierce town hall, focusing on reproductive freedom and Florida's maternal mortality crisis. McGill Johnson and Nixon outlined the leadership they believe Florida families need, including protecting abortion access and expanding comprehensive health care services statewide. "Representative Nixon is a true champion for reproductive freedom," McGill Johnson said. "In the Senate, she is going to stand up for affordable health care and our right to make our own decisions about our own bodies." During the event, Nixon addressed a question about a proposed Islamic center approved for construction in Palm Beach County. Deep Dive: WPBF 25 News Investigates "This is a country where folks should have freedom of religion," Nixon said. "I would speak out against that type of opposition and hate if it was directed at a synagogue being built, if it was directed at a church being built, if it was directed at any other spiritual facility." Nixon also discussed the state of reproductive health care in Florida and other issues raised by voters. "Gas is high, people are struggling to get to and from work, and then they can't even afford the food anymore, let alone taking their children to the movies or out to eat, that's null and void now," one voter said. Nixon won the Democratic primary in St. Lucie County with about 54% of the vote. When asked how she plans to close the gap between herself and Republican incumbent Ashley Moody, Nixon said she intends to continue engaging with voters, including those who may disagree with her. Matt Elliott wants to know whether his brain cancer could be connected to other diagnoses on the Treasure Coast. He also knows he may not live long enough to get an answer. It might take them years to even figure out what the hell’s going on around here, Elliott said. I can’t expect myself to be around at the end of it. Lucie County have raised similar questions for years, pointing to diagnoses just houses apart and, in some cases, among unrelated residents of the same home decades apart. In June, I-Team reporter Katie Bente revisited families’ search for answers. In this second part of her investigation, Bente went street by street with a widow tracking the diagnoses and pressing health officials for updated findings. A few houses apart For Stephanie Ankiel , one stop on the drive through Fort Pierce brings the questions back to her own family. She pointed to her late husband’s childhood home, then another home a few houses away where she said a resident was diagnosed in 2025 with the same type of brain tumor. This is the house my late husband grew up in, Ankiel said. He was diagnosed with the same exact thing as that gentleman in 2025. Both men were initially diagnosed with oligodendroglioma, a different type of brain tumor from glioblastoma . Ankiel said her husband Mark Cunningham’s cancer later progressed to glioblastoma. A few streets away, she identified another home where she said two unrelated residents developed glioblastoma decades apart. This is the house where we’ve had two glioblastoma cases, 20 years apart, no family relation, she said. Elsewhere along the route, Ankiel pointed to neighboring homes where she said a woman and an 18-year-old had been diagnosed with brain cancer. The I-Team is withholding exact addresses to protect families’ privacy. PART 1: Brain cancer diagnoses leave St. Lucie County families searching for answers, again Ankiel helps patients through the Brain Cancer Foundation of the Treasure Coast , including a child who is just 3. She has spent years mapping where patients lived and looking for possible connections. Three additional brain cancer cases were confirmed in August alone in the areas families are tracking. Those diagnoses and the proximity of patients’ homes do not establish a cancer cluster or a common cause. But Ankiel wants officials to examine the range of brain cancers represented on her map, beyond glioblastoma alone. Regardless if it’s Glio at this point, we have too much brain cancer in this area. CDC guidance allows consideration of different cancer types when evidence suggests shared causes or exposures. No such connection has been established among the cases families are tracking. What the state studied and what is new The Florida Department of Health’s 2019 review examined glioblastoma diagnoses from 1998 through 2017 in ZIP codes 34952, 34982 and 34983. It found no statistically significant increase and did not designate a cancer cluster. That review did not include later diagnoses and focused on glioblastoma rather than the range of brain tumors represented on Ankiel’s map. Her husband’s initial diagnosis is one reason she wants officials to examine that broader picture. The I-Team asked whether the department had analyzed cases diagnosed since 2017 and what would trigger new environmental testing. Lucie County Health Officer Clint Sperber said officials have been reviewing cancer registry data and environmental influences. Our latest analysis, which includes data through 2023, shows no indication of higher rates in St. Lucie County or in the specific zip codes people have asked about, Sperber wrote. Lucie’s rates are in line with nearby counties and with the state as a whole. The updated report was not available when he responded. Sperber said officials were finishing a summary to release online. His response did not explain how the analysis handled tumors initially classified as another type and later diagnosed as glioblastoma, or whether other brain cancers were examined separately. It also did not specify what would trigger additional environmental testing. No environmental factor questioned by families has been established as a cause of these cancers. A call for another look Rep. Brian Mast said he has again asked the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention to examine the concerns and provide the data behind its conclusions. You need to give us the receipts, Mast said. Give us the data of where these took place, how many of them took place. The CDC said state and local health departments lead examinations of unusual cancer patterns. It confirmed that it assisted Florida’s investigation in 2018, but did not specifically address whether it had received Mast’s latest request or would open a new review. In a statement to the I-Team, a CDC spokesperson said: CDC is prepared to provide additional assistance upon the Florida Department of Health’s request. Making the most of the time left Elliott was diagnosed this year with glioblastoma, an aggressive, fast-growing grade 4 brain cancer. The former bar manager described struggling to speak after surgery and initially believing his diagnosis was an isolated case. Meeting other local patients changed that. I thought I was the only one, he said. He has decided not to continue treatment, choosing to spend his remaining time with friends and family, going to the beach and swimming. While he wants investigators to find answers, he is focused on the life he still has. I’m not going to be that person that lives to be 65, 70, 80 years old, Elliott said. But I get to hang out with my friends. I get to go take a swim, have some fun.

No arrests have been made in the shooting death of a 17-year-old at a teen meetup near Garcia’s Boat Ramp in Indian River County, with a self-defense claim expected in the case, Indian River County Sheriff Eric Flowers announced Monday. “We got kids out here losing their lives chasing likes and shares on social media,” Flowers said. The shooting occurred late Friday night when approximately 100 teens, ranging in age from 14 to 19, gathered at Garcia’s Boat Ramp in the 3700 block of County Road 512, the sheriff said. Deputies had broken up a similar group earlier that evening before the crowd moved to the boat ramp. “The 17-year-old, and a group of his friends, are approaching a truck, and there are two people, both 18 years old, inside of that truck. The 17-year-old opens the door, and he starts to punch,” Flowers said. “He’s going to punch on the people that are inside of that truck. That shot is the shot that ultimately killed 17-year-old in this case.” The teen’s friends drove him away from the scene, east on County Road 512, while calling 911 and a dispatcher told them to stop at Fellsmere City Hall, where emergency crews performed CPR, the sheriff said. He was taken to Sebastian River Medical Center and later flown to Holmes Regional Medical Center in Melbourne, where he died from his injuries. The two individuals in the truck were identified using the sheriff’s office’s Flock technology, the sheriff said. Flowers said both have been cooperative with investigators, surrendering the weapon used in the shooting and the truck. Additional individuals involved in the incident have also been identified through Flock, though some remain unidentified. Investigators also recovered other weapons from the vehicle in which the 17-year-old was transported from the scene. Flowers said a warrant will be submitted in the case, but it will be up to the state to determine whether charges are filed. “There have been no arrests on this case at this time, because the preliminary investigation shows that the 17-year-old was opening the door to attempt to fight with the two that were inside of the vehicle. They had a history of fighting,” Flowers said. “Self defense plays a part in these, and when these kids go out and videotape these fights, and now guns are involved, there’s going to be more of this.” Names of those involved are not being released as the investigation continues, the sheriff said. Investigators believe at least four fights occurred at the boat ramp on the night of the shooting. Multiple shell casings and rounds were recovered from the scene. During Monday’s news conference, Flowers released video of the shooting, noting the footage had already circulated widely on social media and that the victim’s mother had seen it. One of the 18-year-olds involved in the shooting attends Vero Beach High School. The sheriff said teen meetups like the one at Garcia’s Boat Ramp are coordinated through Snapchat, making them difficult for law enforcement to track in advance. “When it’s Snapchat, it’s basically a private conversation,” Flowers said. “But it quickly can escalate to over 100, 150, 200 people there.” Flowers said the meetups, which have included alcohol, fighting, and firearms, have been taking place for years across Indian River County, Okeechobee, and surrounding areas, but that social media has intensified the danger. “Now we’re adding guns and alcohol into the mix, and we’re adding social media into the mix, and so what we’re seeing is an escalation of each one of these,” Flowers said. There’s guns, and those two just don’t mix. And now add in the fuel of the fire of social media, and now we have a 17-year-old dead.” The sheriff said teens at these gatherings are motivated in part by a desire for online attention. “The kids like to fight, and they like to videotape it, and they like to get their likes and shares because of that,” Flowers said. Parents, you see these videos. You do not want your teens out at these meetups." With Vero Beach High School’s homecoming game scheduled for Friday and the dance on Saturday, Flowers said additional deputies will be on duty. Meanwhile, the sheriff urged parents to monitor their children’s whereabouts and report any information about planned meetups to the sheriff’s office. “Parents, if your kids are telling you that they’re headed out to one of these meetups, ask them where they’re going. Ask, find out the details. Share that with us,” Flowers said. He recommended parents use location-sharing apps such as Life360 to track their children and said a child appearing to be in a remote or unusual location can be an indicator that a meetup is taking place. The investigation remains active. Flowers said anyone who witnessed any of the events that night, including the shooting itself, and has not yet spoken to investigators is urged to come forward. “I can tell you, our investigation is not even remotely over, and if we are able to identify people that were involved in this, from underage drinking to fighting, hurting other people,” Flowers said. " If they did something wrong, they’re going to have to be accountable for that." Anyone with information is asked to call the Indian River County Sheriff’s Office at 772-569-6700 or Treasure Coast Crime Stoppers at 1-800-273-TIPS.

Florida has reported nearly 500 dengue cases this year, including more than 250 infections acquired within the state, as new University of Florida research points to residential yards in Indian River County as a key place to understand mosquito-bite exposure. The Florida Department of Health’s latest weekly surveillance report , covering Sept. 20-26, lists 252 locally acquired dengue cases and 245 travel-associated cases statewide 497 total. The locally acquired cases were reported in Hillsborough, Miami-Dade, Orange, Palm Beach, Pasco, Pinellas and Polk counties. Palm Beach County had one locally acquired case and 12 travel-associated cases; St. Lucie County had six travel-associated cases. No locally acquired dengue cases were listed for Indian River County in the report. The state’s locally acquired total includes 223 cases in Hillsborough County, the center of Florida’s outbreak. Health officials also reported 20 mosquito pools testing positive for dengue statewide. Nationally, the CDC’s most recent weekly provisional report counted 690 dengue cases among U.S. Florida accounted for 403 of those cases in the CDC reporting system, though the state’s more current surveillance report lists a higher total because reporting systems update on different schedules. Against that backdrop, researchers at UF/IFAS’ Florida Medical Entomology Laboratory in Vero Beach found a surprising mosquito pattern in suburban Indian River County. The team expected residential yards to be dominated by Aedes albopictus , also known as the Asian tiger mosquito. Instead, researchers found relatively high numbers of Aedes aegypti the yellow fever mosquito and one of the two species most closely associated with dengue transmission worldwide. The finding does not mean dengue is circulating in Indian River County . But it underscores why backyard mosquito control and personal bite prevention matter, researchers said. See also: Florida stages emergency supplies as Tropical Storm Isaias strengthens in Gulf The first-of-its-kind study paired mosquito trapping at homes with a smartphone-based Bite Diary that let residents document when and where they were bitten. Researchers collected 3,788 female mosquitoes from 78 yards. Of 70 reported bites, nearly 93% happened outdoors and nearly 74% happened at home, according to the peer-reviewed study . The number of mosquitoes trapped in a yard was not associated with the number of bites residents reported. Instead, people who spent more time outside during the evening, from 5 p.m. to 9 p.m., reported more bites. Gardening and walking dogs were among activities commonly reported when bites occurred. Dengue is spread when an infected mosquito bites a person; it does not spread directly from person to person. Symptoms can include fever, severe muscle and joint pain, rash, nausea and pain behind the eyes. People with symptoms should contact a health care provider, especially after travel to an area where dengue is common. Health officials urge residents to use EPA-registered insect repellent, wear long sleeves and pants when practical, repair window and door screens, and dump standing water from containers such as buckets, flowerpots, toys, tires and pool covers.

Hundreds of people gathered Wednesday night at the Farm and Flame restaurant in Vero Beach to honor the life of 17-year-old Sulli Bah, who was fatally shot last Friday. "He was just joyful, happy all the time. Contagious smile," said Chelynn Godfrey, Bah’s mother. Godfrey said she was the only one who called her son Sulliman, while everyone else knew him as Sulli, a young man who always had a kind word for strangers. "That was just very important to him, that he made people feel good, that he made people feel seen," Godfrey said. Bah was killed Friday at a party at the Garcia Boat Ramp. Videos released by the sheriff’s office show Bah opening the door of a white pickup truck, and the passenger inside the truck firing one shot, killing him. The vigil, held at the restaurant where Bah worked, began with a prayer, followed by friends sharing memories of the 17-year-old and praying for justice. "Sulli was a kind soul," said one friend, fighting to hold back tears. No arrests have been made in connection with Bah’s death. A heated debate over Palm Beach County's investment in Israeli bonds unfolded Tuesday as residents packed commission chambers to voice support and opposition to the county's continued participation in the investment program. WATCH BELOW: Debate heats up over Israeli bond investmentThe county currently holds approximately $1 billion in Israeli bonds, making it the world's largest investor in the securities, according to county officials and speakers at the meeting.Supporters argued the investment provides strong financial returns for taxpayers while strengthening ties with a longtime U.S. Opponents said the county should reconsider the investments because of concerns related to Israel's military actions in the Middle East.The discussion comes as Palm Beach County is preparing for an additional $67 million investment in Israeli bonds scheduled to take effect Nov. 1.The debate drew passionate testimony from residents on both sides of the issue.At times, tensions escalated inside commission chambers, with law enforcement removing some attendees from the meeting.Opponents of the investment argued taxpayer funds should not be connected to actions they oppose overseas and called on county leaders to reconsider the county's involvement with Israeli bonds.Supporters countered that the bonds represent a sound financial investment that benefits Palm Beach County residents."This is not about political agenda. It's about investment that benefit all Palm Beach County citizens," said supporter Ifataloni. "We don't want to pay more taxes in here."Among those speaking against the investment was Lydia Singh."What it's about is making sure that no government gets special treatment," Singh said.She also argued county investments should be based on financial performance and fiduciary responsibility."Investments cannot be made for social or political reasons, and they must be made where it's the most prudent investment and most financially profitable investment possible," Singh said.While much of the discussion centered on county government, Palm Beach County Mayor Sara Baxter said the county commission does not directly decide where investment funds are placed."We, the commission, do not decide where those investments get spent. The clerk of courts does," Baxter said.Baxter said she nevertheless chose to allow public comment on the issue because of the strong community interest surrounding the investments."Even though we don't decide, I still chose to let them speak," she said.One of the key arguments from supporters centered on the financial return generated by the investment.Baxter said she has been told the county's investment has produced a return of at least 5.7%."The numbers that I've heard are it's at least a 5.7% return on investment," Baxter said. "That's huge, and the amount of money that it brings into this county is amazing."She said the returns help generate revenue beyond property tax collections and can benefit county residents.The county's planned $67 million investment remains scheduled to take effect Nov. 1 as debate over the issue continues.WPTV will continue following developments and reactions from county leaders and residents.This story was reported on-air by a journalist and has been converted to this platform with the assistance of AI. Family, friends, teachers and classmates gathered at Farm & Flame in Vero Beach on Wednesday to remember 17-year-old Sulliman “Sulli” Bah, who was fatally shot during a meetup at Garcia Boat Ramp last week, according to the Indian River County Sheriff's Office. No arrests have been made, and investigators are examining whether the shooting may have involved self-defense.The celebration of life was held at the Vero Beach restaurant where Bah worked. Through tears and memories, those who knew him described the Sebastian River High School student as kind, funny, hardworking and someone who could light up a room.As rain poured down Wednesday evening, flowers, candles and photographs filled Farm & Flame while people who knew Bah stood together to honor his life.Isaac Rodriguez, who knew Bah, said Bah made an impact on everyone around him. “He touched everybody’s heart and he was just really kind and he always lit up the room,” Rodriguez said.Bah's close friends told WPTV he was focused on his future and enjoyed spending time with the people closest to him.Alex Cortez said he and Bah boxed together, spent time together and shared many memories. “He was a very positive guy. He was always about working, he was intelligent, he had a big future,” Cortez said.Friend Xavi Espinosa remembered Bah as someone who could immediately make others feel welcome. “Even when I first met him, I felt he was such a good soul,” Espinosa said.The Indian River County Sheriff's Office said Bah was at a meetup at Garcia Boat Ramp on Friday when shots were fired. The sheriff's office said investigators are looking into whether the shooting was self-defense. No arrests have been made.Bah's mother, Chelynn Godfrey, described her son as a loving and caring teenager who had his entire life ahead of him. She said she wants investigators to consider all the facts as they determine what happened.“I just ask that law enforcement truly looks at the big picture. I just want them to really look at the facts and I hope that they get this right,” Godfrey said. “I hope his shooter is arrested and I hope he goes to jail.”During the celebration, people took turns sharing memories of Bah and the impact he had on their lives.Angela Sanders, one of Bah's former sixth grade teachers, remembered his personality and smile. “His personality is amazing, his smile lit up a room,” Sanders said.Myan Agosto said Bah was the type of friend who regularly checked on the people around him. “He never failed to make sure everybody was okay,” Agosto said. “He was just a really good friend.”Another friend, Zani Zoutten, remembered spending time with Bah during sixth period and described him as a happy person.The memories shared Wednesday showed how many people Bah touched during his 17 years.“He may not have lived so many years in this room, but the days he made on this earth — look at this room,” another speaker said during the celebration.Bah's funeral is scheduled for Saturday.

A woman fled for her life after she was attacked and later shot at as she drove away in her vehicle. According to the Fort Pierce Police Department , on Saturday, October 3, officers responded to South Sixth Street at 7:12 a.m. after the victim called police and reported that someone was shooting at her. The investigation revealed the victim went to South Sixth Street to speak with her boyfriend about their relationship. Upon her arrival, several people ran out of the residence and began attacking her. See also: Opponents, supporters clash over Palm Beach County Israel Bonds investments Police said the victim was able to escape, get into her vehicle, and drive away. As she fled, one of the suspects grabbed a gun from the property and began shooting at her, according to police. A second person was arrested for allegedly driving the shooter away from the scene. The two suspects arrested were identified as Keibin Lopez-Godoy, 18, and Kailee Yurubi, 18. Godoy faces a charge of first-degree attempted homicide. Yurubi faces a charge of accessory after the fact.
