A West Palm Beach woman is turning her husband’s Huntington’s disease diagnosis into a mission to raise awareness and support families affected by the progressive neurological disease.Madison Donovan says her husband, Brian, was diagnosed with Huntington’s disease at age 21, just four years ago. Now, she is helping organize the Hope for HD Walk this weekend outside the Spanish River Library in Boca Raton.The walk is scheduled for Saturday at 9 a.m. and aims to raise both awareness and money for people and families affected by Huntington’s disease.According to Donovan, Huntington’s disease is a hereditary and progressive neurological disease that can affect movement and behavior.For Donovan, the diagnosis has become a reason to help others better understand a disease she says affects everyday families.“I want to spread awareness. It’s not just a disease that goes into the rare disease book. It’s something that is affecting everyday people,” Donovan said.Donovan is helping organize the Hope for HD Walk as part of an effort to bring more attention to Huntington’s disease and raise funds for those affected by it.Proceeds from the event will benefit the Huntington’s Disease Society of America, Donovan said.The fundraising goal is $10,000. Donovan says organizers are already halfway to that goal.The event will take place Saturday at 9 a.m. outside the Spanish River Library in Boca Raton.

Lucie County Fire District has hit a snag in its effort to create a new policy for handling complaints against its own top leaders as fallout continues from a controversial hazing investigation. During a Fire District Board workshop Wednesday morning, board members had hoped to hear from outside law firms about helping draft a new complaint policy.WATCH BELOW: Fire district's new complaint policy effort stalls amid hazing falloutInstead, St. Lucie County Commissioner and Fire District Board Member Jamie Fowler said one of the law firms contacted never returned her calls, while another disclosed a potential conflict of interest."I appreciated her honesty and forthrightness on that issue," Fowler said of the attorney during the meeting. "That being said, she did provide two references, both on the West Coast." The board discussed now reaching out to additional law firms in hopes of securing outside legal help ahead of its next meeting Oct. 21."I think we'd be doing ourselves an injustice if we at least we don't have a courtesy conversation with these other firms, so that we're at least prepared just in case these two firms aren't available, non-responsive," Board Member and Fort Pierce City Commissioner Curtis Johnson said. "I think we all have some sense of urgency of getting this thing closed, and and I don't want to delay any further." The effort follows a heated special board meeting Sept. 30, when members publicly acknowledged what they described as a significant gap in district policy: There is no clear process for independently handling complaints made against some of the district's own contract employees. "Since this district's inception, we have not had a policy on how they handle complaints against themselves," Fowler said during that meeting. "They — being those positions — have essentially been able to investigate themselves."Those positions include the fire chief, district attorney, clerk treasurer and medical director.The issue came under increased scrutiny amid fallout from a hazing investigation involving three veteran firefighters.A third-party investigator concluded that videos showing firefighters using a modified bug zapper to shock probationary firefighters depicted hazing.Three veteran firefighters — Doug Boudrias, Jordan Hutchinson and Christopher Baldwin — were fired as a result.Hutchinson and Boudrias previously told WPTV they did not consider the conduct hazing and said there was no intent to hurt anyone."It was just us in our downtime, joking around, having fun," Hutchinson said."We're all still friends," Boudrias said. "Us and the victims, there was no ill intent."The controversy has also raised questions about how complaints involving district leadership have been handled.Months before the hazing incident came to light, Baldwin and Hutchinson filed a complaint against Fire Chief Jeff Lee and then-District Attorney Kim Sabol in September 2025. District officials ultimately denied it. Baldwin and Hutchinson later filed additional complaints, including an amended complaint to investigators alleging the hazing investigation and their subsequent terminations were part of a broader pattern of retaliation. Lucie County Fire District told WPTV it is not currently in receipt of any official retaliation complaint from any party involved in this matter."That's not a good process," Fowler previously told WPTV.Sabol submitted her notice of retirement Sept. 30, just minutes after the special board meeting, effective 90 days from her notice. The District stated she will continue to provide services during that 90-day period. Lee previously acknowledged the district lacks a clear complaint process and told WPTV investigative reporter Kate Hussey that he welcomed outside scrutiny."I'm glad this board is finally taking this as a serious issue," Lee said, adding that he "welcomes any investigation from any agency."Lee also defended Sabol following her notice of retirement, calling it a "sad day" and saying she had been a "tremendous attorney for the district."Meanwhile, firefighters have been casting ballots in a union vote of no confidence in Lee."It basically says whether or not they trust and believe in him to lead this district," Fowler previously said. "So that is a huge thing if you have the majority of the men and women underneath you saying they can no longer serve under you, that's a pretty impactful message."Lee previously said he would wait for the results before commenting further on the vote."We'll see what the men and women decide," Lee said. "I came up on the labor side; I've always fought for our men and women on the line."The union is also continuing its legal fight to reinstate Boudrias, Hutchinson and Baldwin.During the Sept. 30 meeting, Fowler questioned whether the fire board itself may have the authority to bring the three firefighters back rather than waiting for the arbitration process to play out."I think we might actually," Fowler said at the time.Board members are expected to continue searching for an outside law firm to help develop the new policy before the Fire District Board meets again Oct.

President Donald Trump wants to transform Trump International Golf Club in Palm Beach County into a permanent presidential retreat for U.S. presidents and visiting foreign leaders, a proposal that would involve county-owned land and a new lodging facility paid for by the golf club.The proposal, outlined in a Sept. 3 letter from Trump International Golf Club attorney Harvey E. Oyer to Palm Beach County commissioners, calls for the golf club to partner with the county and the federal government to create what Trump has described as a Camp David-style retreat.Trump announced the idea Wednesday, saying the concept was suggested by the military and U.S. Secret Service.“They could spend the weekend there like a retreat, like sort of a Camp David retreat,” Trump said. But the location presents a significant security question. Trump International Golf Club was the site of an attempted assassination of Trump in September 2024, when he was a presidential candidate. A former FBI agent who spoke with WPTV's Michael Hoffman says the property's location and surrounding roads could make it difficult to secure as a permanent presidential retreat.The golf club's letter asks Palm Beach County to designate Trump International Golf Club as the “permanent United States Presidential Golf Course.”Under the proposal, the club would make its golf courses and amenities available to past, current and future U.S. presidents, regardless of political party, as well as visiting foreign heads of state, at the discretion of the White House.The letter says Trump International Golf Club would work with the U.S. General Services Administration and U.S. Secret Service to design an appropriate presidential lodging facility.The club says it would pay the cost of constructing the lodging facility and provide access to the facilities at no cost to the federal government.Oyer described the proposal as a gift to future presidents and the American people, noting in the letter that Trump would be out of office before the project could be completed.The letter also points to the golf club's proximity to Palm Beach International Airport, South Florida's weather and existing security measures as reasons the property would be well suited for the proposal.The club called Trump International Golf Club “one of the most secure golf courses in the world” and described it as an ideal site for a presidential retreat.The golf course sits on county-owned land that is leased long term to Trump International Golf Club, according to the club's letter.Under the proposed arrangement, Trump International Golf Club would grant the county a legal right to the land needed for the lodging facility and other structures. The county would then lease that property to the federal government, allowing the county to remain the landlord.The proposal says Palm Beach County would retain control of the property if the federal government no longer wanted to use the facility or defaulted on its lease.That means the proposal would require more than simply building a new facility at the golf course. It would create a new arrangement among the golf club, Palm Beach County and the federal government.The proposal remains in its early stages. WPTV is reaching out to Palm Beach County commissioners about whether they support providing county land for the project.The proposal's security claims come with a notable complication: Trump International Golf Club was the scene of an attempted assassination of Trump on Sept. 15, 2024.Federal prosecutors said Ryan Wesley Routh was convicted in 2025 of attempting to assassinate Trump at the golf course. He was sentenced in February 2026 to life in federal prison plus seven years.According to the Justice Department, a Secret Service agent conducting a security sweep at the golf course spotted Routh along the fence line near the sixth hole with a rifle. The agent fired at Routh, who fled before being arrested in Martin County.The incident demonstrated the security challenges posed by the golf course's perimeter, including areas adjacent to public roads.Former FBI agent Stuart Kaplan told WPTV he believes securing the property as a permanent presidential retreat would be extremely difficult.“I think it would be absolutely impossible to secure the Trump International Golf Course,” Kaplan said.Kaplan pointed to the property's location near major thoroughfares and the need to secure both the perimeter and surrounding airspace.“If you're going to secure this type of retreat, it has to be 24 hours a day, seven days a week, all day long, every single day,” Kaplan said.Kaplan also questioned the need for a permanent presidential retreat in South Florida.Trump's proposal would ultimately require coordination between Palm Beach County, Trump International Golf Club and the federal government.The club has proposed paying for the lodging facility and says the arrangement would come at no cost to the federal government. Palm Beach County, however, would play a central role because the golf course sits on county-owned land.For now, the proposal is only that — a proposal. A new ammunition manufacturing facility in Indiantown is bringing additional manufacturing activity and planned job growth to Martin County as the Treasure Coast continues to contend with unemployment rates above the statewide average.Ikonick Energetics recently expanded its operations into Indiantown, opening a primer manufacturing facility that is part of the company’s broader ammunition production operation in Martin County.Richard Rhatigan, vice president of law enforcement and government sales at Ikonick USA, said the facility has significant production capacity.“At full capacity you're looking at a billion primers per year,” said Rhatigan.Primers are a small part of the larger puzzle in manufacturing ammunition. “It is one of the four components that go into building ammunition, so the primer actually ignites the powder which is incased within the brass,” said Rhatigan.While cameras were not permitted inside the primer manufacturing facility, Ikonick provided a look at its ammunition manufacturing operation in Stuart.At the Stuart facility, workers combine the primer, brass casing and projectile to produce finished ammunition.With the addition of the Indiantown facility, the company says about 75% of each piece of ammunition is now produced in Martin County.Ikonick also plans to hire over 100 additional employees across its two locations. The positions are expected to include both entry-level and more specialized manufacturing jobs.“When you talk about American manufacturing what that really means is, the people who work in our facilities, they live in our community,” said Rhatigan.The company says the expansion reflects the potential for additional manufacturing growth in the area.“The opportunity for expansion is here and it is part of supporting the community in Martin County,” said Rhatigan.The Indiantown Chamber of Commerce said the new facility represents a significant investment in advanced manufacturing for the region.The company also says its Martin County operations will help meet ammunition needs for law enforcement training.“We can support the state and local law enforcement training needs with our ammo with our facility in Stuart and here in Indiantown,” said Rhatigan.The expansion comes as Martin, St. Lucie and Indian River counties report unemployment rates above the statewide average, according to the latest unemployment data.For Indiantown, the facility represents another addition to the community’s manufacturing sector and could provide new employment opportunities as Ikonick continues to expand its operations.Portions of this story were assisted by artificial intelligence tools and reviewed by a WPTV journalists to ensure accuracy, clarity, and adherence to editorial standards.

Isaias strengthened into the first hurricane of the Atlantic season late Wednesday as it surged towards the U.S. Gulf Coast, the National Hurricane Center said.Forecasters warned that it was on track to make landfall between the Mississippi coast and the Florida Panhandle late Friday or early Saturday and was expected to bring heavy rains and potentially flash flooding.The center of the cyclone was about 460 miles (745 kilometers) south-southwest of the Mississippi River, with maximum sustained winds around 75 mph (120 kph), according to an advisory from the Miami-based hurricane center.Isaias is developing more than four months into the Atlantic hurricane season, tying a 121-year-old record for the area’s latest-forming hurricane.According to the National Weather Service, the record dates to 1905, when the year’s first Atlantic hurricane formed on Oct. 8.The Atlantic hurricane season has been unusually quiet this year because of a strong El Niño, which disrupts storm formation over that ocean. Storm activity has been ab After Isaias (pronounced ees-ah-EE’-ahs, according to the hurricane center) became a tropical storm Wednesday in the warm waters off eastern Mexico, communities in its potential path worked quickly to prepare. Some Gulf oil wells paused production while governors in Florida and Alabama declared a state of emergency for dozens of counties.Isaias is expected to strike along a wide swath of coastline that’s very familiar with major hurricanes.One of the 20th century’s worst storms, Hurricane Camille, killed more than 250 people after hitting land near Waveland, Mississippi, in 1969. Hurricane Katrina in 2005 razed neighborhoods in Mississippi, flooded New Orleans and killed nearly 1,400 people. And Hurricane Michael leveled homes and buildings near Panama City, Florida, in 2018.Ahead of the storm, oil and gas producers shut down a significant share of offshore production in the Gulf, which accounts for almost 15% of crude pumped annually in the U.S.As of Wednesday about 25% of the oil production in the region was temporarily halted, taking about 511,000 barrels a day off the market, according to the Marine Minerals Administration. It said eight of the Gulf's 371 manned oil platforms were evacuated.With oil prices already high, the production cuts are steep enough to affect markets, though other Gulf hurricanes have caused larger disruptions, said Jim Burkhard, global head of crude oil market research for S&P Global Energy. More concerning, he said, is whether Isaias strikes as a powerful storm near refineries.“I would characterize the oil market risk as moderate, but rising,” Burkhard said in an email.In Gulf Shores, Alabama, organizers canceled the National Shrimp Festival, which had been scheduled for Thursday through the weekend. The event drew an estimated 325,000 people last year. Gulf Shores and Orange Beach issued a statement encouraging people in low-lying areas to voluntarily evacuate.Gulf Shores resident Maranie Adams gathered water and other supplies as her family moved belongings, including a hot tub motor, to higher ground.Adams said she, her husband and two adult sons planned to ride out the storm at home, roughly a half-mile from shore, sheltering indoors alongside their flock of chickens.“We’re having to get crates to bring them into the house so they don’t blow away,” Adams said. “It’s going to be noisy.”Alabama Gov. Kay Ivey issued a state of emergency for 40 counties, saying on the social platform X that, “While I hope for minimal impacts, we must take preparations seriously.”Florida Gov. Ron DeSantis declared one for 25 counties in the Panhandle and Big Bend regions. The declaration activates the state's emergency management plan for hurricanes, allowing officials to deploy disaster responders and equipment. The state also planned to deploy a Miami-based urban search and rescue task force.In Pensacola, electric utilities were pre-positioning crews to quickly repair any power outages. City officials provided sand for residents to fill sandbags to protect their homes against flooding. Reeves urged people to check on older adult neighbors and others who might need help.“Obviously no need to panic at this point,” Reeves told a news conference. “This is really about preparation.”

Florida has reported nearly 500 dengue cases this year, including more than 250 infections acquired within the state, as new University of Florida research points to residential yards in Indian River County as a key place to understand mosquito-bite exposure. The Florida Department of Health’s latest weekly surveillance report , covering Sept. 20-26, lists 252 locally acquired dengue cases and 245 travel-associated cases statewide 497 total. The locally acquired cases were reported in Hillsborough, Miami-Dade, Orange, Palm Beach, Pasco, Pinellas and Polk counties. Palm Beach County had one locally acquired case and 12 travel-associated cases; St. Lucie County had six travel-associated cases. No locally acquired dengue cases were listed for Indian River County in the report. The state’s locally acquired total includes 223 cases in Hillsborough County, the center of Florida’s outbreak. Health officials also reported 20 mosquito pools testing positive for dengue statewide. Nationally, the CDC’s most recent weekly provisional report counted 690 dengue cases among U.S. Florida accounted for 403 of those cases in the CDC reporting system, though the state’s more current surveillance report lists a higher total because reporting systems update on different schedules. Against that backdrop, researchers at UF/IFAS’ Florida Medical Entomology Laboratory in Vero Beach found a surprising mosquito pattern in suburban Indian River County. The team expected residential yards to be dominated by Aedes albopictus , also known as the Asian tiger mosquito. Instead, researchers found relatively high numbers of Aedes aegypti the yellow fever mosquito and one of the two species most closely associated with dengue transmission worldwide. The finding does not mean dengue is circulating in Indian River County . But it underscores why backyard mosquito control and personal bite prevention matter, researchers said. See also: Florida stages emergency supplies as Tropical Storm Isaias strengthens in Gulf The first-of-its-kind study paired mosquito trapping at homes with a smartphone-based Bite Diary that let residents document when and where they were bitten. Researchers collected 3,788 female mosquitoes from 78 yards. Of 70 reported bites, nearly 93% happened outdoors and nearly 74% happened at home, according to the peer-reviewed study . The number of mosquitoes trapped in a yard was not associated with the number of bites residents reported. Instead, people who spent more time outside during the evening, from 5 p.m. to 9 p.m., reported more bites. Gardening and walking dogs were among activities commonly reported when bites occurred. Dengue is spread when an infected mosquito bites a person; it does not spread directly from person to person. Symptoms can include fever, severe muscle and joint pain, rash, nausea and pain behind the eyes. People with symptoms should contact a health care provider, especially after travel to an area where dengue is common. Health officials urge residents to use EPA-registered insect repellent, wear long sleeves and pants when practical, repair window and door screens, and dump standing water from containers such as buckets, flowerpots, toys, tires and pool covers.

A 14-year-old Treasure Coast High School student is in critical condition after being struck by an SUV while walking to school Wednesday morning in Port St. Officers with the Port St. Lucie Police Department say the crash happened around 6 a.m. near the intersection of SW Port St. Lucie Boulevard and SW Squirrel Avenue. Lucie flooding problem renews focus on city's stormwater spending Officers said the teen was struck from behind by a 2002 Ford Excursion driven by a 72-year-old man. The driver initially believed he had hit a construction barrel and did not realize he had struck a person, according to investigators. Police said the driver made a U-turn at the next available location where he could safely turn around. He returned to the area, activated his hazard lights, and found the teen unconscious on the side of the road. The driver called 911 and has remained cooperative with investigators, police said. A former CIA agent convicted Tuesday of defrauding the government of $194 million reportedly used the majority of the money to acquire properties in Palm Beach and Hobe Sound. According to CBS Miami , court filings say 49-year-old David J. Rush of Virginia, a former high-ranking federal employee, directed $145 million to a holding company he controlled, and that $102 million was used to purchase four Florida properties: Two Palm Beach homes: $21.9 million and $27 million One Palm Beach parcel: $13.65 million One Hobe Sound parcel: $40 million Prosecutors allege Rush intended to eventually resell the properties for a profit. How the scheme unfolded According to the Department of Justice , Rush, of Ashburn, Virginia, pleaded guilty Tuesday, Oct. 6, to wire fraud in federal court in Alexandria, Virginia. According to prosecutors, Rush used his senior-level government position and "Top Secret" clearance to create fictitious government authorities and obtain federal money for his own benefit. Between November 2025 and March 2026, he directed approximately $145 million to a holding company established at his direction, according to court documents. The money was then used to purchase the properties. The Justice Department says Rush fraudulently obtained approximately $193.6 million in government funds. The South Florida real estate was only part of the alleged scheme. Gold bars Prosecutors say Rush separately created a fake "sensitive government activity" to justify acquiring hundreds of gold bars. On May 19, 2026, FBI agents searched Rush's Virginia home and recovered 298 gold bars, approximately $2.1 million in cash, €104,795, and numerous luxury watches. The gold had cost the government approximately $46 million, according to the Justice Department. Rush has agreed to forfeit the gold bars and cash, the Florida properties, luxury watches, and two 2026 BMW Alpina vehicles as part of his plea agreement. What's next Rush is scheduled to be sentenced Jan. He faces a maximum of 20 years in federal prison, along with possible restitution, forfeiture and a fine. The Justice Department said its investigation is continuing. The Director of National Intelligence has also requested an investigation by the Intelligence Community's inspector general. The allegations and admissions are detailed in federal court documents filed as part of Rush's guilty plea.

South Florida commuters are paying more to ride Tri-Rail after the regional rail service implemented a 10% fare increase, a move officials say is necessary as the agency works to address ongoing funding challenges.The fare hike, which took effect Oct. 1, increases one-way fares by roughly 30 cents to $1, depending on the route. Round-trip costs have increased by about $1 to $2, according to Tri-Rail.WATCH: Tri-Rail riders are paying more after a 10% fare increase.For many riders who rely on public transportation every day, the higher cost is already noticeable.The increase comes as transportation costs continue to rise for South Florida residents, with higher gasoline prices and other commuting expenses putting additional pressure on household budgets. For riders who depend on Tri-Rail to get to work, school and appointments, even modest fare increases can have a significant impact.Jordan Bruce, a regular Tri-Rail passenger, said he depends on the train to travel between West Palm Beach and Deerfield Beach."Some people don't have a choice, kind of like me right now," Bruce told WPTV.Bruce said the fare increase has been noticeable."I've definitely seen the price go up. It's very noticeable from before," he said.Without access to a car, Bruce said Tri-Rail remains a necessity."I really depend on the train. So let's say one day I don't have enough, I'm pretty much screwed that day," he said.Another rider, Daniel Presmr, said the need for reliable transportation outweighs the higher costs."At the end of the day, I gotta get home," Presmr said.Victor Garcia, director of public affairs for Tri-Rail, said the fare increase is intended to generate additional revenue, though it represents only a small portion of the agency's overall financial needs."That's one of the things that the board decided we had to do because, right, we got to look for all the means that we can to try to get more money," Garcia said.According to Garcia, the agency is still waiting for $45 million to $60 million in state funding. "That funding is essential for Tri-Rail services. It actually helps operate our train service," Garcia said.Tri-Rail officials say they continue to search for long-term funding solutions while monitoring future financial needs.Garcia said potential service reductions have been discussed if funding challenges persist."Some of the things that we had we've been considering is potentially like weekend service having to cut off," Garcia said.Despite the current fare increase, Tri-Rail officials said they do not anticipate another rate hike as they continue working to close the funding gap.Tri-Rail operates commuter rail service across Palm Beach, Broward and Miami-Dade counties, providing a transportation alternative for thousands of South Florida riders each day.Garcia said keeping those riders on Tri-Rail also helps reduce congestion on South Florida roads."This is 15,000 people a day — the equivalent of about one lane of traffic on I-95. You throw them on the roads, now you’re dealing with that much more traffic," Garcia said.As Tri-Rail works to determine how to address its funding needs, Garcia said the larger question is how much the region is willing to invest in the service."Is Tri-Rail important to the region? And if it is, at what cost? If we know it’s a valuable service, then we need to support it to keep it going," he said.This story was reported on-air by a journalist and has been converted to this platform with the assistance of AI. Lucie County Fire District has hit a snag in its effort to create a new policy for handling complaints against its own top leaders as fallout continues from a controversial hazing investigation. During a Fire District Board workshop Wednesday morning, board members had hoped to hear from outside law firms about helping draft a new complaint policy. WATCH BELOW: Fire district's new complaint policy effort stalls amid hazing fallout Instead, St. Lucie County Commissioner and Fire District Board Member Jamie Fowler said one of the law firms contacted never returned her calls, while another disclosed a potential conflict of interest. "I appreciated her honesty and forthrightness on that issue," Fowler said of the attorney during the meeting. "That being said, she did provide two references, both on the West Coast." The board discussed now reaching out to additional law firms in hopes of securing outside legal help ahead of its next meeting Oct. "I think we'd be doing ourselves an injustice if we at least we don't have a courtesy conversation with these other firms, so that we're at least prepared just in case these two firms aren't available, non-responsive," Board Member and Fort Pierce City Commissioner Curtis Johnson said. "I think we all have some sense of urgency of getting this thing closed, and and I don't want to delay any further." The effort follows a heated special board meeting Sept. 30 , when members publicly acknowledged what they described as a significant gap in district policy: There is no clear process for independently handling complaints made against some of the district's own contract employees. "Since this district's inception, we have not had a policy on how they handle complaints against themselves," Fowler said during that meeting. "They — being those positions — have essentially been able to investigate themselves." Those positions include the fire chief, district attorney, clerk treasurer and medical director. The issue came under increased scrutiny amid fallout from a hazing investigation involving three veteran firefighters. A third-party investigator concluded that videos showing firefighters using a modified bug zapper to shock probationary firefighters depicted hazing. Three veteran firefighters — Doug Boudrias, Jordan Hutchinson and Christopher Baldwin — were fired as a result. Hutchinson and Boudrias previously told WPTV they did not consider the conduct hazing and said there was no intent to hurt anyone. "It was just us in our downtime, joking around, having fun," Hutchinson said. "We're all still friends," Boudrias said. "Us and the victims, there was no ill intent." The controversy has also raised questions about how complaints involving district leadership have been handled. Months before the hazing incident came to light, Baldwin and Hutchinson filed a complaint against Fire Chief Jeff Lee and then-District Attorney Kim Sabol in September 2025. District officials ultimately denied it. Baldwin and Hutchinson later filed additional complaints, including an amended complaint to investigators alleging the hazing investigation and their subsequent terminations were part of a broader pattern of retaliation. Lucie County Fire District told WPTV it is not currently in receipt of any official retaliation complaint from any party involved in this matter. "That's not a good process," Fowler previously told WPTV. Sabol submitted her notice of retirement Sept. 30, just minutes after the special board meeting, effective 90 days from her notice. The District stated she will continue to provide services during that 90-day period. Lee previously acknowledged the district lacks a clear complaint process and told WPTV investigative reporter Kate Hussey that he welcomed outside scrutiny. "I'm glad this board is finally taking this as a serious issue," Lee said, adding that he "welcomes any investigation from any agency." Lee also defended Sabol following her notice of retirement, calling it a "sad day" and saying she had been a "tremendous attorney for the district." Meanwhile, firefighters have been casting ballots in a union vote of no confidence in Lee. "It basically says whether or not they trust and believe in him to lead this district," Fowler previously said. "So that is a huge thing if you have the majority of the men and women underneath you saying they can no longer serve under you, that's a pretty impactful message." Lee previously said he would wait for the results before commenting further on the vote. "We'll see what the men and women decide," Lee said. "I came up on the labor side; I've always fought for our men and women on the line." The union is also continuing its legal fight to reinstate Boudrias, Hutchinson and Baldwin. 30 meeting, Fowler questioned whether the fire board itself may have the authority to bring the three firefighters back rather than waiting for the arbitration process to play out. "I think we might actually," Fowler said at the time. Board members are expected to continue searching for an outside law firm to help develop the new policy before the Fire District Board meets again Oct.

Ron DeSantis announced Tuesday that Florida's intensified effort to root out fraud, waste and abuse in the state's Medicaid program has resulted in more than $1 billion in projected savings and the removal of hundreds of providers from the system.Speaking at the Healthcare District of Palm Beach County alongside Agency for Health Care Administration (AHCA) Secretary Shevaun Harris, DeSantis said the state has expanded oversight and enforcement measures to identify fraudulent billing and improper Medicaid payments.WATCH BELOW: State targets Medicaid fraud, removes hundreds of providers"We want to make sure that what is being spent is being spent well," DeSantis said. "Medicaid dollars must go to healthcare for eligible Floridians, not to people who are gaming the system."According to state officials, AHCA has conducted more than 400 provider site visits since January and increased the use of data analytics, claims monitoring and background screening to uncover suspicious activity.As part of the crackdown, the state said more than 150 fraud-related referrals have been made to the Florida Attorney General's Office over the past year, more than 250 providers have been placed on payment restrictions or had payments suspended, and more than 220 providers have been terminated from Florida Medicaid due to fraud, waste or abuse.State officials said those terminated providers accounted for more than $230 million in Medicaid billing in 2025.A major focus of the effort has been Applied Behavioral Analysis (ABA) services, commonly used to help children with autism. According to Harris, Florida Medicaid spent approximately $6.57 billion on ABA services between 2023 and 2025, nearly four times more than any other state's Medicaid program. At one point, spending was projected to grow by 30% annually.The state moved ABA services into managed care in 2025, a change officials say has improved oversight and slowed spending growth to less than 10% annually. As a result, the state now projects ABA-related expenditures at roughly $2.8 billion, more than $1 billion lower than previous forecasts."That is where we want our funding going," Harris said. "Not in the pockets of crooks."Investigators uncovered instances in which providers billed Medicaid for impossible service schedules, including claims for more than 24 hours of care in a single day and services allegedly provided continuously through weekends and holidays.To strengthen provider screening, AHCA also partnered with identity verification company SentiLink to help identify synthetic identities, suspicious ownership structures and other potential fraud indicators before providers enter the Medicaid system.In July, WPTV chief investigator Jamie Ostroff spoke with families in Palm Beach County whose access to ABA was abruptly cut off by Medicaid. They told her ABA was a lifeline for their children who were able to learn in school, communicate, use the bathroom and control tantrums thanks to the therapy.Despite the enforcement actions, DeSantis and Harris emphasized that the effort is aimed at fraudulent providers and not families who rely on Medicaid services.When Ostroff asked about concerns from families struggling to access ABA therapy, particularly in Palm Beach County, DeSantis replied, "If you have a provider that is doing some legitimate services and much fraudulent — to the extent that those services get interrupted, that's not AHCA's fault. That's that provider's fault."Harris added that managed care plans are working with affected recipients to connect them with new providers when a provider is removed from the program."If there is a parent watching and they're having any issues, they can contact the agency and we will help them ourselves or connect them with their managed care plan," Harris said.DeSantis said the Medicaid initiative is part of a broader effort to ensure taxpayer dollars are spent responsibly while maintaining Florida's fiscal position. The governor highlighted the state's recent budget reductions, debt repayment efforts and tax relief measures as examples of what he described as responsible financial management.State officials said AHCA will continue conducting site visits, monitoring claims and referring suspected fraud cases for further investigation.Ostroff asked Harris for a list of providers accused of fraud. She said she would provide what she could without jeopardizing any ongoing, potentially criminal, investigations."This is kind of just the opening salvo," DeSantis said. "I would anticipate you will see more results coming in the weeks, months and years ahead."

WPTV is taking a closer look at the military operation protecting the skies above Palm Beach County and the number of aircraft that have crossed into restricted airspace around Mar-a-Lago since President Donald Trump returned to office.According to the North American Aerospace Defense Command, or NORAD, fighter pilots have intercepted more than 60 aircraft violating Temporary Flight Restrictions around Palm Beach since January 2025.WATCH BELOW: NORAD intercepted 60+ aircraft near Mar-a-Lago since 2025"Since January of 2025, there have been over 60 intercepts that we've had to accomplish," said Major Anthony Olive, an F-15 pilot and senior operations duty officer with NORAD.When announcing the number during a media briefing held Tuesday at President Donald J. Trump International Airport, Olive's reaction was immediate."I would say so. I would say that's a lot," said Olive.The briefing comes as WPTV continues reporting on the impact the restrictions have had on communities below, including concerns about increased aircraft noise in parts of West Palm Beach and Palm Beach.In May, Palm Beach County Commissioner Gregg Weiss told WPTV the rerouted flight paths have impacted approximately 20,000 residents.The restrictions, known as TFRs, are routinely put in place when Trump is staying at Mar-a-Lago. NORAD officials told WPTV they do not create the restrictions. Instead, the restrictions are established by the Federal Aviation Administration and U.S. Secret Service, while NORAD is responsible for enforcing them."We're here to enforce the TFR and to ensure the safety of everyone, to include the individuals on the ground, the airplanes that are flying in the air as well, to make sure nobody violates the TFR, and if they do, to make sure that they're escorted safely out of the TFR as well, basically to keep the airspace clean," Olive said.NORAD officials shared a demonstration video where WPTV was given a close look at the fighter aircraft and personnel responsible for protecting the restricted airspace.Pilots assigned to the mission are not waiting on the ground for a violation to occur.When asked whether they launch after a violation or patrol routinely, one pilot's answer was simple:"Regularly patrol," the pilot replied.Officials said fighter jets are already in position before the restrictions take effect."When the TFR goes active, we're already airborne, and we're there," Olive said.If a pilot enters restricted airspace without authorization, NORAD receives notification through air traffic control."We're already airborne. They'll give us a point out; we'll find it with our radar, we'll go check it out, and basically get their intention, what they're looking to do," Olive said. "If they're just a person who doesn't know they're not supposed to be there, then we'll help escort them out of the TFR safely."Despite the number of interceptions, officials said the overwhelming majority involve pilots making mistakes, not people attempting to threaten the restricted airspace."I would say the majority, that is correct," Olive said. "There's also a majority of it where they have the proper code, they have the proper clearance, they just forget to squawk the right code, so they take off, they have a clearance, they're good to go, but they haven't punched in that clearance in their airplane, and then they do so on departure, but we still have to scramble on them because we don't know their intention because they're not squawking the right code."Asked whether any of the interceptions he has handled involved bad intentions, Olive said: "Not, I don't, no, not from my experience, no, they're just people who forget or who have not done the proper flight planning."Officials say most of the aircraft involved are not large commercial jets."The majority would be smaller Cessnas, single-engine planes for sure," said Olive.Palm Beach presents unique challenges, according to NORAD, because of the large amount of general aviation traffic in the area."I'd say Mar-a-Lago is interesting. It's different from up north," one pilot said. "There's more general aviation down here due to the nice weather, the amount of flight schools that are around here, people want to fly up and down the coast, the banner towers, so we get more general aviation traffic down here for sure."The restricted airspace itself consists of two zones."It's a temporary flight restriction," a pilot explained. "It encompasses a 10-mile ring centered at the airfield here, and then there's a 30-mile ring as well that extends beyond that. The 10-mile ring is essentially a no-fly zone."Pilots operating inside the larger ring must follow special FAA procedures."You have to be on a flight plan. You have to be squawking a discrete code, and in comms with ATC."Officials emphasized that while most violations are innocent mistakes, every response is treated seriously."We're always training to take it all the way to the conclusion that, hey, this is a person with bad intentions," Olive said. "Obviously that is a last, last resort. We're not there to hand down the judgment or the punishment; we're just there to enforce the TFR and escort them safely either to land or outside of the TFR."Any penalties are handled by the FAA once the aircraft lands."We'll safely escort them out. We'll make sure that they land. We'll monitor them until they land at their destination," Olive said. "Upon landing, they'll be notified that they have a phone number to call that'll be a phone number that leads them to the FAA and then the FAA will deal with that."Officials also stressed how closely NORAD and the FAA work together."It's imperative. We're completely intertwined," Olive said. "The FAA, they can't do their job without us. We can't do our job without them."For residents wondering why military aircraft may be overhead during presidential visits, officials say the mission comes down to safety."Any time you have the president of the United States travel anywhere, that's a very high visibility movement, and it attracts a lot of attention not only within the United States but nationally as well," one pilot said.And for pilots flying near Palm Beach, NORAD had a straightforward message:"If you're going to fly, if you're an avid flyer, check your NOTAMs before you fly, just so everybody's safe, and you're not where you're not supposed to be."When asked whether he had a message for Trump himself, the pilot smiled."Yeah, sir, we'll be above you, keeping you safe in the sky."This story was reported on-air by a journalist and has been converted to this platform with the assistance of AI. Five years have passed, but the shooting death of 20-year-old Gabriella Hanley remains unsolved. Mincey was also struck by gunfire but survived.Investigators said they determined the Kia sustained 37 bullet impacts during the shooting. WPTV is listening to concerns about what could come next following a lot of controversy surrounding a proposed Islamic center, school and daycare in Palm Beach County's Agricultural Reserve near Delray Beach.Now, WPTV's Joel Lopez is getting answers from Palm Beach County Commissioner Maria Sachs, who is asking county staff to review how some projects, including places of worship, receive approval, a move that could affect how similar projects are handled in the future.WATCH BELOW: Islamic Center controversy prompts county review of approval processThe proposed development near Lyons Road in Delray Beach has sparked public debate for months, with residents raising concerns about the project and whether projects of that nature should receive additional public scrutiny.During a recent county commission meeting, Sachs asked county staff to review portions of the county's land development code involving government facilities and places of worship."I would like board direction to staff to research and prepare a presentation on government services and places of worship uses with draft revisions to the ULDC to require their approval as a Class A conditional use approval before the BCC," Sachs said.Later in the discussion, Sachs explained why she wants staff to take another look at the current process."For many years, any government facilities or places of worship were able to get approval through DRO, which is an administrative approval through the zoning staff, and never came before the board for a hearing," Sachs said.Sachs stressed she is not proposing an immediate change to county rules, but to begin the first steps in the process."I'm asking the staff to review that and bring it back to us for a presentation and our consensus on it and what we think about it," Sachs said.The discussion comes as residents continue to question how the proposed Islamic center moved through the approval process."The issue is whether or not we are going to bring all classifications back to the board as opposed to singling out places of worship," said County attorney David Ottey.Lopez has been digging into this project and learned that the school and daycare portion of the project went before county commissioners in 2023. Sachs, then-Commissioner Sara Baxter and former Commissioner Michael Barnett voted against the proposal, but it was ultimately approved in a 4-3 vote.Commissioners Maria Marino, Marci Woodward, Gregg Weiss and then-Commissioner Mack Bernard voted in favor, allowing the project to move forward.The proposed mosque on an adjacent parcel, however, did not come before county commissioners because places of worship can currently be approved administratively by county staff.That process was the focus of several public comments during Tuesday's meeting.One resident urged county commissioners to revisit the issue."Please consider the vote that was made in 2023," said Pamela Higer-Polani, an attorney who lives in the Ag Reserve. "There is precedent that if this body, this esteemed body, reevaluates its decision, you have it within your power to open up the vote again. We are asking you to do so and reconsider."Another resident questioned whether the project has already obtained legal protections that could make changes difficult."My question is whether those approvals have become legally vested and immune from subsequent action from this commission," the resident said.The resident also asked county officials to answer several legal questions publicly, including if the projects will grandfather development rights, and if construction has not commenced and vested rights have not been established, could a moratorium or new Agricultural Reserve development restrictions adopted by the commission legally apply to this project.WPTV got answers from Sachs, who told WPTV that any changes to the approval process would not affect projects that have already received county approval."If we are able to get these amendments passed, do you think that's going to change the projects going forward?" asked Lopez."It won't change any project that's already been approved," answered Sachs.Sachs said changing the status of previously approved projects would likely require legal action. She also said she is considering a moratorium on new applications, and those in the works while county staff reviews the current process and prepares recommendations for commissioners."My message is very clear: I hear your voices, I know that you're upset, and I understand that, and actually I agree," Sachs said. "This has been an issue, and this is something we need to clear up."Not everyone speaking during public comment opposed the project.Rabbi Steve Moss urged county leaders and residents to support religious freedom regardless of faith."As faith leaders and citizens of Delray Beach, we value living in a pluralistic, respectful democracy where faith communities can live side-by-side in peace," Moss said.Moss also defended the ability of religious groups to build facilities in the community."We join communities throughout our country in standing together and defending every faith community's right to build houses of worship and community centers," Moss said.Questions were also raised by commissioners about the legal implications of changing approval standards for houses of worship.Commissioner Maria Marino asked county attorneys whether federal protections could limit what the county can do."Before we go this route, I would like clarification on what we can and can't do when it comes to a religious use or a place of worship," Marino said.County attorneys told commissioners they would return with research and legal analysis, including any federal and state legal considerations.For now, no code changes have been approved, and no action has been taken against previously approved projects. County staff is expected to review the issue and bring findings and recommendations back to commissioners for future discussion.This story was reported on-air by a journalist and has been converted to this platform with the assistance of AI. President Donald Trump is seeking to turn Trump International Golf Club in Palm Beach County into "the permanent United States Presidential Golf Course," according to a letter from the golf club's attorney to county commissioners. "Our client proposes to make the TIGC golf courses and amenities available to all past, current, and future U.S. Presidents regardless of party affiliation and all visiting foreign heads of state, at the discretion of the White House," the letter said. According to the letter, TIGC would work with the General Services Administration and United States Secret Service "to design an appropriate Presidential lodging facility."The Sept. 3 letter touted the course's proximity to the airport, South Florida weather, and in-place security — calling it "one of the most secure golf courses in the world" — as factors that made it "the ideal site for such a use""Just as Camp David, Windsor Castle, or the Elysee Palace are known worldwide, so too will the Presidential Golf Course in Palm Beach County," Attorney Harvey E. Oyer said in the letter TIGC would pay the cost of constructing the lodging facility and would provide access to the facilities "at no cost to the federal government.""This is a gift that the President would like to share with his successors, the people of America, and his fellow Palm Beach County residents," the letter said. "It should be noted that President Trump will be out of office before this proposed project could be completed so this is a gift to his successors."The club is located on county-owned land and is leased long term to the club, according to the letter. The letter proposes an agreement in which TIGC "grants the County a legal right" to the land for the lodging and other structures, with the county entering into a lease agreement with the federal government "so that the County controls the property as landlord."The letter said the county would continue to control the asset if the federal government defaulted or no longer wanted to use the premises. A 14-year-old Treasure Coast High School student is in critical condition after being struck by an SUV while walking to school Wednesday morning in Port St. Officers with the Port St. Lucie Police Department say the crash happened around 6 a.m. near the intersection of SW Port St. Lucie Boulevard and SW Squirrel Avenue. PSLPD says the freshman was walking northbound along Port St. Lucie Boulevard near the edge of the roadway, alongside construction barrels in the area. The incident occurred on National Walk, Bike, & Roll to School Day . A former CIA agent convicted Tuesday of defrauding the government of $194 million reportedly used the majority of the money to acquire properties in Palm Beach and Hobe Sound. According to CBS Miami , court filings say 49-year-old David J. Rush of Virginia, a former high-ranking federal employee, directed $145 million to a holding company he controlled, and that $102 million was used to purchase four Florida properties: Two Palm Beach homes: $21.9 million and $27 million One Palm Beach parcel: $13.65 million One Hobe Sound parcel: $40 million Prosecutors allege Rush intended to eventually resell the properties for a profit. How the scheme unfolded According to the Department of Justice , Rush, of Ashburn, Virginia, pleaded guilty Tuesday, Oct. 6, to wire fraud in federal court in Alexandria, Virginia. According to prosecutors, Rush used his senior-level government position and "Top Secret" clearance to create fictitious government authorities and obtain federal money for his own benefit. Between November 2025 and March 2026, he directed approximately $145 million to a holding company established at his direction, according to court documents. The money was then used to purchase the properties. The Justice Department says Rush fraudulently obtained approximately $193.6 million in government funds. The South Florida real estate was only part of the alleged scheme. Gold bars Prosecutors say Rush separately created a fake "sensitive government activity" to justify acquiring hundreds of gold bars. On May 19, 2026, FBI agents searched Rush's Virginia home and recovered 298 gold bars, approximately $2.1 million in cash, €104,795, and numerous luxury watches. The gold had cost the government approximately $46 million, according to the Justice Department. Rush has agreed to forfeit the gold bars and cash, the Florida properties, luxury watches, and two 2026 BMW Alpina vehicles as part of his plea agreement. What's next Rush is scheduled to be sentenced Jan. He faces a maximum of 20 years in federal prison, along with possible restitution, forfeiture and a fine. The Justice Department said its investigation is continuing. The Director of National Intelligence has also requested an investigation by the Intelligence Community's inspector general. The allegations and admissions are detailed in federal court documents filed as part of Rush's guilty plea.

Lucie County Fire District has hit a snag in its effort to create a new policy for handling complaints against its own top leaders as fallout continues from a controversial hazing investigation. During a Fire District Board workshop Wednesday morning, board members had hoped to hear from outside law firms about helping draft a new complaint policy.Instead, St. Lucie County Commissioner and Fire District Board Member Jamie Fowler said one of the law firms contacted never returned her calls, while another disclosed a potential conflict of interest."I appreciated her honesty and forthrightness on that issue," Fowler said of the attorney during the meeting. "That being said, she did provide two references, both on the West Coast." The board discussed now reaching out to additional law firms in hopes of securing outside legal help ahead of its next meeting Oct. 21."I think we'd be doing ourselves an injustice if we at least we don't have a courtesy conversation with these other firms, so that we're at least prepared just in case these two firms aren't available, non-responsive," Board Member and Fort Pierce City Commissioner Curtis Johnson said. "I think we all have some sense of urgency of getting this thing closed, and and I don't want to delay any further." The effort follows a heated special board meeting Sept. 30, when members publicly acknowledged what they described as a significant gap in district policy: There is no clear process for independently handling complaints made against some of the district's own contract employees. "Since this district's inception, we have not had a policy on how they handle complaints against themselves," Fowler said during that meeting. "They — being those positions — have essentially been able to investigate themselves."Those positions include the fire chief, district attorney, clerk treasurer and medical director.The issue came under increased scrutiny amid fallout from a hazing investigation involving three veteran firefighters.A third-party investigator concluded that videos showing firefighters using a modified bug zapper to shock probationary firefighters depicted hazing.Three veteran firefighters — Doug Boudrias, Jordan Hutchinson and Christopher Baldwin — were fired as a result.Hutchinson and Boudrias previously told WPTV they did not consider the conduct hazing and said there was no intent to hurt anyone."It was just us in our downtime, joking around, having fun," Hutchinson said."We're all still friends," Boudrias said. "Us and the victims, there was no ill intent."The controversy has also raised questions about how complaints involving district leadership have been handled.Months before the hazing incident came to light, Baldwin and Hutchinson filed a complaint against Fire Chief Jeff Lee and then-District Attorney Kim Sabol in September 2025. District officials ultimately denied it. Baldwin and Hutchinson later filed additional complaints, including an amended complaint to investigators alleging the hazing investigation and their subsequent terminations were part of a broader pattern of retaliation. Lucie County Fire District told WPTV it is not currently in receipt of any official retaliation complaint from any party involved in this matter."That's not a good process," Fowler previously told WPTV.Sabol submitted her notice of retirement Sept. 30, just minutes after the special board meeting, effective 90 days from her notice. The District stated she will continue to provide services during that 90-day period. Lee previously acknowledged the district lacks a clear complaint process and told WPTV investigative reporter Kate Hussey that he welcomed outside scrutiny."I'm glad this board is finally taking this as a serious issue," Lee said, adding that he "welcomes any investigation from any agency."Lee also defended Sabol following her notice of retirement, calling it a "sad day" and saying she had been a "tremendous attorney for the district."Meanwhile, firefighters have been casting ballots in a union vote of no confidence in Lee."It basically says whether or not they trust and believe in him to lead this district," Fowler previously said. "So that is a huge thing if you have the majority of the men and women underneath you saying they can no longer serve under you, that's a pretty impactful message."Lee previously said he would wait for the results before commenting further on the vote."We'll see what the men and women decide," Lee said. "I came up on the labor side; I've always fought for our men and women on the line."The union is also continuing its legal fight to reinstate Boudrias, Hutchinson and Baldwin.During the Sept. 30 meeting, Fowler questioned whether the fire board itself may have the authority to bring the three firefighters back rather than waiting for the arbitration process to play out."I think we might actually," Fowler said at the time.Board members are expected to continue searching for an outside law firm to help develop the new policy before the Fire District Board meets again Oct.

After viewer videos showed water covering roads and vehicles struggling through several Port St. Lucie neighborhoods, the city's own budget documents show where it plans to put money to reduce flooding. The city says that work is still in its early stages. Lucie has received about 4 inches of rain over the past 48 hours , and another 2 to 4 inches could fall by the end of the week. City crews are monitoring conditions as water recedes, and officials are reminding drivers and pedestrians to stay out of flooded roads because it is hard to tell how deep the water is. Frank Camarda, who has lived in the area for more than 20 years near SW California Boulevard and SW Plantation Terrace, said Tuesday night's flooding turned his street into a detour. He said drivers piled in while trying to bypass flooded roads, and he believes Savona Boulevard was also underwater. Camarda said he has not seen flooding on his own street before, but he has watched water pool near Oak Hammock a couple of times. He also said city crews used to clean the swale in front of his home about once a month, and he believes that has stopped. "I've been waiting for these guys to clean up. I haven't seen them," Camarda said. City spokesperson Scott Samples said the rain came in too fast for the system to keep up. He said the canals, swales and retention ponds were already full, which makes it harder for water to move. At one location the city monitored, he said, about two feet of water arrived in roughly 30 minutes. Samples said the water had receded from most roadways by about 8:30 p.m. Tuesday, and he described that as the stormwater system doing what it is designed to do. He said Public Works checks drainage before heavy rain and is working to keep swales, drains and canals clear, but there is only so much crews can do when that much water arrives at once. See also: Florida stages emergency supplies as Tropical Storm Isaias strengthens in Gulf Samples said residents who cannot get home should find another place to stay if they can, and that the city is working closely with police on safety. The city's proposed capital plan for fiscal years 2027 through 2031, submitted to City Council on April 13, includes the Oak Hammock Watershed Improvement Project. It would add new retention ponds, pump systems and upgraded valves. The plan shows $8 million in each of the first two years and $7 million in each of the next two, for $30 million in all, paid for through stormwater bond financing. Samples said the city has just begun early data analysis for Oak Hammock, which he placed in the California Boulevard area. He said that work will guide the design of a multi-phase project that could include new retention ponds, pumps for canals, or even raising the roadway at California and Savona boulevards so water drains off. He said it is hard to predict when residents will see construction or a finished project, because the city must first gather data, settle on a design and line up funding. He called Oak Hammock a priority for the city. "It will move as fast as it possibly can," Samples said. According to the city, the project covers a large area east of Interstate 95, north of the C-23 Canal and Port St. Lucie Boulevard, and west of Florida's Turnpike. The money would come partly from a $6 increase in the annual stormwater assessment, which the city's website lists as proposed. That would raise the assessment from $183 to $189. The city says the assessment helps pay for five projects aimed at flooding and water flow: Oak Hammock, the Elkcam Basin, the E-8 Canal, Hogpen Slough, and faster replacement of swales and culverts. The city says its drainage system includes about 200 miles of canals, 1,200 miles of swales, and more than 6,000 culverts. It also notes that maintaining swales and driveway culverts, from the edge of the pavement to the property line, is the property owner's responsibility under city code.

A 14-year-old Treasure Coast High School student is in critical condition after being struck by a vehicle while walking to school Wednesday morning, according to the Port St. Lucie Police Department.Police said the crash happened around 6 a.m. near the intersection of Southwest Port St. Lucie Boulevard and Southwest Squirrel Avenue.WATCH BELOW: Student critically injured after being struck by SUVInvestigators said the freshman was walking northbound along Port St. Lucie Boulevard on his way to school and was near the edge of the roadway alongside construction barrels in the area when he was struck from behind by a 2002 Ford Excursion driven by a 72-year-old man.According to police, the driver initially believed he had hit a construction barrel and did not realize he had struck a person. Authorities said the driver later made a U-turn at the next location where it was safe to do so and returned to the scene.Once back in the area, the driver activated his hazard lights and found the teen unconscious on the side of the roadway. Police said he immediately called 911 and has remained cooperative throughout the investigation.The student suffered life-threatening injuries and remains hospitalized in critical condition, according to police.Investigators said there were no apparent signs of impairment involving the driver, though they noted the assessment is preliminary and could change as the investigation continues.The crash remains under investigation.Police are asking anyone who witnessed the incident or who may have dash camera, surveillance or other video footage from the area around the time of the crash to come forward.Anyone with information is asked to contact the Port St. Lucie Police Department at 772-871-5000.

Buc-ee’s may be best known for its massive travel centers, barbecue sandwiches and loyal fan base, but on the Treasure Coast, county leaders say the proposed development could signal something even bigger: a wave of growth along the Indrio Road corridor in northern St. After years of planning and review, the proposed Buc-ee’s at Interstate 95 and Indrio Road has completed the county’s planning process, bringing the long-discussed project one step closer to reality. The proposed 76,000-square-foot travel center would feature approximately 120 fuel pumps and could become the largest Buc-ee’s location in Florida. Buc-ee’s Nearing Construction Phase According to St. Lucie County Planning and Development Services Director Benjamin Balcer, the project has cleared its local planning hurdles. "They are completely 100% finished with the planning process," Balcer said. "Our board will not see this again." Balcer said the company is now awaiting final approvals from the Florida Department of Transportation and the Florida Department of Environmental Protection before construction can begin. "As far as the county is concerned, their building permit and their site development permit is pretty much at the tail end and ready to go," Balcer said. "It's really just pulling the trigger on Buc-ee's end to start the process." Buc-ee's has previously targeted a 2028 opening date. Development Interest Growing Along Indrio Road While the travel center itself would bring jobs and tax revenue, county officials say its presence also shines a spotlight on a corridor already attracting significant development interest. For now, much of the area remains undeveloped, with cattle grazing across wide stretches of rural land. But Balcer said developers are increasingly looking at opportunities along Indrio Road. "It's kind of an untapped resource," he said. "At the moment, we're seeing a lot of development interest, whether that's pre-application meetings, developers coming in and talking about concept plans, or actual formal applications." Balcer stopped short of calling Buc-ee's the direct catalyst for that interest, but acknowledged that a major national company can influence future investment decisions. "I don't know if Buc-ee's is a catalyst that actually drives development," he said. "But whenever you have a large national commercial entity like Buc-ee's, it does move the needle whenever people see that type of investment." Why the Corridor Is Attracting Attention The area has benefited from recent road and utility improvements, making it increasingly attractive for future residential and commercial projects. County officials say they are already seeing proposals emerge throughout the area. "But all through that Indrio Road corridor, we do see more retail, mixed-use residential projects that are starting to come in and gain traction," Balcer said. Several large developments are either proposed or moving through the review process near the future Buc-ee's site. The proposed Club at Indrio Creek , located south of Indrio Road, could bring hundreds of new homes to the area. Another proposal, Indrio Town Center , would transform approximately 85 acres near Indrio Road and Emerson Avenue into a mixed-use development featuring retail, office space and residential uses. Perhaps the most controversial proposal was Indrio Groves , a development planned near Spanish Lakes Fairways that could add more than 3,000 homes to the area. The size of that proposal has raised concerns among nearby residents who worry about traffic and infrastructure demands. The discussion was tabled over the summer. Residents Voice Infrastructure Concerns But as development proposals continue to stack up, some residents worry infrastructure isn't keeping pace. "That's what people are concerned about," said Jeff Bourassa, president of the Spanish Lakes Fairways Homeowners Association. If they put another 3,000 homes, we're in trouble." Bourassa said residents are worried local roads are not equipped to handle the level of growth being proposed. They're cowpaths," Bourassa said. "There's nothing that was put in for infrastructure." County officials say they understand those concerns. "People are concerned," Balcer said. "Traffic impacts, changing their lifestyle. This is a historical agricultural kind of community." Looking Ahead Whether Buc-ee's ultimately becomes a transformational project remains to be seen. County leaders say the larger story is what comes next for the surrounding area. If Buc-ee's opens and several proposed developments move forward, the character of the Indrio Road corridor could change dramatically over the next decade. "If Buc-ee's does come online, and the projects that are in the pipeline do develop," Balcer said, "you'll see a big difference in the Indrio Road corridor."

The city of Westlake is considering installing speed enforcement cameras in a school zone near Seminole Ridge High School, a proposal that city leaders say would improve student safety.The topic is expected to come before the Westlake City Council during its meeting Tuesday at 6 p.m., as officials discuss a potential agreement with RedSpeed, the company that would provide the camera technology.WATCH BELOW: Westlake considers speed cameras near Seminole Ridge HighAccording to Westlake City Manager Howard Brown Jr., the city has been discussing school zone speed cameras for about a year. A speed zone study conducted by the city found a need for additional enforcement in the area surrounding Seminole Ridge High School."Seminole Ridge High School will be the target area," Brown said.City officials say the cameras would serve as an additional tool to address speeding drivers in the school zone."Some people are busy, and they are not paying attention that they are going through a school zone," Brown said.Brown, who has a young child at home, said protecting children is a top priority."I have a little one at home. That's an area where we really want to protect our children and provide law enforcement with additional tools," he said.Under the proposal, drivers caught traveling more than 10 mph over the posted speed limit on Seminole Pratt Whitney Road within the school zone would face a $100 citation."We are trying to break some of those bad driving habits," Brown said.Not everyone is convinced the cameras are necessary.Westlake resident Nicole Haley said she worries speed cameras could worsen existing traffic congestion."I think it would back up traffic even more than it already is," Haley said.Instead of adding cameras, Haley believes roadway improvements may be a better solution."I think integrating a roundabout like the one they have on Stribling would be better," she said.If approved, the cameras could be operational before the end of the year. The city says there would also be a 30-day warning period before citations are issued.At this time, Seminole Ridge High School is the only school in the city being considered for speed camera enforcement.The speed camera discussion is one of several items on Tuesday night's council agenda. City officials have also indicated they will not move forward with license plate reader technology at this time. The meeting will be held at the Lodge at 6 p.m.

By: Emma Romano Posted and last updated WEST PALM BEACH, Fla. — The scene has been cleared after West Palm Beach police investigated a suspicious package at the Palm Beach County courthouse Tuesday. The Palm Beach County Sheriff’s Office initially said the West Palm Beach Police Department was investigating a suspicious object at the courthouse.
