A woman fled for her life after she was attacked and later shot at as she drove away in her vehicle. According to the Fort Pierce Police Department , on Saturday, October 3, officers responded to South Sixth Street at 7:12 a.m. after the victim called police and reported that someone was shooting at her. The investigation revealed the victim went to South Sixth Street to speak with her boyfriend about their relationship. Upon her arrival, several people ran out of the residence and began attacking her. See also: Opponents, supporters clash over Palm Beach County Israel Bonds investments Police said the victim was able to escape, get into her vehicle, and drive away. As she fled, one of the suspects grabbed a gun from the property and began shooting at her, according to police. A second person was arrested for allegedly driving the shooter away from the scene. The two suspects arrested were identified as Keibin Lopez-Godoy, 18, and Kailee Yurubi, 18. Godoy faces a charge of first-degree attempted homicide. Yurubi faces a charge of accessory after the fact.

The city of Westlake is moving forward with plans to install school zone speed cameras at Seminole Ridge High School after city council members unanimously approved the measure during a final hearing.WPTV reporter Christy Waite has been tracking speed cameras that are popping up across western Palm Beach County.WATCH BELOW: Westlake approves school zone speed cameras Westlake City Council voted 5-0 to authorize the cameras along Seminole Pratt Whitney Road, making Seminole Ridge High School the first and only school in the city to have the technology at this time.City Manager Howard Brown Jr. said the cameras are being implemented to improve safety around students and provide law enforcement with another tool to enforce speed limits in school zones.According to city leaders, a recent speed zone study found a need for additional enforcement in the area, helping drive the decision to move forward with the program."That's an area where we really want to protect our children and provide law enforcement with additional tools," Brown said.The city says children's safety is the top priority. They hope the cameras will encourage drivers to slow down and pay closer attention when traveling through active school zones."We are just trying to correct behavior in those school zones because people are busy, they are not paying attention that they are even going through a school zone," Brown said.Under the program, drivers caught traveling more than 10 mph over the posted speed limit in the school zone will receive a $100 citation.The city will partner with RedLine to operate the speed camera system.City leaders said there was no public comment submitted either for or against the cameras during the hearing. The city also says they are discussing the program and have included topics such as safety, security and privacy.Westlake expects the cameras to be installed by the end of the year. Once activated, the city plans to offer a 30-day warning period before citations are issued to drivers.

Florida has reported nearly 500 dengue cases this year, including more than 250 infections acquired within the state, as new University of Florida research points to residential yards in Indian River County as a key place to understand mosquito-bite exposure. The Florida Department of Health’s latest weekly surveillance report , covering Sept. 20-26, lists 252 locally acquired dengue cases and 245 travel-associated cases statewide 497 total. The locally acquired cases were reported in Hillsborough, Miami-Dade, Orange, Palm Beach, Pasco, Pinellas and Polk counties. Palm Beach County had one locally acquired case and 12 travel-associated cases; St. Lucie County had six travel-associated cases. No locally acquired dengue cases were listed for Indian River County in the report. The state’s locally acquired total includes 223 cases in Hillsborough County, the center of Florida’s outbreak. Health officials also reported 20 mosquito pools testing positive for dengue statewide. Nationally, the CDC’s most recent weekly provisional report counted 690 dengue cases among U.S. Florida accounted for 403 of those cases in the CDC reporting system, though the state’s more current surveillance report lists a higher total because reporting systems update on different schedules. Against that backdrop, researchers at UF/IFAS’ Florida Medical Entomology Laboratory in Vero Beach found a surprising mosquito pattern in suburban Indian River County. The team expected residential yards to be dominated by Aedes albopictus , also known as the Asian tiger mosquito. Instead, researchers found relatively high numbers of Aedes aegypti the yellow fever mosquito and one of the two species most closely associated with dengue transmission worldwide. The finding does not mean dengue is circulating in Indian River County . But it underscores why backyard mosquito control and personal bite prevention matter, researchers said. See also: Florida stages emergency supplies as Tropical Storm Isaias strengthens in Gulf The first-of-its-kind study paired mosquito trapping at homes with a smartphone-based Bite Diary that let residents document when and where they were bitten. Researchers collected 3,788 female mosquitoes from 78 yards. Of 70 reported bites, nearly 93% happened outdoors and nearly 74% happened at home, according to the peer-reviewed study . The number of mosquitoes trapped in a yard was not associated with the number of bites residents reported. Instead, people who spent more time outside during the evening, from 5 p.m. to 9 p.m., reported more bites. Gardening and walking dogs were among activities commonly reported when bites occurred. Dengue is spread when an infected mosquito bites a person; it does not spread directly from person to person. Symptoms can include fever, severe muscle and joint pain, rash, nausea and pain behind the eyes. People with symptoms should contact a health care provider, especially after travel to an area where dengue is common. Health officials urge residents to use EPA-registered insect repellent, wear long sleeves and pants when practical, repair window and door screens, and dump standing water from containers such as buckets, flowerpots, toys, tires and pool covers.

Governor Ron DeSantis was in Indian River County on Monday to celebrate the completion of a new I-95 interchange at Oslo Road, a $100 million project state officials say will improve traffic flow, emergency response times and freight movement. The interchange, which opened about a year ahead of schedule, marks the first new I-95 interchange built in Indian River County in nearly 50 years. DeSantis said the project will provide a new direct connection to I-95 while easing congestion at nearby interchanges at Indrio Road and State Road 60. “This is going to bring a new critical connection to I-95 for a part of the state that has changed quite a bit,” DeSantis said. According to the governor, drivers using Oslo Road to access I-95 can expect travel times to be cut roughly in half. State transportation officials also project traffic along the corridor will continue growing through 2045. DeSantis said the project is expected to have significant public safety benefits as well. The state estimates emergency response times in the area could be reduced by as much as 56%, allowing first responders to reach crashes and other emergencies more quickly. “This will ultimately save some lives because time is of the essence in some of these situations,” DeSantis said. Florida Department of Transportation Secretary Jared Perdue said improved access to I-95 for first responders was one of the project’s most important features. “Every single second counts when it comes to saving lives, and this is going to reduce the time it takes for first responders to get to incidents substantially,” Perdue said. The new interchange is also expected to improve freight movement for businesses in southern Indian River County by providing a more direct route to the interstate for trucks and commercial traffic. State officials said the project was accelerated through Florida’s Moving Florida Forward initiative, a transportation funding program launched by the DeSantis administration to speed up major road projects across the state. Perdue said FDOT worked with contractors through a “voluntary acceleration” program that rewarded construction teams for finding ways to complete projects more quickly. As a result, the Oslo Road interchange was finished approximately 400 days ahead of schedule. In addition to transportation improvements, FDOT acquired land near the interchange to establish a dedicated gopher tortoise habitat. State officials said the site will serve as the only relocation area of its kind in Southeast Florida, allowing protected tortoises to be moved while infrastructure projects continue. The Oslo Road interchange is part of nearly $1 billion in planned transportation investments across Florida’s Treasure Coast region. “This interchange sets a clear example of how Florida delivers infrastructure that improves quality of life today while building more capacity for the future,” DeSantis said.

After viewer videos showed water covering roads and vehicles struggling through several Port St. Lucie neighborhoods, the city's own budget documents show where it plans to put money to reduce flooding. The city says that work is still in its early stages. Lucie has received about 4 inches of rain over the past 48 hours , and another 2 to 4 inches could fall by the end of the week. City crews are monitoring conditions as water recedes, and officials are reminding drivers and pedestrians to stay out of flooded roads because it is hard to tell how deep the water is. Frank Camarda, who has lived in the area for more than 20 years near SW California Boulevard and SW Plantation Terrace, said Tuesday night's flooding turned his street into a detour. He said drivers piled in while trying to bypass flooded roads, and he believes Savona Boulevard was also underwater. Camarda said he has not seen flooding on his own street before, but he has watched water pool near Oak Hammock a couple of times. He also said city crews used to clean the swale in front of his home about once a month, and he believes that has stopped. "I've been waiting for these guys to clean up. I haven't seen them," Camarda said. City spokesperson Scott Samples said the rain came in too fast for the system to keep up. He said the canals, swales and retention ponds were already full, which makes it harder for water to move. At one location the city monitored, he said, about two feet of water arrived in roughly 30 minutes. Samples said the water had receded from most roadways by about 8:30 p.m. Tuesday, and he described that as the stormwater system doing what it is designed to do. He said Public Works checks drainage before heavy rain and is working to keep swales, drains and canals clear, but there is only so much crews can do when that much water arrives at once. See also: Florida stages emergency supplies as Tropical Storm Isaias strengthens in Gulf Samples said residents who cannot get home should find another place to stay if they can, and that the city is working closely with police on safety. The city's proposed capital plan for fiscal years 2027 through 2031, submitted to City Council on April 13, includes the Oak Hammock Watershed Improvement Project. It would add new retention ponds, pump systems and upgraded valves. The plan shows $8 million in each of the first two years and $7 million in each of the next two, for $30 million in all, paid for through stormwater bond financing. Samples said the city has just begun early data analysis for Oak Hammock, which he placed in the California Boulevard area. He said that work will guide the design of a multi-phase project that could include new retention ponds, pumps for canals, or even raising the roadway at California and Savona boulevards so water drains off. He said it is hard to predict when residents will see construction or a finished project, because the city must first gather data, settle on a design and line up funding. He called Oak Hammock a priority for the city. "It will move as fast as it possibly can," Samples said. According to the city, the project covers a large area east of Interstate 95, north of the C-23 Canal and Port St. Lucie Boulevard, and west of Florida's Turnpike. The money would come partly from a $6 increase in the annual stormwater assessment, which the city's website lists as proposed. That would raise the assessment from $183 to $189. The city says the assessment helps pay for five projects aimed at flooding and water flow: Oak Hammock, the Elkcam Basin, the E-8 Canal, Hogpen Slough, and faster replacement of swales and culverts. The city says its drainage system includes about 200 miles of canals, 1,200 miles of swales, and more than 6,000 culverts. It also notes that maintaining swales and driveway culverts, from the edge of the pavement to the property line, is the property owner's responsibility under city code.

It takes an army of 38 staff members to create all the video, replays and entertainment fans enjoy at Florida Panthers games at Amerant Bank Arena.WPTV Florida Panthers anchor and Panthers 360 Mike Trim went one-on-one with Mike Masino, vice president of entertainment and operations, who gave Trim a tour of the newly renovated control room and front-of-house operations. Masino compared the director's role to one familiar to those in television news."Mark, who's TDing, and you've got Scott who is our director. They're locked in all game, but it's what they do, and it's what they love to do," Masino said.The first pre-season game for the Panthers also marked a significant technology upgrade for the arena."So tonight's actually a milestone for us, moving from a baseband video infrastructure where you're hard patching cables to a networked routable video infrastructure," Masino said."All of our cabling throughout the building was replaced to bring us to the highest quality broadcast infrastructure that sports are doing these days," Masino said.This story was reported on-air by a journalist and has been converted to this platform with the assistance of AI. After months of talking to viewers and responding to emails, WPTV reporter Matt Sczesny and WPTV anchor Hollani Davis are hearing from experts on the ballot referendum and diving into money issues that matter to you.WATCH: WPTV Let's Hear It: Property Tax Town Hall on Amendment 3 (Part 1)WPTV hosted its Property Tax Town Hall at Palm Beach State College, Lake Worth Campus, on Tuesday, inside the Public Safety Conference Center. WPTV is working to get answers to questions residents raised about a controversial Islamic center approved in Palm Beach County's Agricultural Reserve. After Friday's heated public meeting, many viewers reached out asking who is behind the project, how it was approved and what happens next.The proposed development would be located off Lyons Road and 152nd Place South in Delray Beach, on what is currently a dirt road and grassy field. The project includes a mosque, school and daycare.WATCH BELOW: Who's behind the Ag Reserve Islamic Center? Residents seek answersDuring Friday's meeting, several residents questioned who is involved with the project and where funding is coming from. One speaker told county leaders, "If credible documented evidence exists connecting specific individuals or organizations associated with this project to extremist organizations, residents deserve to know what authorities have investigated and determined. Who controls this organization? Who is financing this project? Where is the money coming from? And what security review has been conducted?"The project also drew protesters outside the meeting."Where are they from, who are they, were they vetted? Build it and they shall come," said a woman pushing back against the Islamic center, calling the developments part of a "Muslim takeover."Sachs pushed through the feedback from the crowd and said places of worship of all faiths go through a review process."Yes, an investigation was made into every house of worship, whether it is Christian, Jewish, Muslim, Hindu and we do have Hindu temples if anybody here is interested," Sachs said. there's an investigation made as to who owns it, who's going to run it, and whether or not they're going to abide by the rules of the county and the United States Constitution."Inside the meeting, a woman who identified herself as a Latina Muslim convert questioned the nature of the concerns being raised. Her comments drew a strong reaction from the crowd as some wanted to focus on traffic impacts and nearly caused the meeting to be shut down."I want to be safer again; will this development help my community to be safe? My mosque welcomes people of other faith to ask questions," she said.Questions about who is behind the project have remained a focal point for residents.The project consists of a 15-acre Islamic center featuring 5 acres for the mosque and 10 for the school and daycare along Lyons Road.County documents reviewed by WPTV appear to identify the applicant as the Islamic Center School of west Delray Beach. The organization also appears to own an additional 5 acres on the north side of 152nd Place South. Plans for that portion are uncertain.Seeking more context on the concerns raised at the meeting, WPTV spoke with former Rabbi David Steinhardt, who retired about 16 months ago after serving for more than 30 years as senior rabbi at B'nai Torah Congregation in Boca Raton. He also served as co-president of the Boca Raton Interfaith Clergy Association.When asked what his message would be to residents expressing concern about a mosque coming into the area and the impacts on the Jewish community, Steinhardt said, "No one's trying to take their place. The issue is how do we live together."He said fear often grows when people lack familiarity with one another."I think that when you don't know people, then you suspect people, and when you're suspicious, you fear people. And so when you fear people, then you don't necessarily act rationally. This is not a new group of people. These are people that have been in town for decades. We have worked together at the hospitals, in the courts, in business, in all different arenas of public uh public uh society. And in our community, we have shared in various efforts to bring peace to the world. And so, I know that community. I have been in conversation with that community and its leadership for decades."Steinhardt said he knows the president of the mosque approved for the site and said they are members of the Islamic Center of Boca Raton seeking a second mosque to provide better access for members."I don't know if it's a need, if it's a desire; that should be enough. Is there a need for the number of synagogues we have in our Community? I'm not sure, but there's a desire for more, and we all have the right to do that."WPTV also learned the project is represented by Brian Seymour with the Gunster law firm. A request for additional details has been sent, and WPTV is working to hear back.Another issue repeatedly raised Friday involved notification requirements. Several residents questioned why people living more than 500 feet from the site were not notified.The county's Planning and Zoning Division told WPTV that only property owners within 500 feet were notified because the project is located within the U/S, AGR and Glades tiers. Had the project been located within the Exurban and Rural tiers, a 1,000-foot notification radius would have applied.To see which growth tier a property falls under, open the Palm Beach County GIS Map Viewer. Once you're in the map, click the menu icon (the "pancake" in the upper corner), then use the "Search Layers" tool and type in "Managed Growth Tier System." That layer will show all of the county's designated growth tiers and allow you to see exactly where a property is located within the system.Palm Beach County Commissioner Maria Sachs is planning a second public meeting focused on projects in the Agricultural Reserve following feedback from Friday's meeting. Her staff told WPTV details are still being worked out.Sachs also told WPTV she is working with county staff to find an appropriate date to propose changes to the Unified Land Development Code regarding the Development Review Officer process for places of worship and governmental entities.The issue has become a focal point because several projects residents protested were approved through an administrative review process that has existed for years and allows certain government entities and houses of worship to move forward without direct approval from county commissioners."I think for the most part people had their voices heard, but what they said is they want to have a voice in what comes to development in this county. I respect that I hear them," Sachs said Friday.While the mosque was approved through the administrative process, the proposal for an Islamic school and daycare next door did require a vote by county commissioners.WPTV reviewed records from a 2023 county meeting and learned the project was approved by a 4-3 vote.Sachs, former Commissioner Michael Barnett and then-Commissioner Sara Baxter voted against the proposal, citing concerns that not enough input from residents had been collected.Vice Mayor Marci Woodward, Commissioner Maria Marino, Commissioner Gregg Weiss and former Commissioner Mack Bernard voted in favor of the project.This story was reported on-air by a journalist and has been converted to this platform with the assistance of AI. Our editorial team verifies all reporting on all platforms for fairness and accuracy.

No arrests have been made in the shooting death of a 17-year-old at a teen meetup near Garcia’s Boat Ramp in Indian River County, with a self-defense claim expected in the case, Indian River County Sheriff Eric Flowers announced Monday. “We got kids out here losing their lives chasing likes and shares on social media,” Flowers said. The shooting occurred late Friday night when approximately 100 teens, ranging in age from 14 to 19, gathered at Garcia’s Boat Ramp in the 3700 block of County Road 512, the sheriff said. Deputies had broken up a similar group earlier that evening before the crowd moved to the boat ramp. “The 17-year-old, and a group of his friends, are approaching a truck, and there are two people, both 18 years old, inside of that truck. The 17-year-old opens the door, and he starts to punch,” Flowers said. “He’s going to punch on the people that are inside of that truck. That shot is the shot that ultimately killed 17-year-old in this case.” The teen’s friends drove him away from the scene, east on County Road 512, while calling 911 and a dispatcher told them to stop at Fellsmere City Hall, where emergency crews performed CPR, the sheriff said. He was taken to Sebastian River Medical Center and later flown to Holmes Regional Medical Center in Melbourne, where he died from his injuries. The two individuals in the truck were identified using the sheriff’s office’s Flock technology, the sheriff said. Flowers said both have been cooperative with investigators, surrendering the weapon used in the shooting and the truck. Additional individuals involved in the incident have also been identified through Flock, though some remain unidentified. Investigators also recovered other weapons from the vehicle in which the 17-year-old was transported from the scene. Flowers said a warrant will be submitted in the case, but it will be up to the state to determine whether charges are filed. “There have been no arrests on this case at this time, because the preliminary investigation shows that the 17-year-old was opening the door to attempt to fight with the two that were inside of the vehicle. They had a history of fighting,” Flowers said. “Self defense plays a part in these, and when these kids go out and videotape these fights, and now guns are involved, there’s going to be more of this.” Names of those involved are not being released as the investigation continues, the sheriff said. Investigators believe at least four fights occurred at the boat ramp on the night of the shooting. Multiple shell casings and rounds were recovered from the scene. During Monday’s news conference, Flowers released video of the shooting, noting the footage had already circulated widely on social media and that the victim’s mother had seen it. One of the 18-year-olds involved in the shooting attends Vero Beach High School. The sheriff said teen meetups like the one at Garcia’s Boat Ramp are coordinated through Snapchat, making them difficult for law enforcement to track in advance. “When it’s Snapchat, it’s basically a private conversation,” Flowers said. “But it quickly can escalate to over 100, 150, 200 people there.” Flowers said the meetups, which have included alcohol, fighting, and firearms, have been taking place for years across Indian River County, Okeechobee, and surrounding areas, but that social media has intensified the danger. “Now we’re adding guns and alcohol into the mix, and we’re adding social media into the mix, and so what we’re seeing is an escalation of each one of these,” Flowers said. There’s guns, and those two just don’t mix. And now add in the fuel of the fire of social media, and now we have a 17-year-old dead.” The sheriff said teens at these gatherings are motivated in part by a desire for online attention. “The kids like to fight, and they like to videotape it, and they like to get their likes and shares because of that,” Flowers said. Parents, you see these videos. You do not want your teens out at these meetups." With Vero Beach High School’s homecoming game scheduled for Friday and the dance on Saturday, Flowers said additional deputies will be on duty. Meanwhile, the sheriff urged parents to monitor their children’s whereabouts and report any information about planned meetups to the sheriff’s office. “Parents, if your kids are telling you that they’re headed out to one of these meetups, ask them where they’re going. Ask, find out the details. Share that with us,” Flowers said. He recommended parents use location-sharing apps such as Life360 to track their children and said a child appearing to be in a remote or unusual location can be an indicator that a meetup is taking place. The investigation remains active. Flowers said anyone who witnessed any of the events that night, including the shooting itself, and has not yet spoken to investigators is urged to come forward. “I can tell you, our investigation is not even remotely over, and if we are able to identify people that were involved in this, from underage drinking to fighting, hurting other people,” Flowers said. " If they did something wrong, they’re going to have to be accountable for that." Anyone with information is asked to call the Indian River County Sheriff’s Office at 772-569-6700 or Treasure Coast Crime Stoppers at 1-800-273-TIPS.

Florida has reported nearly 500 dengue cases this year, including more than 250 infections acquired within the state, as new University of Florida research points to residential yards in Indian River County as a key place to understand mosquito-bite exposure. The Florida Department of Health’s latest weekly surveillance report , covering Sept. 20-26, lists 252 locally acquired dengue cases and 245 travel-associated cases statewide 497 total. The locally acquired cases were reported in Hillsborough, Miami-Dade, Orange, Palm Beach, Pasco, Pinellas and Polk counties. Palm Beach County had one locally acquired case and 12 travel-associated cases; St. Lucie County had six travel-associated cases. No locally acquired dengue cases were listed for Indian River County in the report. The state’s locally acquired total includes 223 cases in Hillsborough County, the center of Florida’s outbreak. Health officials also reported 20 mosquito pools testing positive for dengue statewide. Nationally, the CDC’s most recent weekly provisional report counted 690 dengue cases among U.S. Florida accounted for 403 of those cases in the CDC reporting system, though the state’s more current surveillance report lists a higher total because reporting systems update on different schedules. Against that backdrop, researchers at UF/IFAS’ Florida Medical Entomology Laboratory in Vero Beach found a surprising mosquito pattern in suburban Indian River County. The team expected residential yards to be dominated by Aedes albopictus , also known as the Asian tiger mosquito. Instead, researchers found relatively high numbers of Aedes aegypti the yellow fever mosquito and one of the two species most closely associated with dengue transmission worldwide. The finding does not mean dengue is circulating in Indian River County . But it underscores why backyard mosquito control and personal bite prevention matter, researchers said. See also: Florida stages emergency supplies as Tropical Storm Isaias strengthens in Gulf The first-of-its-kind study paired mosquito trapping at homes with a smartphone-based Bite Diary that let residents document when and where they were bitten. Researchers collected 3,788 female mosquitoes from 78 yards. Of 70 reported bites, nearly 93% happened outdoors and nearly 74% happened at home, according to the peer-reviewed study . The number of mosquitoes trapped in a yard was not associated with the number of bites residents reported. Instead, people who spent more time outside during the evening, from 5 p.m. to 9 p.m., reported more bites. Gardening and walking dogs were among activities commonly reported when bites occurred. Dengue is spread when an infected mosquito bites a person; it does not spread directly from person to person. Symptoms can include fever, severe muscle and joint pain, rash, nausea and pain behind the eyes. People with symptoms should contact a health care provider, especially after travel to an area where dengue is common. Health officials urge residents to use EPA-registered insect repellent, wear long sleeves and pants when practical, repair window and door screens, and dump standing water from containers such as buckets, flowerpots, toys, tires and pool covers.

We're getting murderers, drug dealers, rapists, people that have been really bad people for a long period of time. People with terrible records. People that came out of prisons. That's our first priority. We're getting them out, and we're getting them out fast, and we're getting them out. You see, in record numbers,” Trump said when pressed recently on the sentiment around his immigration and economic policies.

As Florida voters prepare to decide Amendment 3 on Nov. 3, residents, elected officials and policy experts gathered in Palm Beach County to discuss how the proposed constitutional amendment could affect homeowners, local governments and public services.WATCH: WPTV Let's Hear It: Property Tax Town Hall on Amendment 3 (Part 1)The discussion took place during WPTV's "Let's Hear It" community event and town hall at Palm Beach State College's Lake Worth Beach campus, where attendees asked questions and heard arguments from both supporters and opponents of the referendum.For many voters, the amendment could have significant financial implications. Supporters argue it would provide property tax relief for homeowners, while critics warn it could reduce funding for local services and shift key decisions to future lawmakers.WATCH: WPTV Let's Hear It: Property Tax Town Hall on Amendment 3 (Part 2)The evening began with WPTV's "Let's Hear It" event, giving residents an opportunity to learn more about the amendment before voting.Rich Bartholomew, advocacy chair for the League of Women Voters, said he appreciated the effort to help residents better understand the proposal."I have been watching everything that WPTV has been doing on this," Bartholomew said. "I think this is a very important event."Bartholomew also expressed concern that voters may not fully understand the long-term consequences of the amendment based solely on what appears on the ballot."There's nothing showing you on your ballot how all these things, these dominoes would fall," he said.Some residents in attendance said they support Amendment 3 because of rising property tax costs.John, a Palm Beach County resident, argued that continued increases in residential tax bills are becoming increasingly difficult for homeowners to manage."If you think about the tax we're paying now, where's it going to be in five years or 10 years at the rate we keep growing the tax on residences?" he said. "It's unsustainable."Rosey Gekas, another supporter of the amendment, said local governments should focus on budgeting and spending accountability."The scare tactics that I'm continuously hearing is just beyond," Gekas said. "The last five years, the amount of money that has come in from property taxes is skyrocketing. Where is all that money going? We just need to budget."WATCH: Residents, elected officials and policy experts talk Amendment 3 at WPTV Let's Hear It eventSeveral elected officials speaking during the town hall urged voters to consider how reduced tax revenues could affect essential government functions.West Palm Beach Mayor Keith James said the amendment could result in significant financial losses for municipalities."You have to factor in the impact on services," James said.According to James, the City of West Palm Beach could lose $21.7 million in the first year and more than $31 million during the first two years if the measure passes.State Sen. Tina Polsky also raised concerns about potential long-term consequences."This is unchangeable," Polsky said. "If we make this huge mistake on Nov. 3, we are stuck with it forever."Polsky argued that future legislative decisions tied to the amendment could expand its effects beyond what voters initially expect.Supporters of the amendment included state lawmakers who said homeowners deserve relief from rising costs.Florida Rep. Toby Overdorf said homeowners could see significant savings if the amendment is approved."They deserve money back in their pockets," Overdorf said. "Anywhere from $1,700 to as much as $4,000. That's what we're looking at."Amendment 3 will appear on Florida's Nov. Like all proposed constitutional amendments in Florida, it must receive at least 60% voter approval to be adopted into the state constitution.WPTV will continue covering the amendment and providing resources for voters seeking information ahead of Election Day.This story was reported on-air by a journalist and has been converted to this platform with the assistance of AI. Our editorial team verifies all reporting on all platforms for fairness and accuracy.

Susan Collins distanced herself from President Donald Trump during her first Maine Senate debate with Democrat Troy Jackson, arguing she has maintained her political independence by repeatedly voting against Trump's agenda and saying that she's “not exactly his favorite senator.”Democrats are trying to flip the Maine Senate seat as they work to win control of the Senate. Trump lost the state in 2024, giving Democrats hope of defeating the five-term moderate Republican, who has been targeted by Democrats in previous elections and survived.RELATED STORY | Senate Republicans move cash from purple North Carolina to red Kansas as battle for majority shiftsDuring the hourlong debate, Jackson focused largely on attempting to connect Collins to Trump. He kicked off the night by pointing out she cast a critical vote to confirm Supreme Court Justice Brett Kavanaugh, a Trump nominee who eventually helped overturn the constitutional right to abortion. Collins supports abortion rights and said Kavanaugh assured her it was settled law, but she has said recently that she does not regret her vote to confirm him.“Would you trust her to pick the next Supreme Court justice?” asked Jackson, a former state lawmaker and logger.He also repeatedly brought up her procedural vote to advance the president’s 2025 tax and spending bill — though Collins ultimately broke with her party to vote against it.Collins countered that she has voted against Trump more than she did Joe Biden when the Democrat was president, and has pushed back against Trump on tariffs, immigration enforcement and the war in Iran.“I voted against my party more than another other senator on either side of the aisle,” Collins said.The attention on Trump comes as only 31% of U.S. adults approved of how the Republican is handling the presidency, according to a September AP-NORC poll. That’s well below where his approval stood when he took office last year.The president has started holding rallies around the country in an effort to help GOP candidates win in November, telling voters to pretend he is on the ballot. At Tuesday's debate, a moderator noted Trump has floated the idea of campaigning in Maine, and asked Collins if she would stand beside him if he does.RELATED STORY | Trump holds Ohio midterm rally, urging voters to consider him on the ballot during 32-day campaign tour“I’m not exactly his favorite senator,” she said, adding “I would say that he’s not coming to Maine.”Collins, who has said she didn’t vote for Trump in 2016, voted to convict the president after his 2021 impeachment over his role in the Jan. In January, Collins joined a handful of Republican colleagues in backing a failed effort to limit the president’s ability to unilaterally use force in Venezuela. The move prompted Trump to say on social media that they “should never be elected to office again.”Collins argued that her seniority and experience in the Senate have resulted in money and resources for Maine, saying: “Leadership matters in Washington.”She also spent Tuesday evening attempting to turn the focus of Maine’s high cost of energy and housing on Jackson, arguing that he had a larger role in making a difference when he was the state Senate president and criticizing “Augusta’s failed policies” as a way to connect Jackson’s to the state’s struggle to address affordability.Other moments showed how the two candidates were approaching their appeal to working class Maine voters. For example, as Collins touted her ability to remove certain items from Trump’s trade war with Canada, including pulp, concrete and road salt. Jackson pushed back by quipping “we can’t eat road salt.”Jackson and Collins are scheduled to participate in three more debates later this month.

No arrests have been made in the shooting death of a 17-year-old at a teen meetup near Garcia's Boat Ramp in Indian River County, with a self-defense claim expected in the case, Indian River County Sheriff Eric Flowers announced Monday.WATCH BELOW: Sheriff Eric Flowers give update on shooting death of teen"We got kids out here losing their lives chasing likes and shares on social media," Flowers said.The shooting occurred late Friday night when approximately 100 teens, ranging in age from 14 to 19, gathered at Garcia's Boat Ramp in the 3700 block of County Road 512, the sheriff said. Deputies had broken up a similar group earlier that evening before the crowd moved to the boat ramp."The 17-year-old, and a group of his friends, are approaching a truck, and there are two people, both 18 years old, inside of that truck. The 17-year-old opens the door, and he starts to punch," Flowers said. "He's going to punch on the people that are inside of that truck. That shot is the shot that ultimately killed 17-year-old in this case."The teen's friends drove him away from the scene, east on County Road 512, while calling 911 and a dispatcher told them to stop at Fellsmere City Hall, where emergency crews performed CPR, the sheriff said. He was taken to Sebastian River Medical Center and later flown to Holmes Regional Medical Center in Melbourne, where he died from his injuries.The two individuals in the truck were identified using the sheriff's office's Flock technology, the sheriff said. Flowers said both have been cooperative with investigators, surrendering the weapon used in the shooting and the truck. Additional individuals involved in the incident have also been identified through Flock, though some remain unidentified. Investigators also recovered other weapons from the vehicle in which the 17-year-old was transported from the scene.WATCH: 17-year-old dies after shooting near Garcia's Boat RampFlowers said a warrant will be submitted in the case, but it will be up to the state to determine whether charges are filed."There have been no arrests on this case at this time, because the preliminary investigation shows that the 17-year-old was opening the door to attempt to fight with the two that were inside of the vehicle. They had a history of fighting," Flowers said. "Self defense plays a part in these, and when these kids go out and videotape these fights, and now guns are involved, there's going to be more of this." Names of those involved are not being released as the investigation continues, the sheriff said.Investigators believe at least four fights occurred at the boat ramp on the night of the shooting. Multiple shell casings and rounds were recovered from the scene.During Monday's news conference, Flowers released video of the shooting, noting the footage had already circulated widely on social media and that the victim's mother had seen it. One of the 18-year-olds involved in the shooting attends Vero Beach High School.The sheriff said teen meetups like the one at Garcia's Boat Ramp are coordinated through Snapchat, making them difficult for law enforcement to track in advance."When it's Snapchat, it's basically a private conversation," Flowers said. "But it quickly can escalate to over 100, 150, 200 people there."Flowers said the meetups, which have included alcohol, fighting, and firearms, have been taking place for years across Indian River County, Okeechobee, and surrounding areas, but that social media has intensified the danger."Now we're adding guns and alcohol into the mix, and we're adding social media into the mix, and so what we're seeing is an escalation of each one of these," Flowers said. There's guns, and those two just don't mix. And now add in the fuel of the fire of social media, and now we have a 17-year-old dead."The sheriff said teens at these gatherings are motivated in part by a desire for online attention."The kids like to fight, and they like to videotape it, and they like to get their likes and shares because of that," Flowers said. Parents, you see these videos. You do not want your teens out at these meetups."With Vero Beach High School's homecoming game scheduled for Friday and the dance on Saturday, Flowers said additional deputies will be on duty. Meanwhile, the sheriff urged parents to monitor their children's whereabouts and report any information about planned meetups to the sheriff's office."Parents, if your kids are telling you that they're headed out to one of these meetups, ask them where they're going. Ask, find out the details. Share that with us," Flowers said.He recommended parents use location-sharing apps such as Life360 to track their children and said a child appearing to be in a remote or unusual location can be an indicator that a meetup is taking place.The investigation remains active. Flowers said anyone who witnessed any of the events that night, including the shooting itself, and has not yet spoken to investigators is urged to come forward."I can tell you, our investigation is not even remotely over, and if we are able to identify people that were involved in this, from underage drinking to fighting, hurting other people," Flowers said. " If they did something wrong, they're going to have to be accountable for that."Anyone with information is asked to call the Indian River County Sheriff's Office at 772-569-6700 or Treasure Coast Crime Stoppers at 1-800-273-TIPS.

With less than a month until Election Day, Democrats are looking beyond the traditional battlegrounds as new signs emerge that the fight for control of Congress could be spreading into states Republicans once had little reason to worry about. Kansas and Florida are among the states receiving new attention, while President Donald Trump’s own campaign schedule is taking him into reliably Republican territory. RELATED STORY | Trump holds Ohio midterm rally, urging voters to consider him on the ballot during 32-day campaign tourThe shift can also be seen in campaign spending. Conservative groups have recently moved money from North Carolina, where the Senate contest was expected to be one of the year’s most competitive races, to Kansas as Democrats perform better in both states. Kansas has not elected a Democratic senator in nearly a century. “Since Labor Day, the numbers have only gotten worse for Republicans,” said Kyle Kondik, a nonpartisan election analyst with the University of Virginia Center for Politics. Florida is another state to watch. Democrats are increasingly campaigning there even though the state appeared on relatively few lists of major battlegrounds earlier this year. RELATED STORY | Trump takes midterm push to Nebraska amid economic concerns among farmersKondik said Florida could become an important early indicator on election night if Democrats are having an especially strong showing. “That’s a state that counts very quickly,” Kondik said. Trump, meanwhile, campaigned this week in Nebraska, a state he carried by nearly 200,000 votes two years ago. The president frequently calls polls fake, and Kondik cautioned that the current political picture could still be affected by inaccurate polling. “I am always concerned about there being some systematic polling error,” he said. Republicans currently hold 218 seats in the House, while the Senate has 53 Republicans and 47 Democrats. Democrats need 51 Senate votes to hold a majority, while Republicans need 50 because the vice president breaks ties. The final weeks of the campaign will help determine whether the activity in Kansas, Florida and other states marks a genuine expansion of the political battlefield or whether the fight for Congress ultimately returns to more familiar battlegrounds.

Boca Raton police have released new video, dispatch audio and 911 calls from a fatal officer-involved shooting that occurred in December 2024, weeks after the Palm Beach County State Attorney's Office determined the shooting was justified.During his first official news conference on the case, Boca Raton Police Chief Jarad Phelps outlined the events leading up to the shooting of 39-year-old Morey Clemmons and addressed questions surrounding the investigation, including why the involved officer's body camera was not activated.The release of the evidence comes after prosecutors concluded Officer Michael Super was legally justified in using deadly force. Boca Raton police say a separate administrative review remains underway.Police released video showing Officer Super arriving near Northwest Second Avenue after receiving reports of a man causing a disturbance in the area.According to 911 calls released by the department, callers reported a man who appeared disoriented and was in the roadway near Mizner Boulevard and the post office."Hi, there is a gentleman seems very out of it, in the middle of the street on Mizner by the post office," one caller told dispatchers.Police said Clemmons began running after Officer Super arrived. Video released by the department shows the encounter escalating moments later.According to Chief Phelps, Clemmons was seen yelling and moving toward the officer while ignoring commands. Police said Officer Super deployed his Taser twice within about seven seconds, but the attempts were unsuccessful.The encounter ended when Officer Super fired his weapon, striking and killing Clemmons.One of the key questions raised during the news conference centered on Officer Super's body camera.Chief Phelps confirmed the officer was wearing a body camera at the time of the shooting but said it was not activated.When asked why the camera was not turned on, Phelps said he did not yet know the reason."We will complete our administrative review," Phelps said, adding that determining why the body camera was not activated will be part of that process.Phelps also discussed reports that a backup officer responding to the scene was delayed by a passing train.The chief called it a broader transportation challenge affecting the city."That's a much larger transportation issue. I would love to have an underpass or overpass over the railroad so that we don't have those issues," Phelps said.Phelps said he recently met with Clemmons' wife to discuss the investigation and provide information that had not previously been released publicly.According to the chief, the meeting was cordial and focused on helping the family better understand what occurred."They're looking for closure. These have been happening since before I was in high school, since before many of you were in high school. This has been going on for a long time. Heavy rain flooded roads across Port St. Lucie Tuesday afternoon, leaving some vehicles stranded, forcing children to walk through standing water after school and prompting a response from police officers and city crews. According to the City of Port St. Lucie , a large amount of rain fell in a short period of time, leading to temporary road closures and flooding in multiple areas. Public Works crews responded to flooding near Savona Boulevard and California Boulevard, closing the roadway until it was safe for travel. The city also reported high-water conditions near Thornhill Drive and Floresta Drive, where Phase 3 construction is underway. On Southwest Thornhill Drive, school buses continued dropping off students despite flooded streets. CBS12 News saw children step off buses carrying their shoes and walk barefoot through standing water to reach home. Along Southwest Broadview Avenue near Crosstown Parkway, residents watched as water spilled across the roadway, making it difficult for drivers to tell where the street ended and floodwater began. "If you didn't see the grass here, you wouldn't know where the road is," resident Kevin Burke told CBS12 News. "It was steady sheets of rain for a good hour. Non-stop, and I mean heavy, heavy." Police officers directed traffic while Public Works crews set up barricades and monitored conditions during the evening commute. Burke said flooding in the area has become a familiar problem during heavy downpours. "When it rains heavy like it did today, it's like this all the time, from that canal coming up," he said. Burke said standing water presents concerns beyond traffic issues. "We have a pond over there by Crosstown and Bayshore. It's got signs all around it saying there are gators in it. It's a long shot, but it could happen, and that's what worries me, with kids and the animals," he said. For some residents, the flooding disrupted everyday tasks. "She has her elderly brother, who's 83 years old, and she's in her 60s, and she was going to run out and get Chinese food, and now she's still sitting here waiting because she can't get to it," Burke said. Earlier in the day, Port St. Lucie police reported flooding at several intersections, including SE Evans Avenue and SE Airoso Boulevard, SE Eyerly Avenue and SE Airoso Boulevard, SW Bayshore Boulevard and SW Thornhill Drive, and NE Floresta Drive and NE Ardsley Drive. See also: Opponents, supporters clash over Palm Beach County Israel Bonds investments City officials said Public Works crews continued monitoring conditions as water slowly receded Tuesday evening. Officials also reminded residents not to walk or drive through flooded roadways because it can be difficult to determine how deep the water is.

Senate candidate Angie Nixon visited Fort Pierce on Tuesday to speak with voters about reproductive health care, the economy, and other issues as part of her campaign across Florida ahead of the general election. Nixon, who represents a Jacksonville-area district in the Florida House of Representatives and describes herself as a Democratic Socialist, is holding town hall meetings across the state to connect with voters. Planned Parenthood President and CEO Alexis McGill Johnson hosted the Fort Pierce town hall, focusing on reproductive freedom and Florida's maternal mortality crisis. McGill Johnson and Nixon outlined the leadership they believe Florida families need, including protecting abortion access and expanding comprehensive health care services statewide. "Representative Nixon is a true champion for reproductive freedom," McGill Johnson said. "In the Senate, she is going to stand up for affordable health care and our right to make our own decisions about our own bodies." During the event, Nixon addressed a question about a proposed Islamic center approved for construction in Palm Beach County. Deep Dive: WPBF 25 News Investigates "This is a country where folks should have freedom of religion," Nixon said. "I would speak out against that type of opposition and hate if it was directed at a synagogue being built, if it was directed at a church being built, if it was directed at any other spiritual facility." Nixon also discussed the state of reproductive health care in Florida and other issues raised by voters. "Gas is high, people are struggling to get to and from work, and then they can't even afford the food anymore, let alone taking their children to the movies or out to eat, that's null and void now," one voter said. Nixon won the Democratic primary in St. Lucie County with about 54% of the vote. When asked how she plans to close the gap between herself and Republican incumbent Ashley Moody, Nixon said she intends to continue engaging with voters, including those who may disagree with her. "They have someone who is going to put them first," Nixon said when asked about the message she hopes attendees took away from Tuesday's event. She added that her campaign for U.S. Senate is focused on putting money back in people's pockets. Nixon spoke with voters for about an hour. Her next stop is in the Orlando area. Parents, students and grandparents gathered outside the Okeechobee County School Board on Monday, demanding greater accountability over bullying concerns after a 14-year-old student said relentless harassment pushed her to a breaking point.Signs lined the street as protesters chanted "no more bullying" and "hold bullies accountable," rallying around 14-year-old Estrella Ventura Meras, a student at Okeechobee Achievement Academy.WATCH BELOW: Parents demand action after girl jumps from school busLast week, WPTV reported on a video showing Estrella jumping from the window of a moving school bus. WPTV is not showing the video.Estrella told WPTV she jumped to escape students who had been bullying her since the start of the school year. She said she later went home and attempted to take her own life."I thank God he gave me another chance to live," Estrella said, holding back tears.Her mother, Estela Meras, said she found her daughter pale and lying next to a pill bottle. She said Estrella had left behind a note saying she was tired."What if I hadn't found her there lying in bed?" Meras said as she became emotional. Now, Estrella and her mother are calling for change."I just hope there's justice and the students responsible," said Estela Meras. "Everybody was on the bus laughing about her instead of helping her. If it was me, I would have been helping somebody."Estrella told WPTV she repeatedly reported the alleged bullying to teachers and administrators at Okeechobee Achievement Academy but said nothing changed. Her mother said she also previously raised concerns about bullying involving her daughter and now wants the district to reevaluate how it handles those reports.Other families at Monday's protest told WPTV they have also raised concerns about bullying at Okeechobee Achievement Academy and believe more needs to be done. "Somebody has to take some accountability somewhere," protester Maria Rodriguez said. Okeechobee County Schools said it shares parents' belief that "bullying has no place in our schools" and that every student deserves to feel safe, supported and heard.The district said the allegations involving Estrella remain under investigation. Citing federal student privacy law, district officials said they could not publicly discuss details of the investigation, education records or any potential student discipline.The district said schools are responsible for investigating bullying allegations reported by students and parents. If a family believes a school has failed to act on a complaint, district officials said the family should contact the district office so administrators can review both the allegations and the school's response."We take allegations that reports have gone unaddressed seriously," district spokesperson Dr. Joseph Stanley said in a statement to WPTV.Under School Board Policy 5.321, bullying reports can be made verbally, in writing or anonymously, and no specific reporting form is required. The policy calls for separate, confidential interviews and a review of evidence, with investigative procedural steps to be completed within a maximum of 10 school days, according to the district.The district said the policy also requires parents to be promptly notified when an investigation begins and requires a written report and recommendations for corrective action. It also includes provisions for counseling, intervention and follow-up measures intended to protect students.The district told WPTV that Okeechobee Achievement Academy has completed investigations into four other reports of alleged bullying during the current school year. Those cases involved four alleged victims and nine alleged perpetrators.None of the four complaints was substantiated as bullying, according to the district. Those cases are separate from the investigation involving Estrella, which remains open.However, the district stressed that an allegation being unsubstantiated as "bullying" does not necessarily mean no inappropriate behavior occurred. Florida law defines bullying as "systematically and chronically inflicting physical hurt or psychological distress" on one or more students. The district said a single incident generally does not meet that definition on its own, although one incident could reveal a broader pattern. Conduct that does not legally qualify as bullying could also constitute harassment or another violation requiring intervention or discipline.District officials said cooperation from students and parents is important during investigations because details about incidents, witnesses, previous reports and other evidence can help investigators determine what happened. The district said limited participation can restrict the information available to investigators but does not prevent officials from reviewing the evidence they can obtain.Despite calls from some parents for changes, Okeechobee County Schools said it believes its existing policies comply with Florida law and provide a thorough framework for responding to bullying allegations. The district said no procedural, staffing, disciplinary or policy changes are currently under consideration in response to the concerns raised by families.Instead, officials said their focus is on consistently implementing existing requirements, conducting thorough investigations and taking appropriate action based on the evidence.For Estrella's mother and the families who stood alongside her Monday, however, the protest was about making sure their concerns are heard before another child reaches a breaking point."All we want is answers for Estrella," Rodriguez said.

A deadly school bus crash in Polk County is raising new questions about how students are protected inside Florida school buses and why state law still falls short of federal safety recommendations.One student, a 10th grader on her way to Winter Haven High School, was killed Monday morning when a school bus carrying 39 people was involved in a crash. The circumstances surrounding the crash remain under investigation, including what happened outside the bus and what took place inside it.Watch report from Katie Lagrone"We have one fatality of a beautiful high school girl. It's just heartbreaking," Polk County Sheriff Grady Judd said during a morning news briefing.Investigators have not released details about how many students were wearing seat belts, what type of restraints were in use, or whether the belts played a role in the outcome of the crash.Florida law requires school buses built since 2001 to be equipped with seat belts. However, students are not required to wear them, and state law does not require the more protective lap-and-shoulder belts recommended by federal safety investigators. Instead, many Florida school buses continue to use standard lap belts.The federal recommendation followed an investigation by investigative reporter Katie LaGrone more than a decade ago.In 2012, a St. Lucie County school bus collided with a semi-truck, killing 9-year-old Aaron Beauchamp. Aaron was wearing the bus's standard lap belt at the time of the crash.Several years later, investigators with the National Transportation Safety Board (NTSB) examined that crash and studied how different types of seat belts affect student safety.The agency's testing showed significant differences between standard lap belts and lap-and-shoulder restraints. Simulations demonstrated that lap-and-shoulder belts provide greater protection by better controlling a passenger's movement during a crash.As a result, the NTSB recommended that all school buses nationwide be equipped with lap-and-shoulder belts.The NTSB specifically urged Florida to change state law to require lap-and-shoulder belts on new large school buses.That recommendation was never adopted.Today, it remains unclear how many Florida school districts have voluntarily upgraded their fleets to meet the federal recommendation.In St. Lucie County, nearly 15 years after Aaron's death, about 20% of district school buses still use only standard lap belts.In Polk County, a district spokesperson confirmed on Monday that all the district’s school buses are equipped with just lap belts.The latest crash has renewed questions about whether stronger seat belt requirements could better protect students who are traveling to and from school on a school bus.Despite the concerns raised by this tragedy, transportation safety experts continue to emphasize that deadly school bus crashes are extremely rare, and that school buses remain the safest form of transportation for students traveling to and from school.For families in Polk County and across Florida, the crash could prompt renewed scrutiny of whether the state's school bus safety standards should be updated to reflect federal recommendations."No one will ever understand how heavy this weighs on our hearts," Polk County Schools Superintendent Fred Heid said following the crash.

The political committee supporting Amendment 3 — which would raise Florida's homestead tax exemption — received an $18 million cash infusion in September, campaign finance records show. The two committees opposing the amendment raised a combined $680,000, a margin of more than 26 to 1.In the coming days and weeks, voters can expect to see significant messaging urging a "yes" vote on the amendment.WATCH BELOW: Amendment 3 backers outraise opponents 26-to-1Digging deeper into those campaign finance records, I found the "No" committees received donations from numerous corporate, individual and nonprofit contributors. Yes on 3's $18 million came from a single source: Florida Realtors.Margy Grant is the chief executive of Florida Realtors and the sole contributor to "Yes on 3.""As the voice of real estate, Florida Realtors is a longtime advocate for homeowners," Grant said. "Families are struggling with the affordability of so many things. When you go to the grocery store, when you go to the gas station, prices just continue to climb. The one thing we can possibly control is property taxes." Jackson Peel, spokesman for "Floridians for Shared Prosperity" — one of the two "No" groups — said his side has an advantage despite the funding gap."Well, we have the advantage of the facts on our side," Peel said. "This is not the savings that is promised on the mailers in your mailbox from the realtors— that this is a scam and a tax shift. You're gonna end up paying more in other ways."While the political committees against Amendment 3 have a much smaller war chest, Peel said Florida voters are still hearing their warnings through opposition from groups like the Florida Sheriff's Association and the Florida Association of Firefighters."I'm on the side of the sheriffs, the police, and the firefighters who say that this is bad for our community's public safety. I'm on the side of the teachers who say, yeah, this is gonna cut after-school programs that help our kids." Peel said.On the question of funding for public services, Grant said she has full confidence in elected officials."If you look at the increase in revenue over the past 10 years, it has doubled. Services have not doubled," Grant said. "I have full faith and confidence in our elected officials that they will be able to implement Amendment 3 successfully and effectively." Matt Elliott wants to know whether his brain cancer could be connected to other diagnoses on the Treasure Coast. He also knows he may not live long enough to get an answer. It might take them years to even figure out what the hell’s going on around here, Elliott said. I can’t expect myself to be around at the end of it. Lucie County have raised similar questions for years, pointing to diagnoses just houses apart and, in some cases, among unrelated residents of the same home decades apart. In June, I-Team reporter Katie Bente revisited families’ search for answers. In this second part of her investigation, Bente went street by street with a widow tracking the diagnoses and pressing health officials for updated findings. A few houses apart For Stephanie Ankiel , one stop on the drive through Fort Pierce brings the questions back to her own family. She pointed to her late husband’s childhood home, then another home a few houses away where she said a resident was diagnosed in 2025 with the same type of brain tumor. This is the house my late husband grew up in, Ankiel said. He was diagnosed with the same exact thing as that gentleman in 2025. Both men were initially diagnosed with oligodendroglioma, a different type of brain tumor from glioblastoma . Ankiel said her husband Mark Cunningham’s cancer later progressed to glioblastoma. A few streets away, she identified another home where she said two unrelated residents developed glioblastoma decades apart. This is the house where we’ve had two glioblastoma cases, 20 years apart, no family relation, she said. Elsewhere along the route, Ankiel pointed to neighboring homes where she said a woman and an 18-year-old had been diagnosed with brain cancer. The I-Team is withholding exact addresses to protect families’ privacy. PART 1: Brain cancer diagnoses leave St. Lucie County families searching for answers, again Ankiel helps patients through the Brain Cancer Foundation of the Treasure Coast , including a child who is just 3. She has spent years mapping where patients lived and looking for possible connections. Three additional brain cancer cases were confirmed in August alone in the areas families are tracking. Those diagnoses and the proximity of patients’ homes do not establish a cancer cluster or a common cause. But Ankiel wants officials to examine the range of brain cancers represented on her map, beyond glioblastoma alone. Regardless if it’s Glio at this point, we have too much brain cancer in this area. CDC guidance allows consideration of different cancer types when evidence suggests shared causes or exposures. No such connection has been established among the cases families are tracking. What the state studied and what is new The Florida Department of Health’s 2019 review examined glioblastoma diagnoses from 1998 through 2017 in ZIP codes 34952, 34982 and 34983. It found no statistically significant increase and did not designate a cancer cluster. That review did not include later diagnoses and focused on glioblastoma rather than the range of brain tumors represented on Ankiel’s map. Her husband’s initial diagnosis is one reason she wants officials to examine that broader picture. The I-Team asked whether the department had analyzed cases diagnosed since 2017 and what would trigger new environmental testing. Lucie County Health Officer Clint Sperber said officials have been reviewing cancer registry data and environmental influences. Our latest analysis, which includes data through 2023, shows no indication of higher rates in St. Lucie County or in the specific zip codes people have asked about, Sperber wrote. Lucie’s rates are in line with nearby counties and with the state as a whole. The updated report was not available when he responded. Sperber said officials were finishing a summary to release online. His response did not explain how the analysis handled tumors initially classified as another type and later diagnosed as glioblastoma, or whether other brain cancers were examined separately. It also did not specify what would trigger additional environmental testing. No environmental factor questioned by families has been established as a cause of these cancers. A call for another look Rep. Brian Mast said he has again asked the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention to examine the concerns and provide the data behind its conclusions. You need to give us the receipts, Mast said. Give us the data of where these took place, how many of them took place. The CDC said state and local health departments lead examinations of unusual cancer patterns. It confirmed that it assisted Florida’s investigation in 2018, but did not specifically address whether it had received Mast’s latest request or would open a new review. In a statement to the I-Team, a CDC spokesperson said: CDC is prepared to provide additional assistance upon the Florida Department of Health’s request. Making the most of the time left Elliott was diagnosed this year with glioblastoma, an aggressive, fast-growing grade 4 brain cancer. The former bar manager described struggling to speak after surgery and initially believing his diagnosis was an isolated case. Meeting other local patients changed that. I thought I was the only one, he said. He has decided not to continue treatment, choosing to spend his remaining time with friends and family, going to the beach and swimming. While he wants investigators to find answers, he is focused on the life he still has. I’m not going to be that person that lives to be 65, 70, 80 years old, Elliott said. But I get to hang out with my friends. I get to go take a swim, have some fun.

At Hillcrest Memorial Gardens, Marc Raczkoski stares painfully at a place he's often tried to avoid. "Richard Raczkoski, beloved son, corporal, sheriff's department, Indian River County," reads Marc Raczkoski, blinking back tears. WATCH BELOW: Brother finally gets closure as Florida deputy killer's execution date setIt's the grave of his older brother, who was just 29 years old when he was buried at the Fort Pierce cemetery. "I was 22," Marc said quietly. "I was 22." It's always been an agonizing place for Marc — one that's brought up too many painful memories. Yet this time, his grief feels a little lighter. This time, for the first time in the 40 years he's come to visit his older brother, he finally has the answer he's been longing to give. And it's finally over," Marc said.Gov. Ron DeSantis on Friday signed the death warrant for William Reaves, the man convicted of killing Raczkoski in 1986. If carried out, the execution will mark Florida's 18th this year. 20, and Reaves has one last chance at an appeal."It gives closure," Marc said. "Now, when everybody asks me, 'What happened to the guy that murdered my brother?' That the first question I get, and I got to say, 'He's still — still hasn't happened." "You'll finally have a different answer," investigative reporter Kate Hussey supplied. "Yes, finally have a different answer," Marc replied. 23, 1986, 29-year-old Deputy Richard Raczkoski answered a 911 call at a convenience store in Indian River County. Minutes later, he was shot four times and killed, launching a multi-agency manhunt for the killer.Days later, authorities arrested 37-year-old William Reaves in Albany, Georgia, who was extradited to Indian River County, where he confessed to killing Raczkoski, saying he "panicked" when a gun fell out of his shorts, and that he was under the influence of drugs at the time. Forty years later, Marc said the memories of that night are still fresh and painful, recalling the middle-of-the-night knock on the door that changed everything. "One of the friends that was on the police department in Fort Pierce, my brother's friend, was at the back door. He took me up in the car and raced me up to the hospital, but I knew when they were talking to me in there for too long, I knew he didn't make it. I knew he didn't make it, and from then, it was just a blur of everything else after that," Marc told WPTV. "How could somebody do something like that? Richard was calling him a cab, for God's sake's. To empty his gun into him is beyond me. How could somebody do something like that?" In 1987, Reaves was convicted of murder and sentenced to death, yet for nearly four decades, Reaves sat on death row while Marc stood beside his brother's grave, waiting and wondering."Wondering what's happened. Feels like everybody forgot," Marc said.Marc said the years without resolution took a toll on his entire family."It's something I wouldn't wish on anybody to have to go through. And watch your parents go through," Marc said. "No more Christmas trees in the house. Holidays were never the same. Mom didn't decorate." When DeSantis signed Reaves' death warrant, Marc said the weight of the wait finally lifted."It's finally over. It's finally over," Marc said.The news also brought relief to the Indian River County Sheriff's Office, and Sheriff Eric Flowers himself, who has pushed for Reaves' death warrant to be signed. "All of that is very heavy on our agency, and knowing that this execution is coming in October gives a little weight lifted off. I think it's going to be a moment of healing for our agency," Flowers told WPTV. Flowers said he plans to attend Reaves' execution. "Because I want to make sure the last thing he sees is an Indian River County Deputy uniform," said Flowers. Reaves' execution would mark Florida's 18th this year, following 19 executions in 2025, which set a modern-day record. The rapid pace has prompted concern from groups like Floridians Against the Death Penalty, who, along with capital defense attorneys, have raised concerns about how quickly executions are being carried out."One I think is around the transparency of this process. We don't know how people are being chosen for execution or why. We also don't know the impact this is having on corrections staff and those who are involved," Grace Hanna of Floridians Against the Death Penalty said.Hanna, though, knows the pain Raczkowski's family is experiencing. Her own family member was murdered, and said she understands everyone processes that grief differently. "And far be it for me to tell any family how they should feel. I can only speak to my own experience and my family's experience of having a loved one who was murdered, and I can say that I came out of that feeling that another death and another family's pain was not going to give us closure or peace," said Hanna. "Though certainly don't hold any ill will towards those who feel that this is what gives them closure." For Marc, standing at his brother's grave — a place that will always hold pain — he's reminded of all he's lost. "The time I never got to spend with him," Marc said, holding back tears. "Mom and Dad didn't see any closure in this, time that they didn't get to spend with him, time he didn't get to spend with my children, his nieces and nephews. It's all very much to take in." Marc described his brother as someone always focused on public service. "He was quick to make you laugh. He was always focused on public service, to serve people. He had found a man — an elderly man — that wandered away from a facility one time, and he's the one that found him out in the woods by the facility," Marc recalled. "He liked to fish and he liked the outdoors. And he was just basically fun to be around." Yet as he walks away from the grave, knowing the grief will never go away, he hopes the coming execution will bring something he has long sought."There is finally closure for Richard," Marc said. "For what he [Reaves] did to Richard, yes. What he did and the way he did it, yes, it gives me some closure, but still the pain will still always be there."
