A Fort Pierce senior center is expected to close, leaving some of the older adults who rely on it worried about losing a gathering place in their own community.The Council on Aging of St. Lucie confirmed the senior center at 1505 Orange Avenue in Fort Pierce is expected to close in the near future. The property is currently listed for sale for $2.2 million.The news came as a surprise to some seniors who use the center regularly, including 77-year-old Sandy Pietrewicz. She has relied on the center for nearly a decade. “That's the community center that I go to for lunch and friendship and social activities with other elderly women,” said Pietrewicz.After hearing the center could be closing, Pietrewicz said she and other seniors were left with questions about what would happen to the services they depend on.“We were all talking about who we could contact, and I thought of WPTV immediately,” she said.WPTV reporter Brooke Chau went to the center to get answers and hear directly from the seniors who use it.The Council on Aging said the closure will not mean an end to the services provided to seniors.“You're going to get the same treatment. You're going to get the same love. You're going to get the same meals,” said Trekina Smith with the Council on Aging.Once the property sells, seniors who currently use the Orange Avenue location are expected to transition to the Council on Aging's facility on Bayshore Boulevard in Port St. Lucie.The organization said transportation will be provided to help seniors get to the new location.But some seniors say the location itself is important.“That makes us even angrier. We can't have something in our own community,” Pietrewicz said.Geneira Lovett, who also uses the center, told WPTV that seniors in Fort Pierce want to be able to access services close to where they live.“We live here, we want rights to do thing, besides trouble,” Lovett said.The Council on Aging said it understands those concerns, but says change is necessary.For now, the Council on Aging says services at the Orange Avenue center are continuing. There is no finalized timeline for the closure because the transition is tied to the sale of the property.“We understand the concerns, it's a change for us too. But hey, change comes, and you got to go with the change,” Smith said.The organization said seniors will continue to have access to meals, activities, social opportunities and transportation once services move to the Port St.

Five years after the shooting death of a 20-year-old woman, the Port St. Lucie Police Department is still seeking answers. Lucie police responded to reports of multiple gunshots near Southeast Green River Parkway and Southeast Charleston Drive. Police said Gabriella Gina Hanley was driving south on Southeast Green River Parkway in a black Kia Forte with her boyfriend, Darrick Mincey Jr., when another vehicle pulled alongside them and fired multiple rounds into their car. Officers and rescue personnel began life-saving measures after finding Hanley with multiple gunshot wounds. She was pronounced dead Oct. Mincey was also struck by gunfire but survived. See also: Teen identified after deadly Fellsmere shooting involving 100-plus teens Investigators found the Kia had 37 bullet impacts. Numerous 9mm cartridge casings were recovered, and forensic evidence indicated the bullets were fired from two separate rifles, police said. Five years later, detectives are continuing to conduct interviews and examine forensic and digital evidence. At the time of her death, Hanley left behind a 20-month-old baby. CBS12 reported in 2022 that investigators had identified three people of interest, but no charges were filed against them. Anyone with information is asked to call the Port St. Lucie Police Department at 772-871-5000 or Treasure Coast Crime Stoppers at 1-800-273-TIPS (8477) .

A wrong-way driver sparked a deadly three-vehicle crash early Sunday morning on I-95 in West Palm Beach, killing one person and seriously injuring two others, according to the Florida Highway Patrol (FHP).The crash happened around 5:30 a.m. Sunday on the northbound lanes of I-95 near Palm Beach Lakes Boulevard.Investigators say a GMC Sierra pickup truck was traveling south in the inside lane of northbound I-95, driving the wrong way as it approached Palm Beach Lakes Boulevard. A Palm Beach County Sheriff's deputy spotted the vehicle traveling the wrong way and paced it at about 60 to 65 mph before losing sight of it shortly before the crash.A Dodge Grand Caravan was traveling north in the inside lane when its driver, later identified as Angelo Genova, 68, of West Palm Beach, attempted to swerve right to avoid the oncoming pickup but was unable to avoid a collision.Following the initial impact, the pickup rotated and came to rest in the inside northbound lane. The van spun across the roadway from west to east.A Cadillac El Dorado was traveling north behind the van and was unable to avoid the wreckage. The Cadillac then struck the rear of the van, according to FHP.Genova was pronounced dead at the scene.The wrong-way driver, identified in an arrest report as Edwin Castro, 26, of West Palm Beach, and the Cadillac driver suffered serious injuries and were transported to St. Mary's Medical Center for treatment. FHP said the driver of the Cadallic suffered incapacitating injuries. According to the arrest report, deputies and troopers observed that Castro showed signs of impairment after the crash, including a strong odor of alcohol, bloodshot eyes and slurred speech. Hospital toxicology results showed Castro's blood alcohol level was 0.239, nearly three times Florida's legal limit of 0.08, investigators said.Castro was arrested and charged with DUI causing death, vehicular homicide, DUI causing serious bodily injury, reckless driving causing serious bodily injury, two counts of DUI causing property damage or injury and two counts of reckless driving causing property damage or injury. He was also cited for driving the wrong way on the interstate.The arrest report also states that U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement told investigators that Castro had a final order of removal after a denied asylum claim from Guatemala.All northbound lanes of I-95 at Palm Beach Lakes Boulevard remained closed while the crash was being investigated but have since reopened.

Western Delray Beach residents are voicing concerns about growth and development in the Agricultural Reserve as three major projects move forward along Lyons Road, including a new driver's license office, a nursing home and an Islamic school and daycare. The debate intensified Friday after a public meeting hosted by Palm Beach County Commissioner Maria Sachs that drew hundreds of residents seeking answers about traffic, zoning and public notification.WATCH BELOW: 3 Ag Reserve projects spark debate in western DelrayThe projects are already at various stages of approval and construction, but some neighbors say they were not adequately informed about developments that could significantly change the character of the area.As Palm Beach County continues to experience rapid population growth, development in the Ag Reserve has become a recurring issue for residents concerned about traffic congestion, infrastructure demands and preservation of open land. The latest projects have reignited that debate in western Delray Beach.Hundreds of residents attended a public meeting Friday hosted by Commissioner Sachs to discuss development activity in the Agricultural Reserve.Residents raised concerns about traffic, density and transparency in the approval process.One resident, Michelle, said she believes nearby homeowners should have received more notice before projects advanced."We were not notified," Michelle said. "This is a natural reserve and if you're going to destroy the natural reserve you need to notify residents who live in the neighborhood."Others questioned whether development should continue in the area at all, arguing the Agricultural Reserve should remain protected from additional growth.1. New DMV under constructionOne of the projects is a new Palm Beach County Tax Collector's Office facility, which WPTV previously reported on.According to county officials, Palm Beach County Tax Collector Anne Gannon purchased the property for approximately $4.3 million. The facility will replace the current office on Congress Avenue.Construction is already underway on the 4.2-acre site, with the new location expected to open in 2027.2. Nursing home plannedAnother proposal moving forward is All Seasons, a nursing home development planned on nearly 9 acres.Project documents show the facility will include more than 150 units. Developers expect construction to be completed in spring 2028.3. Islamic school and daycareThe third project is a nearly 10-acre Islamic school and daycare facility planned along Lyons Road.Project information reviewed by WPTV indicates the development is expected to generate an estimated 1,084 daily vehicle trips and could be completed by 2027.The proposal has become a focal point of community discussion, with some residents urging officials to reconsider or pause the project.Michelle said she has contacted state representatives in hopes of stopping the development.However, some residents who support the proposal told WPTV they believe the school would bring additional diversity and educational opportunities to the area.Sachs said the projects were able to move through the approval process under existing county regulations that she believes should be revised."If you're a government entity or a place of worship, then you don't need to come to the Board of County Commissioners," Sachs said. All you have to do is check the boxes for zoning and you get a DRO, which is an administrative leap to build what you want. That's wrong."Sachs is encouraging residents to support zoning reforms and contact county commissioners if they want changes to the development review process.She also told WPTV she plans to hold another public meeting to continue discussing development concerns in the Agricultural Reserve. Details on a date, time and location have not yet been announced.For residents living along Lyons Road and throughout western Delray Beach, the debate reflects broader questions about balancing growth, infrastructure and land preservation as Palm Beach County continues to expand.This story was reported on-air by a journalist and has been converted to this platform with the assistance of AI. Our editorial team verifies all reporting on all platforms for fairness and accuracy.

The mother of a 17-year-old boy shot and killed during a party Friday night at a boat ramp in Indian River County said she believes her son was protecting others when he was killed. She has identified her son as Sulliman Bah. Indian River County Sheriff Eric Flowers held a news conference about the shooting Monday afternoon. He said there were about 1,000 teenagers gathered at Garcia's Boat Ramp, just south of Fellsmere. Flowers showed two videos of the shooting from different angles. The videos start with Bah approaching a white pickup truck. "Seventeen-year-old opens the door, and he starts to punch. He's going to punch on the people that are inside of that truck. One shot is fired," Flowers said. The sheriff said the shot was fired by the passenger in the truck, killing Bah. Flowers stated that Bah had a history with the two 18-year-olds in the truck, noting that they had fought before. The 18-year-olds told investigators they had the gun to protect themselves. "At this time, it looks as though there will be a self-defense claim," Flowers said. Bah’s mother, however, disputes the self-defense claim. In a text message to WPBF 25 News reporter Ari Hait, she said, "Sulliman was a defender of his friends. Always protecting the underdog, and I believe he was trying to save the crowd from that gun that he knew was about to be used...He was there to protect his friends from the thugs that had previously threatened him and many others multiple times." She added that she does not see her son throwing a punch in the video. "If anything, I believe he was attempting to push the gun away," she said. The sheriff has not released the identities of the two 18-year-olds in the truck but said they are cooperating with investigators. No arrests have been made so far. "It's going to be up to the state on whether charges ultimately will be filed. But I can tell you self-defense plays a part in these," Flowers said. The sheriff emphasized that the investigation is ongoing and urged anyone who attended the party to contact his office. No arrests have been made in the shooting death of a 17-year-old at a teen meetup near Garcia's Boat Ramp in Indian River County, with a self-defense claim expected in the case, Indian River County Sheriff Eric Flowers announced Monday.WATCH BELOW: Sheriff Eric Flowers give update on shooting death of teen"We got kids out here losing their lives chasing likes and shares on social media," Flowers said.The shooting occurred late Friday night when approximately 100 teens, ranging in age from 14 to 19, gathered at Garcia's Boat Ramp in the 3700 block of County Road 512, the sheriff said. Deputies had broken up a similar group earlier that evening before the crowd moved to the boat ramp."The 17-year-old, and a group of his friends, are approaching a truck, and there are two people, both 18 years old, inside of that truck. The 17-year-old opens the door, and he starts to punch," Flowers said. "He's going to punch on the people that are inside of that truck. That shot is the shot that ultimately killed 17-year-old in this case."The teen's friends drove him away from the scene, east on County Road 512, while calling 911 and a dispatcher told them to stop at Fellsmere City Hall, where emergency crews performed CPR, the sheriff said. He was taken to Sebastian River Medical Center and later flown to Holmes Regional Medical Center in Melbourne, where he died from his injuries.The two individuals in the truck were identified using the sheriff's office's Flock technology, the sheriff said. Flowers said both have been cooperative with investigators, surrendering the weapon used in the shooting and the truck. Additional individuals involved in the incident have also been identified through Flock, though some remain unidentified. Investigators also recovered other weapons from the vehicle in which the 17-year-old was transported from the scene.WATCH: 17-year-old dies after shooting near Garcia's Boat RampFlowers said a warrant will be submitted in the case, but it will be up to the state to determine whether charges are filed."There have been no arrests on this case at this time, because the preliminary investigation shows that the 17-year-old was opening the door to attempt to fight with the two that were inside of the vehicle. They had a history of fighting," Flowers said. "Self defense plays a part in these, and when these kids go out and videotape these fights, and now guns are involved, there's going to be more of this." Names of those involved are not being released as the investigation continues, the sheriff said.Investigators believe at least four fights occurred at the boat ramp on the night of the shooting. Multiple shell casings and rounds were recovered from the scene.During Monday's news conference, Flowers released video of the shooting, noting the footage had already circulated widely on social media and that the victim's mother had seen it. One of the 18-year-olds involved in the shooting attends Vero Beach High School.The sheriff said teen meetups like the one at Garcia's Boat Ramp are coordinated through Snapchat, making them difficult for law enforcement to track in advance."When it's Snapchat, it's basically a private conversation," Flowers said. "But it quickly can escalate to over 100, 150, 200 people there."Flowers said the meetups, which have included alcohol, fighting, and firearms, have been taking place for years across Indian River County, Okeechobee, and surrounding areas, but that social media has intensified the danger."Now we're adding guns and alcohol into the mix, and we're adding social media into the mix, and so what we're seeing is an escalation of each one of these," Flowers said. There's guns, and those two just don't mix. And now add in the fuel of the fire of social media, and now we have a 17-year-old dead."The sheriff said teens at these gatherings are motivated in part by a desire for online attention."The kids like to fight, and they like to videotape it, and they like to get their likes and shares because of that," Flowers said. Parents, you see these videos. You do not want your teens out at these meetups."With Vero Beach High School's homecoming game scheduled for Friday and the dance on Saturday, Flowers said additional deputies will be on duty. Meanwhile, the sheriff urged parents to monitor their children's whereabouts and report any information about planned meetups to the sheriff's office."Parents, if your kids are telling you that they're headed out to one of these meetups, ask them where they're going. Ask, find out the details. Share that with us," Flowers said.He recommended parents use location-sharing apps such as Life360 to track their children and said a child appearing to be in a remote or unusual location can be an indicator that a meetup is taking place.The investigation remains active. Flowers said anyone who witnessed any of the events that night, including the shooting itself, and has not yet spoken to investigators is urged to come forward."I can tell you, our investigation is not even remotely over, and if we are able to identify people that were involved in this, from underage drinking to fighting, hurting other people," Flowers said. " If they did something wrong, they're going to have to be accountable for that."Anyone with information is asked to call the Indian River County Sheriff's Office at 772-569-6700 or Treasure Coast Crime Stoppers at 1-800-273-TIPS.

A 17-year-old was killed in a shooting Friday night at Garcia's Boat Ramp in Indian River County, and investigators are examining whether the shooting was an act of self-defense, according to Sheriff Eric Flowers.WATCH: WPTV'S Coverage of Teen killed in Garcia's Boat Ramp shootingThe shooting happened during a confrontation at the popular waterfront gathering spot, which authorities say has become a frequent meetup location for teenagers.According to Flowers, investigators reviewed video that showed the 17-year-old opening the door of a truck and throwing punches at people inside before a shot was fired."The 17-year-old opens the door, and he starts to punch. He's going to punch the people that are inside of that truck," Flowers said during a news conference. That shot is the shot that ultimately killed the 17-year-old in this case."Video released by the Indian River County Sheriff's Office shows the confrontation moments before the shooting.Flowers said social media has played a role in drawing large groups of teens to locations like Garcia's Boat Ramp and warned that the presence of firearms is increasing the risks associated with those gatherings."We got kids out here losing their lives chasing likes and shares on social media," Flowers said. "Now we're adding guns into the mix, and we're adding social media into the mix, and so what we're seeing is an escalation of each one of these."Authorities said both the shooter and the driver of the truck have cooperated with investigators, turning over the firearm and the vehicle involved in the incident.As of Monday, no arrests had been made."It's gonna be up to the state on whether charges are ultimately filed, but I can tell you, self-defense plays a part in these," Flowers said.The investigation remains active. The sheriff is asking anyone with video footage or information about the shooting, as well as future teen meetup events, to contact investigators.Flowers also urged parents to know where their children are and suggested location-tracking tools as one way to help keep them safe.

A Fort Pierce man is facing an aggravated assault charge after two tow trucks were hit with a U-Haul truck. On Thursday, Fort Pierce Police officers responded to the 5400 block of Jamboree Drive, east of Interstate 95, regarding a report of a U-Haul box truck crashing into two vehicles. Officers learned that the U-Haul had been parked in violation of homeowner association restrictions, and the contracted tow company was attempting to remove it. During the tow attempt, the person intervened, police said. A second tow truck was positioned behind the U-Haul to prevent it from leaving. After the person refused to pay a drop fee, he entered the U-Haul, backed off the tow truck and struck the tow truck parked behind him, police said. He then continued to drive forward and reverse repeatedly until he freed the U-Haul from between the two vehicles, police said. The person drove down the street, where responding officers located him shortly afterward. No injuries were reported. The U-Haul was towed and the man was taken to the St. Police didn't identify him. Matt Elliott wants to know whether his brain cancer could be connected to other diagnoses on the Treasure Coast. He also knows he may not live long enough to get an answer. It might take them years to even figure out what the hell’s going on around here, Elliott said. I can’t expect myself to be around at the end of it. Lucie County have raised similar questions for years, pointing to diagnoses just houses apart and, in some cases, among unrelated residents of the same home decades apart. In June, I-Team reporter Katie Bente revisited families’ search for answers. In this second part of her investigation, Bente went street by street with a widow tracking the diagnoses and pressing health officials for updated findings. A few houses apart For Stephanie Ankiel , one stop on the drive through Fort Pierce brings the questions back to her own family. She pointed to her late husband’s childhood home, then another home a few houses away where she said a resident was diagnosed in 2025 with the same type of brain tumor. This is the house my late husband grew up in, Ankiel said. He was diagnosed with the same exact thing as that gentleman in 2025. Both men were initially diagnosed with oligodendroglioma, a different type of brain tumor from glioblastoma . Ankiel said her husband Mark Cunningham’s cancer later progressed to glioblastoma. A few streets away, she identified another home where she said two unrelated residents developed glioblastoma decades apart. This is the house where we’ve had two glioblastoma cases, 20 years apart, no family relation, she said. Elsewhere along the route, Ankiel pointed to neighboring homes where she said a woman and an 18-year-old had been diagnosed with brain cancer. The I-Team is withholding exact addresses to protect families’ privacy. PART 1: Brain cancer diagnoses leave St. Lucie County families searching for answers, again Ankiel helps patients through the Brain Cancer Foundation of the Treasure Coast , including a child who is just 3. She has spent years mapping where patients lived and looking for possible connections. Three additional brain cancer cases were confirmed in August alone in the areas families are tracking. Those diagnoses and the proximity of patients’ homes do not establish a cancer cluster or a common cause. But Ankiel wants officials to examine the range of brain cancers represented on her map, beyond glioblastoma alone. Regardless if it’s Glio at this point, we have too much brain cancer in this area. CDC guidance allows consideration of different cancer types when evidence suggests shared causes or exposures. No such connection has been established among the cases families are tracking. What the state studied and what is new The Florida Department of Health’s 2019 review examined glioblastoma diagnoses from 1998 through 2017 in ZIP codes 34952, 34982 and 34983. It found no statistically significant increase and did not designate a cancer cluster. That review did not include later diagnoses and focused on glioblastoma rather than the range of brain tumors represented on Ankiel’s map. Her husband’s initial diagnosis is one reason she wants officials to examine that broader picture. The I-Team asked whether the department had analyzed cases diagnosed since 2017 and what would trigger new environmental testing. Lucie County Health Officer Clint Sperber said officials have been reviewing cancer registry data and environmental influences. Our latest analysis, which includes data through 2023, shows no indication of higher rates in St. Lucie County or in the specific zip codes people have asked about, Sperber wrote. Lucie’s rates are in line with nearby counties and with the state as a whole. The updated report was not available when he responded. Sperber said officials were finishing a summary to release online. His response did not explain how the analysis handled tumors initially classified as another type and later diagnosed as glioblastoma, or whether other brain cancers were examined separately. It also did not specify what would trigger additional environmental testing. No environmental factor questioned by families has been established as a cause of these cancers. A call for another look Rep. Brian Mast said he has again asked the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention to examine the concerns and provide the data behind its conclusions. You need to give us the receipts, Mast said. Give us the data of where these took place, how many of them took place. The CDC said state and local health departments lead examinations of unusual cancer patterns. It confirmed that it assisted Florida’s investigation in 2018, but did not specifically address whether it had received Mast’s latest request or would open a new review. In a statement to the I-Team, a CDC spokesperson said: CDC is prepared to provide additional assistance upon the Florida Department of Health’s request. Making the most of the time left Elliott was diagnosed this year with glioblastoma, an aggressive, fast-growing grade 4 brain cancer. The former bar manager described struggling to speak after surgery and initially believing his diagnosis was an isolated case. Meeting other local patients changed that. I thought I was the only one, he said. He has decided not to continue treatment, choosing to spend his remaining time with friends and family, going to the beach and swimming. While he wants investigators to find answers, he is focused on the life he still has. I’m not going to be that person that lives to be 65, 70, 80 years old, Elliott said. But I get to hang out with my friends. I get to go take a swim, have some fun.

Kyler Murray and the Minnesota Vikings' offense would've appreciated a touchdown for their progress down the stretch, but there was only one way to truly secure this victory.T.J. Hockenson fittingly took the winning slide.The Vikings stayed undefeated with more dominance by their defense and five field goals from Will Reichard, sidestepping their early passing game problems to beat the winless Miami Dolphins 15-10 on Sunday.Hockenson tied a career high with 13 receptions for 119 yards on 13 targets from Murray, including the game-sealing 8-yard catch on third-and-5 from the 10. The eighth-year tight end was wide open and could've coasted into the end zone, but he wisely slid in front of the goal line to drain the clock to the two-minute warning."Once you get the first down, you've got to get down," said Hockenson, who had his highest yardage total since Week 10 of the 2023 season. I saw that goal line and I wanted it, but it's for the betterment of the team that we ended on offense."With the Dolphins out of timeouts, the Vikings had Murray take three straight kneel-downs to move to 4-0 for the second time in three years — despite going without a touchdown in two games."If we want to score, we should do it earlier," Vikings coach Kevin O'Connell said.Murray finished 27 for 37 for 247 yards without a turnover, but he took four sacks for 34 yards against a Dolphins defense that had none in the first three games and was often tentative and unsteady in the pocket until Hockenson helped him open up the field with a handful of clutch and difficult catches.The Dolphins, who are 0-4 for the first time since starting 0-7 in 2019 in their first season under then-coach Brian Flores, were crushed by a combination of unforced mistakes — including nine penalties for 55 yards.New Dolphins quarterback Malik Willis went just 9 for 17 for 85 yards, losing a fumble during one of the two sacks by Dallas Turner. The four teams the Dolphins have faced in coach Jeff Hafley's first year are 15-1."You hate the feeling of continuing to get better without actually gaining wins on the win column, but as we see, we're going out there and competing," Willis said.Willis thought he had escaped the relentless Vikings pass rush to float a 68-yard touchdown pass to Chris Bell early in the second quarter, but Bell was flagged for illegal touching after stepping out of bounds as he moved to get open.The Vikings had 11 penalties for 85 yards, but they dodged one when Ivan Pace Jr. had a call for roughing the kicker waved off by the video replay assist system's determination that he tipped Bradley Pinion's punt and therefore didn't commit a penalty.After netting just 76 yards on 21 plays in the first half and failing to finish any possession across midfield, the Dolphins finally found a couple of creases in Minnesota's suffocating defense directed by Flores.Ollie Gordon, in an elevated role following the season-ending knee injury to star running back De'Vone Achane, ripped off a career-best 53-yard run on third-and-5 to set up Riley Patterson's 27-yard field goal. Gordon, who ended the game with 100 yards rushing, had a 12-yard touchdown run on the next drive to pull the Dolphins within 12-10.Reichard, who stretched the NFL's longest active streak to 31 consecutive made field goals, drew a loud roar when he was shown on the videoboard during the two-minute warning. Murray, on the other hand, heard some mild rounds of boos as the unproductive possessions began to pile up.But the Vikings had the ball for 14 of 15 minutes in the fourth quarter, accumulating eight first downs.Aaron Jones also carried another heavy load with 20 carries for 94 yards and four receptions for 34 yards, with the Vikings missing star wide receiver Justin Jefferson (ankle) for the first time since Week 12 of the 2023 season and running back Jordan Mason (thumb) for the third game in a row."That door will get kicked down soon," Murray said.The Vikings played most of the second half without two of their best blockers. Left guard Donovan Jackson (knee) was sidelined in the first quarter and left tackle Christian Darrisaw (neck) was hurt in the second after going head-first into the pile at the end of a run. Darrisaw returned after halftime, only to be pulled again as a precaution for a concussion evaluation following a second hit.Dolphins: Host Cincinnati next Sunday.Vikings: Play at New Orleans next Sunday.

It takes an army of 38 staff members to create all the video, replays, and entertainment fans enjoy at Florida Panthers games at Amerant Bank Arena.WPTV Florida Panthers Anchor and Panthers 360 Mike Trim went one-on-one with Mike Masino, vice president of entertainment and operations, who gave Trim a tour of the newly renovated control room and front-of-house operations.WATCH: Newly renovated control room at Amerant Bank Arena brings Panthers games to lifeThe front-of-house operations area serves as the hub of game-day activity. It houses the public address announcer, primary producer, music operations, a spotter, and a gold horn operator. Lighting operations and building lights are also managed from the same space, along with social media stations used for interactive fan games."Yeah, so this is our front-of-house operations area. This is where we have our public address announcer. We have our primary producer, music operations, our spotter, and our gold horn operator. We've got our lighting operations team as well as building lights. And then up here we have some of our fun stuff. We've got social media stations for some of our interactive games," Mike Masino said.What is now one open workspace was once 3 separate rooms."This was actually 3 rooms," Masino said."Flow communication becomes a lot easier. Direct line of sight is also helpful, and it actually created some more space for the operators," Masino said.The tour also included the broadcast control room — the engine room of the entire production."Now we've got the actual broadcast control room; this is where the real magic happens," Masino said.Inside, Mark serves as the technical director, and Scott is the director. Masino compared the director's role to one familiar to those in television news."Mark who's TDing, and you've got Scott who is our director. Our director, just like in news, they're actually calling the cameras, calling the angles. Queuing videos," Masino said.When Trim asked how the team handles milestone moments — whether anticipated or unexpected — Masino said the control room is always plugged in and prepared."We're directly plugged in with our public relations team and our communications team who communicates that milestone to us. We're prepared ahead of time," Masino said.Masino noted that the 38-person team is a critical part of the operation, pointing to significant growth in both staff size and talent."We've doubled the staff. Talent level is continuing to increase every year, and it's really become a wonderful, wonderful team," Masino said."They're on it. They're locked in all game, but it's what they do, and it's what they love to do," Masino said.The first pre-season game for the Panthers also marked a significant technology upgrade for the arena."So tonight's actually a milestone for us, moving from a baseband video infrastructure where you're hard patching cables to a networked routable video infrastructure," Masino said."All of our cabling throughout the building was replaced to bring us to the highest quality broadcast infrastructure that sports are doing these days," Masino said.This story was reported on-air by a journalist and has been converted to this platform with the assistance of AI. Our editorial team verifies all reporting on all platforms for fairness and accuracy.

Florida center Aleksander Barkov has been placed on long-term injured reserve by the Panthers, meaning the injury to his left leg will keep him sidelined for at least the next 10 games and quite possibly beyond.The Panthers are still unclear on the extent of Barkov's injury, coach Paul Maurice said, adding that Barkov will see Florida team physicians on Monday.>> RELATED: More Panthers news"We know it’s going to be 10 (games) anyway," Maurice said after the Panthers practiced in Irvine, California. "We’ll see what they say Monday. Whatever they say."Florida made a pair of roster additions after placing Barkov on the injured list Saturday, bringing up center Sam Lafferty and defenseman Alexander Petrovic.Barkov was hurt midway through the second period of Florida's 4-3 overtime loss to the San Jose Sharks on Thursday night. He was jostling for the puck along the boards, got pushed by the Sharks' Darnell Nurse and awkwardly fell to the ice with his left leg at an unnatural angle. It appeared his knee buckled on the play.Barkov remained down for a few moments, then got up and headed toward the tunnel leading to the Florida dressing room. He walked with a bit of a limp and appeared to angrily try to throw off his gloves as he moved toward the room.Barkov — Florida's captain and a huge part of the Panthers' runs to Stanley Cup championships in 2024 and 2025 — missed the entire 2025-26 season with torn ligaments in his right knee. He went scoreless in his first two appearance of this season for Florida, which plays Sunday at Anaheim.There was some good injury news Saturday, with Maurice saying that forward Brad Marchand is getting closer to making his season debut — "real close," Maurice said — and that defenseman Gustav Forsling, who had the overtime goal in the opener at Carolina but was a last-minute scratch at San Jose with an upper body issue, is a game-time decision for Sunday.

A Fort Pierce senior center is expected to close, leaving some of the older adults who rely on it worried about losing a gathering place in their own community.The Council on Aging of St. Lucie confirmed the senior center at 1505 Orange Avenue in Fort Pierce is expected to close in the near future. The property is currently listed for sale for $2.2 million.The news came as a surprise to some seniors who use the center regularly, including 77-year-old Sandy Pietrewicz. She has relied on the center for nearly a decade. “That's the community center that I go to for lunch and friendship and social activities with other elderly women,” said Pietrewicz.After hearing the center could be closing, Pietrewicz said she and other seniors were left with questions about what would happen to the services they depend on.“We were all talking about who we could contact, and I thought of WPTV immediately,” she said.WPTV reporter Brooke Chau went to the center to get answers and hear directly from the seniors who use it.The Council on Aging said the closure will not mean an end to the services provided to seniors.“You're going to get the same treatment. You're going to get the same love. You're going to get the same meals,” said Trekina Smith with the Council on Aging.Once the property sells, seniors who currently use the Orange Avenue location are expected to transition to the Council on Aging's facility on Bayshore Boulevard in Port St. Lucie.The organization said transportation will be provided to help seniors get to the new location.But some seniors say the location itself is important.“That makes us even angrier. We can't have something in our own community,” Pietrewicz said.Geneira Lovett, who also uses the center, told WPTV that seniors in Fort Pierce want to be able to access services close to where they live.“We live here, we want rights to do thing, besides trouble,” Lovett said.The Council on Aging said it understands those concerns, but says change is necessary.For now, the Council on Aging says services at the Orange Avenue center are continuing. There is no finalized timeline for the closure because the transition is tied to the sale of the property.“We understand the concerns, it's a change for us too. But hey, change comes, and you got to go with the change,” Smith said.The organization said seniors will continue to have access to meals, activities, social opportunities and transportation once services move to the Port St.

President Trump announced that more than 20 million seniors on Medicare will soon receive a direct deposit of nearly $100, drawing Democratic criticism and questions about whether the payments — made without congressional approval — are legal."I am pleased to announce over 20 million seniors on Medicare will still be receiving a deposit of nearly $100 directly into their bank accounts," Trump said.RELATED STORY | Trump announces $500 refunds for nearly 1 million 'Obamacare' enrolleesTrump said the money will come from the Medicare Improvement Fund. A White House fact sheet says most eligible seniors will receive $90 via direct deposit in early October. Those without direct deposit will receive a check.The Medicare payment is not the only check the administration is cutting. Last month, Trump announced refunds to some people enrolled in Affordable Care Act health plans, saying they had been previously overcharged."Nearly 1 million hardworking Americans in 30 states will soon be getting refunds of $500 each," Trump said.On the campaign trail, Trump has also promised more money if Republicans win in the November midterm elections.IN CASE YOU MISSED IT | $5K reality check: Experts say Trump's promise of midterm checks would strain the economySo far, no legal challenge has resulted in a court blocking either the $500 ACA refunds or the $90 Medicare payments, though Democrats have been sharply critical of both."If you want to BUY midterm votes, maybe start by not gutting everyone's health care in the first place," Oregon Sen. Ron Wyden said, referring to the $500 ACA checks.Also drawing scrutiny on Capitol Hill is Trump's use of taxpayer dollars to pay for commercials this campaign season. The White House says the spending is legal, but others disagree. Complaints have been filed with the FCC and broadcasters, though no judge has yet blocked the commercials from airing.

Ron DeSantis opened the new I-95 interchange at Oslo Road in Indian River County on Monday, calling it a critical connection for drivers, emergency crews and the region’s growing population. The roughly $100 million project opened one year ahead of schedule , according to the governor’s office and the Florida Department of Transportation. This is the first new interchange built in this area in almost 50 years, DeSantis said. It’s going to bring [a] new critical connection [to] I-95 for a part of the state that has changed quite a bit. The new exit is expected to ease congestion at nearby Indrio Road and State Road 60 interchanges, DeSantis said. Drivers traveling from Oslo Road to I-95 can expect their travel times to be cut in half, he added. With the number of daily vehicles on the corridor still expected to grow between now and 2045 significantly, the Oslo Road interchange sets a clear example of how Florida delivers infrastructure that improves quality of life today while building more capacity for the future, DeSantis said. The governor also said the direct interstate connection will help emergency crews respond faster in southern Indian River County. See also: Two killed, including 10th-grade girl, after rollover school bus crash in Polk County We anticipate that just for the local community on a normal basis, for local, like non-hurricane-type emergencies, that the emergency response time will be reduced by up to 56%, DeSantis said. That will ultimately save some lives, of course, because time is of the essence in some of these situations. FDOT Secretary Jared Perdue said the project was completed 400 days early through what the agency calls voluntary acceleration, which lets contractors propose ways to speed construction and share in the savings. This is going to reduce the time it takes for first responders to get to incidents substantially, Perdue said. We’re really excited about that, to include cutting commute time in half and so many other benefits. DeSantis said FDOT also acquired land near the interchange for a dedicated gopher tortoise habitat. He said the site will be the only relocation area of its kind in Southeast Florida. Florida [is] showing that it’s possible to do the projects that we need done while also buttressing environmental stewardship, DeSantis said. Perdue said nearly $1 billion in transportation investment is planned for the Treasure Coast region. Indian River County Commissioner Joseph Flescher recounted his reaction when he first heard about the opening. "When I got the phone call, I said, ' We're not near completion. I had been here just two weeks ago. We were nowhere near where we're at.' This team worked an incredible operation, said Flescher. Flescher also highlighted how important this new entrance ot I-95 is to the growing population across the county. This interchange is very much needed in the development of our county. And I don't mean the future development. I mean the current development, Flescher said.

Video above: News and weather for Monday, October 5, 2026 A Port St. Lucie resident accused of theft at a Palm Beach County apartment complex more than two years ago entered a plea agreement. According to court documents in Palm Beach County, Ashley R. Clayton, 38, pleaded guilty on Monday, Oct. 5, to money laundering, organized scheme to defraud and making false entry in book of business entity. Clayton agreed to the plea agreement on Sept. Clayton was sentenced to five years of probation for each charge, but will serve the penalties at the same time, credited with 12 days of time served in Palm Beach County jail, ordered to pay court costs and complete community service. As part of the plea agreement, Clayton and the victim will determine the amount of restitution Clayton owes to the property management company of the apartment complex. Stay up-to-date: The latest headlines and weather from WPBF 25 Clayton is banned from performing any financial transaction for any business or person and was ordered to complete mental health and substance abuse evaluations. According to a Riviera Beach Police Department report, Clayton was an employee at Berkeley Landing Apartments located at 3100 Broadway for three months. On June 13, 2024, a regional manager for the apartment complex told police that Clayton was the community manager who oversaw payments for rent, deposits, application fees, background checks, credit checks and compliance application process for the apartment complex. It was determined that Clayton was collecting money by having residents use Zelle, which allows users to electronically transfer money. The residents’ money went to Clayton’s banking account. Some residents even gave Clayton blank money orders. The police report said Clayton sent residents a letter on apartment complex letterhead stating, “They are currently working on making sure all payment ledgers are up-to-date. We are asking that rent payments be made in the form of money orders until further notice.” The apartment complex did not give Clayton permission to send the letter. Clayton was fired but returned to the property and returned 20 money orders totaling $14,798.22 to the apartment complex management. The police report noted that Clayton kept three money orders and attempted to cash them at an Amscot in Miami. One of the three money orders was cashed, and the apartment complex was missing at least $11,999.23. Clayton collected $31,249.32 through Zelle, and at least $58,046.77 was stolen. The police report lists five additional individuals from whom Clayton took money from under false terms while working for the apartment complex. Indiantown residents remain concerned about flooding after heavy rain left streets covered in water last week, with more rain and storms in the forecast for this week. CBS12 crews captured video of vehicles driving through standing water on roadways in parts of the village. Residents say flooding can quickly become expensive when water affects homes and property. The sad part is, if you don’t have insurance or anything like that you’re just stuck, your stuck with the bill, said Mary Brown, a Booker Park resident. The flooding has renewed questions about the more than $2 million drainage and roadway project in Booker Park. The project began in 2022 to help reduce flooding, but residents say heavy rain is still leaving some streets underwater. Village leaders have said they are working with Martin County on longer-term drainage solutions, including the possible repair or replacement of broken pipes. The next Indiantown Village Council meeting is Thursday night. With more rain possible this week, Martin County Fire Rescue and the Florida Department of Health in Martin County have tips available online for residents to plan ahead and avoid driving or walking through floodwater. You can CLICK HERE to view the entire list. Officials say water on a roadway may be deeper or more contaminated than it appears. Drivers who encounter a flooded road should turn around rather than attempt to drive through it. Martin County Fire Rescue responds to flooding-related emergencies, including when a vehicle becomes stuck in floodwater. Residents should call 911 during an emergency. For ongoing drainage problems or flooded roadways, residents can submit a report through Martin County’s online Request for Service system . The county asks residents to include the specific address or location and details about the issue, such as standing water, a blockage or a low spot near a drainage structure. CLICK HERE to submit a request. Health officials also advise residents whose wells flood to use bottled or boiled water until the well can be tested.

The mother of a 17-year-old boy shot and killed during a party Friday night at a boat ramp in Indian River County said she believes her son was protecting others when he was killed. She has identified her son as Sulliman Bah. Indian River County Sheriff Eric Flowers held a news conference about the shooting Monday afternoon. He said there were about 1,000 teenagers gathered at Garcia's Boat Ramp, just south of Fellsmere. Flowers showed two videos of the shooting from different angles. The videos start with Bah approaching a white pickup truck. "Seventeen-year-old opens the door, and he starts to punch. He's going to punch on the people that are inside of that truck. One shot is fired," Flowers said. The sheriff said the shot was fired by the passenger in the truck, killing Bah. Flowers stated that Bah had a history with the two 18-year-olds in the truck, noting that they had fought before. The 18-year-olds told investigators they had the gun to protect themselves. "At this time, it looks as though there will be a self-defense claim," Flowers said. Bah’s mother, however, disputes the self-defense claim. In a text message to WPBF 25 News reporter Ari Hait, she said, "Sulliman was a defender of his friends. Always protecting the underdog, and I believe he was trying to save the crowd from that gun that he knew was about to be used...He was there to protect his friends from the thugs that had previously threatened him and many others multiple times." She added that she does not see her son throwing a punch in the video. "If anything, I believe he was attempting to push the gun away," she said. The sheriff has not released the identities of the two 18-year-olds in the truck but said they are cooperating with investigators. No arrests have been made so far. "It's going to be up to the state on whether charges ultimately will be filed. But I can tell you self-defense plays a part in these," Flowers said. The sheriff emphasized that the investigation is ongoing and urged anyone who attended the party to contact his office. A 17-year-old died after being shot near a boat ramp in Indian River County late Friday night, according to the Indian River County Sheriff's Office. Deputies responded to reports of a juvenile shot in the 3700 block of County Road 512, near Garcia's Boat Ramp, at approximately 11:24 p.m. WATCH: 17-year-old dies after shooting near Garcia's Boat Ramp The sheriff's office said deputies found the 17-year-old and began lifesaving measures until Indian River County Fire Rescue arrived. A 17-year-old was killed in a shooting Friday night at Garcia's Boat Ramp in Indian River County, and investigators are examining whether the shooting was an act of self-defense , according to Sheriff Eric Flowers. WATCH: WPTV'S Coverage of Teen killed in Garcia's Boat Ramp shooting The shooting happened during a confrontation at the popular waterfront gathering spot, which authorities say has become a frequent meetup location for teenagers. According to Flowers, investigators reviewed video that showed the 17-year-old opening the door of a truck and throwing punches at people inside before a shot was fired. "The 17-year-old opens the door, and he starts to punch. He's going to punch the people that are inside of that truck," Flowers said during a news conference. A 17-year-old was killed in a Fellsmere shooting Friday night after a meetup of more than 100 teens turned violent, according to the sheriff. The shooting happened at around 11:24 p.m. at Garcia’s Boat Ramp , where about 100 teens had gathered. Sheriff Eric Flowers said the group included teens ages 14 to 19, with drinking and fighting reported. These have been happening since before I was in high school, since before many of you were in high school. This has been going on for a long time. But now we're adding guns into the mix, and we're adding social media into the mix. CBS12 confirmed with the family that the slain 17-year-old was Sulliman Bah, a senior at Sebastian River High School. He and a group of friends approached a pickup truck with two 18-year-olds inside. The Bah opened the door and attempted to punch someone inside when a shot was fired. See also: What Florida voters need to know about the 3 constitutional amendments on the Nov. ballot Bah, who was shot, was taken by friends toward Fellsmere. Deputies and EMS met them at Fellsmere City Hall and performed CPR before he was taken to Sebastian River Medical Center and later transported to Holmes Regional Medical Center in Melbourne, where he succumbed to his injuries. No arrests have been made. Flowers said the driver and passenger inside the truck have cooperated with investigators and turned over the truck and firearm. The sheriff said the preliminary investigation indicates a self-defense claim may apply. We will be submitting a warrant in the case, but at this time it looks as though there will be a self-defense claim as a result, Flowers said. The sheriff said the state will ultimately decide whether charges are filed. Investigators used Flock technology to identify people connected to the truck and shooting. Deputies also recovered additional guns and multiple shell casings. Flowers said investigators believe the meetup was part of a growing trend of teens gathering at remote locations arranged through Snapchat , where fights are recorded and shared online. He said there may have been as many as four fights at the boat ramp that night, and investigators are still working to identify people who were there. The sheriff urged parents to ask their children whether they attended the meetup and encouraged anyone who witnessed the shooting or recorded it to contact investigators.

Ron DeSantis opened the new I-95 interchange at Oslo Road in Indian River County on Monday, calling it a critical connection for drivers, emergency crews and the region’s growing population. The roughly $100 million project opened one year ahead of schedule , according to the governor’s office and the Florida Department of Transportation. This is the first new interchange built in this area in almost 50 years, DeSantis said. It’s going to bring [a] new critical connection [to] I-95 for a part of the state that has changed quite a bit. The new exit is expected to ease congestion at nearby Indrio Road and State Road 60 interchanges, DeSantis said. Drivers traveling from Oslo Road to I-95 can expect their travel times to be cut in half, he added. With the number of daily vehicles on the corridor still expected to grow between now and 2045 significantly, the Oslo Road interchange sets a clear example of how Florida delivers infrastructure that improves quality of life today while building more capacity for the future, DeSantis said. The governor also said the direct interstate connection will help emergency crews respond faster in southern Indian River County. See also: Two killed, including 10th-grade girl, after rollover school bus crash in Polk County We anticipate that just for the local community on a normal basis, for local, like non-hurricane-type emergencies, that the emergency response time will be reduced by up to 56%, DeSantis said. That will ultimately save some lives, of course, because time is of the essence in some of these situations. FDOT Secretary Jared Perdue said the project was completed 400 days early through what the agency calls voluntary acceleration, which lets contractors propose ways to speed construction and share in the savings. This is going to reduce the time it takes for first responders to get to incidents substantially, Perdue said. We’re really excited about that, to include cutting commute time in half and so many other benefits. DeSantis said FDOT also acquired land near the interchange for a dedicated gopher tortoise habitat. He said the site will be the only relocation area of its kind in Southeast Florida. Florida [is] showing that it’s possible to do the projects that we need done while also buttressing environmental stewardship, DeSantis said. Perdue said nearly $1 billion in transportation investment is planned for the Treasure Coast region.

hero.headline: Vero Beach Mermaid Brandee Anthony Turns Decade-Old Hobby Into Full Business
hero.body:
Brandee Anthony, known as the Vero Beach Mermaid, has spent the past decade building a business around a childhood fantasy, offering mermaid makeovers, beach photoshoots and poolside swimming lessons to clients of all ages. Anthony is an elite level PADI dive instructor who combines her diving credentials with 15 years of experience as a professional photographer to create the underwater and beach experiences.

Anthony said the idea began with her work as a professional live streamer. "I was a professional live streamer a long time ago, so I thought it would be really cool to take all my viewers underwater, but how can I make that interesting and magical?" she said. That early curiosity turned into a career. "That was 10 years ago and I'm a little in love with mermaiding for sure," she said.

Each session starts inside what Anthony calls her magical closet, stocked with tropical-inspired tails, tops and accessories designed specifically for mermaid gear. The silicone tails each weigh about 30 to 35 pounds, and clients can choose from crowns, armbands and other embellishments to complete their look. Anthony said she helps each client pick options suited to them, pairing a tail, top, accessories and crown before heading to the beach for photos. Tail styles include designs she calls the wind trader and a leafy sea dragon pattern.

Once clients are suited up, Anthony walks them through posing on the shoreline, instructing them to move toward the water like a sea turtle and turn their fin, or fluke, toward the camera. She guides beginners through a seated pose first, telling them to relax and let the wind take their hair for what she calls a little water love. The experience then moves poolside for a basic mermaiding lesson, where Anthony teaches clients to flex their foot toward the surface and push down to feel the water's resistance, which propels the tail. She also leads clients through a back float and a brief underwater dive, counting down before they breathe out and dive down to surface again, the same technique she uses to shoot video underwater.

hero.headline: Former Fort Pierce City Manager Nick Mimms Convicted of Official Misconduct
hero.teaser: A St. Lucie County jury acquitted former Fort Pierce City Manager Nick Mimms of bid tampering but convicted him of official misconduct over a Lincoln Park nonprofit lease tied to his niece. He remains free on bond ahead of sentencing.
hero.body:
A St. Lucie County jury convicted former Fort Pierce City Manager Nick Mimms of official misconduct Thursday, finding he improperly obstructed, delayed or prevented information about a possible felony involving the city from being communicated. Jurors acquitted Mimms of bid tampering, the first count he faced, but found him guilty on the official-misconduct charge. They specifically determined the misconduct involved obstructing, delaying or preventing communication of information related to a possible felony that directly involved or affected the city government he served.

The trial, which began Sept. 29, centered on allegations that Mimms improperly influenced the city's bidding process for two vacant lots in the Lincoln Park area. Prosecutors alleged Mimms steered the process toward Lincoln Park Young Professionals, a nonprofit whose board included his niece and another city employee. The organization sought a lease involving the properties, located near the Lincoln Theater.

During trial, FDLE Agent Derek Brisky testified about emails, city records and the request-for-proposals process. Prosecutors pointed to communications showing Mimms continued to discuss the RFP's evaluation criteria and committee makeup after the matter had already been referred to the city's purchasing department. The defense argued the purchasing department controlled the RFP's publication and administration, and challenged the state's claim that the process amounted to an improper sole-source arrangement.

Court records show Circuit Judge Michael James Linn denied the state's request to take Mimms into custody pending sentencing. Mimms will remain free on bond. Sentencing is scheduled for 9:30 a.m. in St. Lucie County Circuit Court.

hero.headline: MARTY Bus Service Suspended Across Martin County With No Restart Date
hero.body:
MARTY public transit service across Martin County came to an abrupt halt Thursday, leaving riders without their regular transportation while county officials scrambled for a fix. County officials said they received no advance warning that service would stop. According to the county, MARTY's operator, Martin County Transit LLC, had requested a significant increase in its contract, citing rising insurance, fuel and maintenance costs that have caused significant financial losses since it began operating the service in July 2025. Negotiations between the county and the company failed to produce an agreement.

County officials said Martin County Transit LLC gave formal notice about two weeks ago that it intended to terminate its contract in 180 days. Then on Thursday morning, the company told the county it was discontinuing service immediately, with no transition period. The sudden shutdown left residents who depend on MARTY without their usual way of getting to work, medical appointments and stores. County officials said they are working with community partners, including United Way, to help residents affected by the suspension, though no timeline has been given for when the service might resume. Officials said they would post updates on social media and notify residents once a solution is reached.

George Stokus, assistant Martin County administrator, said the county is now working on both short-term and long-term solutions to bring the service back. "We are doing everything we can humanly do right now to restore service as soon as we can," Stokus said. "It's just not an easy operation or switch to turn it back on. It's going to take some time, and we are working to get to that."

The disruption has already hit riders hard. Leticia Chaclan, of Martin County, waited for her usual bus in Stuart on Thursday, but it never came. She had not heard that MARTY service had been suspended until she was told by a reporter. Chaclan said she has relied on the bus for years and considers it essential for many in the community. "We really need the bus," she said. "Especially people within the Hispanic community, who don't have a driver's license, and need it to go to places like the clinic, to go to the hospital, and for other things we need. It's very necessary, and we use the bus a lot. In my case, I don't drive. But I really need the bus, and I use it a lot. I don't drive, and we go everywhere to shop." Another rider, Steven Godell, said he had to get around on his bicycle Thursday after the bus failed to show up that morning. "It's crazy, but I will move on and do something different," he said.

cards.headline: Hobe Sound Woman Accused of Burying Cats Alive, Calling Them Demons
cards.teaser: A Hobe Sound woman is in custody after the Martin County Sheriff's Office said she buried at least four of her cats alive in her yard, believing they were demons. Deputies are still searching the property.
cards.body:
A Hobe Sound woman is in custody after the Martin County Sheriff's Office said she buried at least four cats alive in her yard because she believed they were demons. Alba Chavez, 37, was arrested following what the sheriff's office called a disturbing animal cruelty case at a home in a Hobe Sound mobile home park in the 11,000 block of Southeast Federal Highway.

Patrol deputies and investigators with MCSO Animal Services responded to the home after Chavez told them about the burials. Deputies managed to rescue two of the cats, but two others were found dead. Crews are digging up portions of the property as part of the investigation.

Chavez will face multiple counts of aggravated animal cruelty, the sheriff's office said. The agency said the investigation remains active and deputies are continuing to search the property.

cards.headline: Fort Pierce Police Arrest 2 After Woman Shot At on South Sixth Street
cards.body:
Fort Pierce police have arrested two people after a woman was attacked and then shot at as she fled the scene on South Sixth Street. Officers responded to the area at 7:12 a.m. on Saturday, October 3, after the victim called police to report someone was shooting at her, according to the Fort Pierce Police Department.

The investigation found the victim had gone to a residence on South Sixth Street to speak with her boyfriend about their relationship. When she arrived, several people ran out of the home and attacked her. Police said the victim managed to break free, get into her vehicle and drive away.

As she fled, one of the suspects grabbed a gun from the property and opened fire on her vehicle, according to police. A second suspect was arrested on allegations of driving the shooter away from the scene afterward.

Police identified the suspects as 18 year old Keibin Lopez-Godoy and 18 year old Kailee Yurubi. Lopez-Godoy faces a charge of first-degree attempted homicide. Yurubi faces a charge of accessory after the fact.

hero.headline: Vero Beach Mourns Teen Sulli Bah as Family Seeks Accountability in Shooting
hero.body:
Family, friends, teachers and classmates gathered at Farm & Flame in Vero Beach on Wednesday to remember 17-year-old Sulliman "Sulli" Bah, who was fatally shot during a meetup at Garcia Boat Ramp last week. The Indian River County Sheriff's Office says investigators are looking into whether the shooting involved self-defense, and no arrests have been made. The celebration of life was held at the restaurant where Bah worked, and mourners described the Sebastian River High School student as kind, funny, hardworking and someone who could light up a room.

As rain fell Wednesday evening, flowers, candles and photographs filled Farm & Flame as people who knew Bah gathered to honor him. Isaac Rodriguez, who knew Bah, said he left a mark on everyone around him. "He touched everybody's heart and he was just really kind and he always lit up the room," Rodriguez said. Friend Alex Cortez, who boxed alongside Bah and shared many memories with him, said Bah was focused on building a future for himself. "He was a very positive guy. He was always about working, he was intelligent, he had a big future," Cortez said. Another friend, Xavi Espinosa, remembered Bah's welcoming nature from the moment they met. "Even when I first met him, I felt he was such a good soul," Espinosa said.

The sheriff's office said Bah was at the meetup at Garcia Boat Ramp on Friday when shots were fired, and the investigation into whether the shooting was self-defense remains open. Bah's mother, Chelynn Godfrey, described her son as a loving and caring teenager who had his whole life ahead of him. She is calling on investigators to weigh every detail of the case. "I just ask that law enforcement truly looks at the big picture. I just want them to really look at the facts and I hope that they get this right," Godfrey said. "I hope his shooter is arrested and I hope he goes to jail."

During the celebration, those who knew Bah took turns sharing memories of him. Angela Sanders, one of his former sixth grade teachers, recalled his personality and smile. "His personality is amazing, his smile lit up a room," Sanders said. Friend Myan Agosto said Bah consistently looked out for the people around him. "He never failed to make sure everybody was okay," Agosto said. "He was just a really good friend." Another friend, Zani Zoutten, remembered spending time with Bah during sixth period and described him as a happy person. One speaker at the gathering reflected on the reach of Bah's short life: "He may not have lived so many years in this room, but the days he made on this earth, look at this room." Bah's funeral is scheduled for Saturday.

cards.headline: Family of Death Row Inmate Pleads for Clemency in Deputy's 1986 Murder
cards.teaser: William Reaves is scheduled to be executed Oct. 20 for killing Indian River County Deputy Richard Raczkowski in 1986. His family is now publicly asking Gov. Ron DeSantis to commute his sentence to life in prison.
cards.body:
William Reaves has spent nearly four decades on death row for the 1986 murder of Indian River County Sheriff's Deputy Richard Raczkowski, who was 29 when he was killed. With Reaves' execution scheduled for Oct. 20, his family is speaking publicly for the first time, asking Gov. Ron DeSantis to grant clemency and commute the death sentence to life in prison.

"I mean, he's my uncle, and I love him," said Meredith Farrington, Reaves' nephew. Farrington said his family does not dispute the gravity of the crime or the pain it caused Raczkowski's family. "I can't be upset. I can't be mad at the governor or the decision," he said. "I mean, my uncle did take a life." Still, Farrington said he wants DeSantis "to look at the whole picture" before the execution proceeds.

According to court records, Reaves called 911 from a convenience store in Indian River County on Sept. 23, 1986, after he was unable to get a taxi. Raczkowski responded to help him call a cab when a gun fell from Reaves' pants. A struggle followed, and Reaves shot Raczkowski four times in the back, killing him. A stretch of road near the scene now bears Raczkowski's name. His brother, Marc Raczkowski, has lived with the loss for nearly 40 years. "Why? Why?" he said near his brother's gravesite. "It's something I wouldn't wish on anybody... The pain will still always be there."

DeSantis signed Reaves' death warrant on Sept. 22, setting the execution for Oct. 20. Farrington is not asking for a pardon or release, but wants the sentence commuted so Reaves, now 77, spends the rest of his life in prison. Farrington points to Reaves' service as a Vietnam War veteran and decades of appeals raising questions about his mental health, substance abuse and trial representation. Court records show Reaves argued his trial attorney failed to adequately investigate evidence of his drug use and mental health. "The attorney wasn't an effective attorney for that type of case," Farrington said. "That was his first death row case." Testimony at sentencing described Reaves as suffering from what was then called "Vietnam syndrome," while later experts testified he suffered from PTSD and substance abuse.

Farrington said none of that excuses the killing. "I'm not going to say that his PTSD, his drug use, his being on cocaine and all the other stuff excuses what he did," he said. "He's being punished by being in prison, and he's 77. The governor can let him stay in prison for the rest of his life, and still he's being punished without killing him and taking another life." Farrington said he understands if Raczkowski's family wants the execution to proceed. "I know that the family, the officer... I would probably want the same thing, and I can't even imagine," he said. Reaves has lost his latest bid to stop the execution in Indian River County court and has appealed to the Florida Supreme Court. Unless a court intervenes or DeSantis grants clemency, the execution remains scheduled for Oct. 20 and would mark Florida's 18th execution in 2026.

cards.headline: Vero Beach Mermaid Brandee Anthony Turns Diving Skills Into Magical Underwater Experiences
cards.teaser: Vero Beach-based PADI dive instructor Brandee Anthony runs a mermaid experience business offering makeovers, beach photoshoots and poolside swimming lessons for clients of all ages.
cards.body:
Brandee Anthony, known as the Vero Beach Mermaid, is an elite-level PADI dive instructor who teaches people of all ages to become mermaids. Her business offers experiences ranging from glamorous mermaid makeovers and beach photoshoots to poolside swimming lessons.

Anthony said the idea grew out of her earlier career as a professional live streamer. "I was a professional live streamer a long time ago, so I thought it would be really cool to take all my viewers underwater, but how can I make that interesting and magical?" she said. That early curiosity became a lasting passion. "That was 10 years ago and I'm a little in love with mermaiding for sure," Anthony said.

Each experience begins with a mermaid makeover inside what Anthony calls her custom fantasy closet, stocked with tropical-inspired tails, tops and accessories made specifically for mermaid gear. The closet includes silicone tails that each weigh about 30 to 35 pounds, along with crowns, armbands and other embellishments meant to complete the look. "Mermaid crowns and armbands and embellishments, kind of the final touches to help people really feel like they have a full ensemble," Anthony said. Armbands come in several styles, including options with a vibrant teal accent. After choosing a tail, top, accessories and crown, clients head to the beach for a photoshoot. Anthony, who has worked as a professional photographer for 15 years, combines elaborate costumes with beach backdrops for the shoot. She guides clients through poses on the shoreline, starting with a seated pose she describes as the easiest for beginners.

The experience also includes a poolside mermaid swimming lesson, where Anthony strips the process back from the glamour of the photoshoot to focus on technique. She teaches clients to flex and push their feet to generate the propulsion needed to swim in a tail, and helps them practice back floating before guiding them through a full underwater dive. Anthony said she tailors each session to a client's comfort level. "Once people get in a tail and they find their groove, it turns into a bunch of people just playing in a pool," she said. Clients seek out the experience for different reasons, she said, from simple fun to deeper personal milestones. "Coming on a retreat or take a course really did change their lives, or changed the trajectory of their lives. I've turned a few people into pro mermaids," Anthony said. She added that mermaiding offers adults a chance to play without losing their maturity. "I think that's what mermaiding as an adult feels like is you don't have to act like a kid but you can be an adult that plays," she said.

hero.headline: Jury Convicts Former Fort Pierce City Manager Nick Mimms of Official Misconduct
hero.body:
A St. Lucie County jury convicted former Fort Pierce City Manager Nick Mimms of official misconduct Thursday, finding he improperly obstructed, delayed or prevented information about a possible felony involving the city from being communicated. Jurors acquitted Mimms of bid tampering, the first count he faced, but found him guilty on the official-misconduct charge, specifically determining the misconduct involved blocking communication of information related to a possible felony that directly involved or affected the city government he served.

The trial, which began Sept. 29, centered on allegations that Mimms improperly influenced the city's bidding process for two vacant lots in the Lincoln Park area. Prosecutors alleged Mimms steered the process toward Lincoln Park Young Professionals, a nonprofit whose board included his niece and another city employee. The organization sought a lease involving the properties, located near the Lincoln Theater.

During trial, FDLE Agent Derek Brisky testified about emails, city records and the request-for-proposals process. Prosecutors pointed to communications showing Mimms continued to discuss the RFP's evaluation criteria and committee makeup after the matter had already been referred to the city's purchasing department. The defense argued the purchasing department, not Mimms, controlled the RFP's publication and administration, and disputed the state's claim that the process amounted to an improper sole-source arrangement.

Circuit Judge Michael James Linn denied the state's request to take Mimms into custody pending sentencing, according to court records. Mimms will remain free on bond. Sentencing is scheduled for 9:30 a.m. in St. Lucie County Circuit Court.

cards.headline: Fort Pierce Women Charged After Neglected Dog Dies at Pine Creek Apartments
cards.teaser: Fort Pierce police say Samya Shanice Bryant and Danielle Amanda Potts failed to get veterinary care for a severely malnourished dog that was later euthanized due to organ failure.
cards.body:
Two Fort Pierce women are facing aggravated animal cruelty charges after a severely neglected dog died from his injuries, according to arrest reports from the Fort Pierce Police Department. Samya Shanice Bryant, 25, and Danielle Amanda Potts, 28, were arrested Oct. 2 in connection with the neglect and death of a dog at Pine Creek Apartments.

Officers first found the dog on Sept. 29 lying outside an apartment. He was severely underweight with visible ribs, had infected sores on his paws, and had no access to food or water, according to police.

Bryant told officers the dog was hers and said he had been sick for weeks after another man allegedly poured boiling water on him. Police said both Bryant and Potts lived in the apartment and had control of the dog but did not get him veterinary treatment.

Animal Control took the dog for emergency care, but he had to be euthanized on Oct. 2 because of his injuries, infections and organ failure. Bryant and Potts were both arrested and charged with aggravated animal cruelty and confining or impounding an animal without sufficient food or water.
